caseno: Writ Petition No. 3488 of 2000 and 6348 of 2011.
lawyer:
SM Harmuz Ahmed with Samar Rahman, Advocates—For the Petitioners. [Writ Petition No. 3488 of 2000]
Yousuf Hossain Humayun with Motiur Rahman, Advocates—For the Respondent No.8. [Writ Petition No. 3488 of 2000]
SM Mahbubul Islam, Advocate—For the Petitioner. [Writ Petition No. 6348 of 2011] 
Amit Talukder, DAG with Toufiq Sajwar Partho, AAG—For the Respondent No. 4. [Writ Petition No. 6348 of 2011]
Yousuf Hossain Humayun with Motiur Rahman, Advocates—For the Respondent No. 8. [Writ Petition No. 6348 of 2011]
parties:
Khondker Abu Taher Noori & others -------- Petitioners
VS
Government of Bangladesh and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Khizir Ahmed Choudhury, J: These Rules being issued on identical matter challenging the same LA proceeding are heard and disposed of analogously by single judgment. 

2. Rule has been issued in writ petition No. 3488 of 2000 in the following terms: "A Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-6 to show cause as to why the impugned acquisition proceedings contained in the notice under section 3 of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Properties Ordinance, 1982 (Annexure-F) in Land Acquisition Case No. 1 of 1999-2000 in respect of acquisition of lands measuring 6.56 acres contained in RS Plot Nos. 23-27, 29 and 41 in RS Khatin Nos. 35, 13, 15, 37, 39 and 38 of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur within PS Saver, District-Dhaka in favour of one Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society's proposed Niribili Housing Scheme should not be declared to have been without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Courts may seem fit and proper." 

3. Similarly Rule has been issued in writ petition No. 6348 of 2011 in the following terms: 
"A Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Gazette Notification under the signature of respondent No. 5 so far it relates to the acquisition of land of the petitioners measuring 2.00 acres situated in RS Plot No. 25 in RS Khatian Nos. 15 of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur under Saver Police Station (now police Station Ashulia), District-Dhaka in connection with LA Case No. 1 of 1999-2000 shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the Respondents shall not be directed to release the acquired 2.00 acres of land situated in RS Plot No. 25 in RS Khatian No. 15 of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur under Savar Police Station, District-Dhaka in connection with LA Case No. 1 of 1999-2000 in favor of the petitioners effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Courts may seem fit and proper." 

4. Short facts as disclosed in the writ petition No. 3488 of 2000 in short is that petitioner No. 1 after his retirement from government service purchased 2.00 acres of land in RS Plot No. 25 having RS Khatian No. 15 in Mouja Uttor Ramchandpur under Police Station vide registered sale deed No. 15071 dated 8-7-1997 with a view to construct residence for himself and for his five sons and daughters having no housing accommodation at Dhaka. After purchase he demarcated boundary, erected barbed were fencing, mutated his name in the record of right and paid government revenues. Similarly petitioner No. 2-5 also with a view to construct residence purchased 0.45 acres of land by separate deeds in their names in 1998. While they have been owning and possessing as mentioned above they came to know that LA case No. 1 of 1999-2000 has been commenced for acquiring an area of 6.55 acres of land covering the case plot for Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society Limited with a view to materialize a housing scheme. The said housing society earlier got acquired 1.50 acres of land for establishing housing scheme. On the proposal of the said housing society Deputy Commissioner Dhaka acquired 1.23 acres of land vide LA Case No. 06 of 1976-1977 purportedly with a view to provide civic facility but no step was taken towards that end. After commencement of acquisition proceeding No.1 of 1999-2000 Ministry of land through its senior Assistant Secretary at the instance of Ministry of land an inquiry was conducted by LA officials and others vide annexure E-1 which was sent by Additional Deputy Commissioner Dhaka to the ministry of land wherein recommendation has been made not to acquire the land as it is not necessary for development project because the project could be implemented in the earlier acquired land, inspite of that the acquisition proceeding has been commenced and notice under section 3 of the acquisition and requisition immovable property ordinance was served beyond the knowledge of the petitioners without issuing public notice but after prolonged search the petitioner collected a copy of the notice issued under section 3 of the ordinance. The proposed acquisition proceeding is not for any public purpose which is Cristal clear from the report submitted by the land acquisition officer and others. Subsequently a notice under section 6 of the acquisition and requisition of immovable property ordinance, 1982 was served beyond the petitioner's knowledge and on coming to know about the said notice the petitioner filed objection against the said process and, as such, the petitioners were constrained to filed the instant writ petition.

5. Respondent No. 5 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition stated that with a view to establish hospital, educational institution, community center, religious and other welfare institution at the auspicious of Niribili Housing Scheme an area of 2.09 acres of land was acquired from RS plot No. 25 along with other land of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur vide LA case No.1 of 1999-2000 and after acquisition of the land the said was duly handed over to Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society upon observing all formalities. After the commencement of the acquisition proceeding notice under section 3 of the ordinance was properly affixed and served and no objection having been filed, notice under section 6 of the ordinance has been issued on 22-2-2000. Thereafter against notification regarding the acquisition of land was published as no order of stay passed by the Hon'ble High Court Division has been served upon respondent No. 5. It is further stated that Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative "Society Limited has allotted most of their plots to the members of the society who took possession accordingly but due to lack of civic facilities namely market, Mosque, Hospital etc the allottees did not construct houses in their plots. It is further stated that a total quantum of 5.56 acres of land of Mouza of Uttar Ramchandrapur was proposed to be acquired for Udyog Co-operative Society and after due approval in 51st meeting of central land allocation committee ministry of land issued direction for completing land acquisition proceeding and, as such, after completion of the procedure the acquired land has been handed over to Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society and hence the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

6. Subsequently petitioner No. 6-10 impleaded themselves as co-petitioners having asserted identical case with the writ petitioners. 

7. In writ petition No. 6348 of 2011, the heirs of writ petitioner No. 1 of writ petition No. 3488 of 2000 being petitioner Nos. 1-4 and along with 2 others as petitioners asserted the same facts as advanced in earlier writ petition and challenged the gazette notification dated 10-8-2006 issued under signature No. 5 so far it relates to acquisition of 2.00 acres of land in plot No. 25 having Khatian No. 15 under Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur, within Savar Police Station present Ashulia Police Station, District-Dhaka. 

8. Respondent No. 8 filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating that Md Rafiqual Alam and 4 others filed Title Suit No. 15 of 2005 before the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court Dhaka against Khandakar Abu Taher Nuri, (petitioner No. 1 of writ petition No. 3488 of 2000) and two others and revisional application is presently pending being civil revision No. 3590 of 2014 before the High Court Division against an interlocutory order passed in title suit. Plaintiff No.3 of title suit No. 15 of 2005 executed a power of attorney on 7-4-2005 in favour of added respondent No. 8 in respect of RS Plot No. 25 who is in possession over the land which has been let-out by respondent No. 8 to RAB-4 and getting monthly rent therefrom. The title regarding plot No. 25 being disputed question of facts the instant writ petition is not maintainable. The petitioners are fully aware about the said title suit and filed the instant writ petition suppressing the said title suit and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

9. Mr SM Harmuz Ahmed along with Mr Sarwar Rahman, Advocates learned advocate appeared for the petitioners and while Mr Yousuf Hosain Humayun and Mr Motiur Rahman advocate appearing for respondent No.8 in writ petition No. 3488 of 2000. 

10. Mr SM Mahbubul Islam advocate appeared for the petitioner in writ petition No. 6348 of 2011 while Mr Amit Talukder, DAG with Mr Toufiq Sajwar Partho, AAG appeared for respondent No. 4 and Mr Yousuf Hossain Humayun and Mr Motiur Rahman learned advocate appeared for respondent No. 8.

11. Mr SM Mahbubul Islam, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner in writ petition No. 6348 of 2011 submits that notice under section 3 issued in LA Case No. 01 of 1999-2000 is vague and indefinite as it is mentioned in the notice that the property in question is needed or lightly to be needed for Niribili Housing scheme keeping in both the options which is illegal, lacking application of mind and, as such, the said notice is of no legal effect. He next submits that the impugned acquisition and consequent gazette notification has been issued acquiring the land of petitioners for not any public purpose or public interest which has been done at the behest to some government officials to give benefit to their relation and friends and, as such, the said proceeding is malafide having not public purpose and, as such, is liable to be declared illegal and is of no legal effect. 

12. The learned advocate next submits that the acquisition in question is violative of the fundamental right of the petitioner grant it under article 42(1) of the constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, the impugned acquisition and consequent gazette notification to be declared as illegal and is of no legal effect. Learned advocate for the petitioner argued that in the report submitted by land Acquisition Officers and others at the instances of Ministry of law it is clearly mentioned that the proposed acquisition is not public purpose and the land acquired is earlier acquisition case for the Udyog co-operative Society has not been utilized by them and, as such, it is incumbent upon the acquiring authority to take cognizance of the said report and drop acquisition proceeding but instead they completed gazette notification regarding the acquired property which is illegal, malafide, ultra virus and is of no legal effect. Learned advocate pointed that the acquisition proceeding has been carried on for the benefit of some individual which is opposed to public policy and which is not for public purpose and, as such, the acquisition in question is liable to be struck down. 

13. Mr Harmuj Ahmed, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner in writ petition No. 6438 of 2011 adopted the submission as of the learned counsel of the writ petition No. 3488 of 2000. 

14. Mr Yousuf Hossain Humayun, learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 8 submits that with a view to establish hospital, educational institution, community center, religious and other welfare institution at the auspicious of Niribili Housing Scheme an area of 2.09 acres of land was acquired from RS plot No. 25 along with other land of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur vide LA case No.01 of 1999-2000 and after acquisition, the said land was duly handed over to Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society upon observing all formalities. He next submits that after the commencement of the acquisition proceeding notice under section 3 of the ordinance was properly affixed and served and no objection having been filed, notice section 6 of the ordinance has been issued on 22-2-2000. He further submits that notice regarding issuance of order of stay passed by the Hon'ble High Court division was not served upon respondent No. 5 and, as such, gazette notification regarding acquisition has been published. He also further submits that Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative "Society Limited has allotted most of their plots to the members of the society who took possession accordingly but due to lack of civic facilities namely market, Mosque, Hospital etc the allottees did not construct houses in their plots. He argued that a total quantum of 5.56 acres of land of Mouza of Uttar Ramchandrapur was proposed to be acquired for Udyog co-operative Society and after due approval in 51st meeting of central land allocation committee, Mnistry of land issued direction for completing land acquisition proceeding and, as such, after completion of all procedures the acquired land has been handed over to Udyog Multipurpose co-operative Society and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

15. Having gone through the writ petitioners, affidavit-in-oppositions and annexures it appears that the acquisition proceeding has been initiated to acquire land for Niribili Housing scheme which is a project of Udyog Multipurpose society vide LA case No.1 of 1999-2000. In the feasibility study report submitted in writ Petition No. 6348 of 2011 annexure-D it is stated that earlier 1.23 acres of land had been acquired for Niribili Housing scheme being run by Udyog Multipurpose society Ltd. vide LA case No. 06/76-77 and possession was made over to the requiring body but till date no installation has been carried out in the said acquired land and infrastructural development namely road, water supply and gas connections as well as other civic facilities has not been provided. The requiring body has huge land in the vicinity where the proposed project can be materialized. So from the said report it is explicitly clear that the land earlier acquired for the purpose of materialization of project remained vacant as yet having no infrastructural facilities although the same has been acquired about 25 years ago from the instant acquisition proceeding from which it can be inferred that the purpose for acquisition of land is anything but public purpose. In the said report it is clearly mentioned that the Udyog Multi-purpose co-operative society has other chunk of land where such project can be materialized and so it is also clear that the purpose of the said society is not to materialize project for the betterment of the people at large, rather to amass property for material gain and, as such, the proposed project cannot be termed for public purpose. In the case of Malik Mehdi Kabir vs Rabitat-al-Alam-aj-Islami, 65 DLR AD 109 it is held that: 
"The explanation public purpose, is therefore, construed according to the times in which particular legislation is enacted is no construed. The acquisition of the immovable property has to be held to have been made for a public purpose and not otherwise. In this particular case, it is seen that the acquisition has been made not for any public purpose rather it is meant for private purpose for office complex of a non-government organization and the acquisition is not needed for public purpose. The High Court Division has totally over looked this aspect of the matter." 

16. In the case of Md Masudul Hussain vs Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others 1995 BLD 493 it is held with reference to 15 DLR 442 that: 
"While the meaning of the expression 'public purpose' is flexible and must be interpreted with reference to the circumstances prevailing at a particular time, such a purpose can only be established if it is shown that the purpose is to benefit the public directly and not incidentally. If the purpose is however, to benefit an individual or a group of individuals directly and the benefit to the public or to a section of it is only prospective or remote or incidental, the purpose is private" 

17. It is further held in the said decision that: 
"In this case the property of the petitioner sought to be requisitioned is for establishing a 3-star Hotel. From the averments made by the respective parties it appears that the hotel is sought to be established at the initiative of an individual and it is a private enterprise. There is absolutely no material to show that either the government has direct financial involvement or that the public has interest in the establishment of the hotel. It appears that it is a commercial concern in which some people might have interest and therefore, such purpose cannot be said to be a public purpose by any stretch or imagination and therefore. The land of the petitioners cannot be taken for the use and enjoyment of some depriving the owner from using and utilizing their own land as guaranteed under the constitution." 

18. It is stated in the writ petition that the petitioner No. 1 of writ petition No. 3488 of 2000 being retired government official purchased certain quantum of land out of the case land for construction of his residential abode and other petitioners also purchased lands with a view to use for their own necessity and, as such, the case land cannot be taken away from them in the garb of public purpose which has been proved to be for ulterior purpose of the cooperative society in question. The petitioners have got unfettered right to enjoy their property as per article 42 of the constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

19. It is also advanced on behalf of the petitioners that notice issued under section 3 of the acquisition and requisition of immovable property ordinance, 1982 is flawed and in effective as definite purpose of acquisition has not been spelt out. It is mentioned that the property may be used or likely to be used in future which is proximate and, as such, not sustainable. In the case of Sanjkar Gopal Chatterjee vs The Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division, 41 DLR 326 it is held that: "Acquisition for a co-operative society per se is not a public purpose. The purpose of which the co-operative society proposes to used the acquired and is the ultimate test for a decision as to whether the acquisition is for a public purpose or not. There is a total lack of disclosure in the Notice under section 3 as to for what purpose the cooperative society needs the acquired land. The need to state the precise public purpose is imperative, because under section 4 of the ordinance any person interested in the disputed property has the right to object to the acquisition of the property challenging the public purpose stated therein, but if no specific public purpose is stated in the notice then the right given to the objection under section 4 rendered nugatory and illusory." 

20. It is specifically asserted that in the writ petition that the acquisition proceeding has been initiated at the behest of some interested government officials with a view to offer benefit to their next of kin which has not been specifically refuted by the respondents rather from the report submitted by land acquisition officers and others wherein they specifically asserted that the proposed land is not necessary for public purpose and in the report it is specifically mentioned that the co-operative society has huge land in the vicinity of the land of acquisition proceeding. So it is clear that acquisition proceeding has been initiated with malafide motive and by colorable exercise of power which, cannot be sustained. In the case of Abdur Rouf vs Abdul Hakim 17 DLR (SC) 515 it is held that: 
"A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction no legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a malafide exercise of power. A malafide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a malafide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order but for some other collateral or ulterior purpose," 

21. We note that inspite of order of stay past by a division bench of this Court the respondents published gazette notification regarding the land under LA case which is nothing but administrative high handedness which we strongly disapprove. Such step also exposed the oblique motive of the respondents to take the petitioners property under any pretext. 

22. It is required to be mentioned here that the subject-matter of the title suit as mentioned hereinabove is relating gazette notification as challenged' in the instant writ petition and, as such, there is no hindrance in maintaining the instant writ petitions. 

23. In the above facts and circumstances and legal provisions we find that both the Rules have merit and those must succeed. Accordingly the Rules are made absolute. 

24. The impugned acquisition proceeding contained in the notice under section 3 of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Properties Ordinance, 1982 (Annexure-F) in Land Acquisition Case No. 1 of 1999-2000 in respect of acquisition of lands measuring 6.56 acres contained in RS Plot Nos. 23-27, 29 and 41 in RS khatian Nos. 35, 13, 15, 37, 39 and 38 of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur within PS Saver, District-Dhaka in favour of one Udyog Multipurpose Co-operative Society's proposed Niribili Housing Scheme is declared to have been initiated and carried without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

25. Equally the impugned gazette notification dated 10-8-2006 (Annexure-A) issued under signature No. 5 so far it relates to acquisition of land of the petitioners measuring 2.00 acres situated in RS Plot No. 25 in RS Khatian No. 15 of Mouza Uttar Ramchandrapur under Savar Police Station (now Police Station Ashulia), District-Dhaka in connection With LA Case No. 1 of 1999-2001 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and respondents are directed to release the said 2.00 acres of land acquired in connection with LA case No.1 of 1999-2000 in favour of the petitioners. 

Communicate the judgment and order. 

End.

lawyer: Mr. Md. Abdur Razzak, Advocate (Appearing Virtually) ------------ For the Applicant-Petitioner.
parties:
Md. Anower Hossain ------------- Applicant-Petitioner.
Vs.
M.A. Nasir and others ----------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
SHEIKH HASSAN ARIF, J,- 1. At the instance of the applicant for addition of party in Vested Property Tribunal Suit No. 247 of 2012, Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and order dated 17.09.2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Narayanganj in Civil Revision No. 14 of 2019 dismissing the same and thereby affirming the order dated 24.04.2019 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court and Vested Property Return Additional Tribunal, Narayanganj in Vested Property Tribunal Suit No. 247 of 2012 rejecting petitioner's application for addition of party, should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders be passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Back Ground Facts:  
2.1 Facts, relevant for the disposal of the Rule, are that the Opposite Party No. 1, as applicant, filed Vested Property Tribunal Suit No. 247 of 2012 before the Vested Property Return Tribunal, Narayangonj and the said case was assigned to the Second Senior Assistant Judge and Arpita Shampatti Return Tribunal, Narayangonj for trial. The case of the opposite party-applicant in the said vested property case is that the suit land originally belonged to Ashok Ali Mir and, accordingly, C.S Khatian was published in his name. Ashok Ali died leaving behind his son Korom Ali Mir and two daughters, Atoronnessa and Oyasi Bibi. That, subsequently, the suit land was taken away by the Zaminder for non-payment of Khajana. Thereupon, Korom Ali and Atoronnessa, by paying Tk. 3,000/- as salami, became owner and possessor of the entire property. 

2.2 That Korom Ali Mir died leaving behind his only son Abdur Rahman Mir, who, subsequently, transferred his share in the property to Atoronnessa by way of deed of exchange and he took some other non-suited lands from his aunt. Thereafter, by rent suit No. 1409/1992, Abdur Rahman and Atoronnessa became owner in possession of the suit land. That at the time of S.A. record preparation, the suit land was wrongly recorded in the names of Giris Chandra Das and Norendra Nath's sons. Being aggrieved by the S.A record, Abdur Rahman and Atoronnessa filed Misc Case No. 12F/1968-69 in the Revenue Court, Narayanganj and the Court, by its order dated 12.09.1968, directed to erase the names of Giris Chandra and others in S.A. Khatian No. 322 and to record the same in the names of Abdur Rahman and Atoronnessa. 

2.3 That, Subsequently, one Ibrahim became owner and possessor of the suit land by way of purchase from the heirs and subsequent purchasers from the said Abdur Rahman and Atoronnessa. Then the suit property was sold to the Managing Director of Nipa Engineering, M.A Nasir, by sale deed No. 16016 dated 27.08.1982 and 16048 dated 27.08.1982, who subsequently gifted the same to 7 (seven) social welfare institutions including the applicants Medical College and Hospital, School and Mosque. However, the said property having been enlisted as returnable vested property under the 'Ka' schedule in the gazette published by the government under Arpita Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001, the applicants filed the said suit for release of the said property mentioned in the schedule to the application. 

2.4 While the said suit was proceeding, the petitioner school, represented by its Secretary, filed an application therein purportedly under Order 1, rule 10(2) read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Section 25 of the Arpita Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 for adding it as party therein stating, inter-alia, that 906 decimals of land mentioned in the schedule to the said application along with other lands originally belonged to one Giris Chandra Das and others as owners of upper title as per C.S. Khatian 295, Plot Nos. 258, 281, 282, 583 under 154 Dapa Indrapur Mouza, Police Station and Sub registry Office Fatullah, Narayangonj and, under him, it was recorded in favour of one Ashok Ali Miah in the column of possession. That, because of the failure of payment of rent, the said property was returned to the Jamidar. That the said Jamidar, Giris Chandra Das, died leaving his five sons as heirs. That one of the sons, Narendra Nath Das, having died, Subod Chandra Das and Sushi! Chandra Das became heirs in his place and the said property was recorded under S.A. Khatian No.322 in the names of Surendra Mohor Das and others. That the said Surendra Mohor Das and others gifted the said property by an unregistered deed in favour of the petitioner-school and handed-over possession and, accordingly, the said 906 decimals land was recorded in the name of the Secretary of the School under R.S. Porcha. But certain property thereof was wrongly recorded in the name of Atorjanbibi, and the said Atorjanbibi then gifted the said property in favour of the said school vide registered deed No. 9245 dated 31.12.1974. Since then, the school has been possessing the said land upon erecting boundary wall and gate and that the school is run by a committee and functioning for about more than sixty years. 

2.5 However, when one M.A. Nasir claimed ownership of certain property of the school, negotiation took place, and the said Nasir gifted the said property in favour of the school vide registered gift deed No. 7636-7642 dated 27.11.1995 and, accordingly, handed over possession of the land. Accordingly, the school became the absolute owner in possession of the said 906 decimals of land. However, the said land along with some other lands having been enlisted in the Arpita Shampatti gazette under schedule 'Ka', the said school filed application for release of the said property from the gazette before the same tribunal, namely Second Senior Assistant Judge and Arpita Shampatti Return Additional Tribunal, Narayangonj and, accordingly, the said application was recorded as Arpita Shampatti Case No. 6325 of 2013. However, since the opposite party No. 1 has filed the instant vested property tribunal case, the petitioner school filed the said application for adding it as one of the opposite parties in the said case. 

2.6 Upon such application, the Tribunal, after hearing the parties, rejected the same vide order dated 24.04.2019 mainly on the ground that the subject matter of the said Arpita Shampatti Return case being the determination of the issue whether the said property should be released from the gazette and since the petitioner filed a separate case for release of its portion of the property, which was pending, there was no scope for adding the petitioner as one of the parties in the said case. Being aggrieved by this order dated 24.04.2019, the petitioner preferred Civil Revision No. 14 of 2019 before the Court of District Judge, Narayangonj. Thereafter, the learned District Judge, after hearing the parties, dismissed the said civil revision vide impugned judgment and order dated 17.09.2020 mainly on the ground that the Additional Tribunal did not commit any illegality in rejecting the application of the petitioner for addition of party. The petitioner then moved this Court invoking civil revisional jurisdiction under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the aforesaid Rule mainly by referring to a decision of a single bench of this Court in Surotunnessa and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 68 DLR(2016)-463 taking the view that civil revisional application against the order of the Arpita Shampatti Return Tribunal was maintainable. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this Court, vide ad-interim order dated 22.02.2021, stayed further proceedings of the said Vested Property Tribunal Suit No. 247 of 2012 for a period of 02(two) months. At the same time, this Court ordered to post this matter in the list on 16.03.2021 for necessary order in order for early disposal of the Rule. Accordingly, the Rule has been fixed at the earliest opportunity for hearing. 

3. Submissions:  
3.1 Mr. Md. Abdur Razzak, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that certain portion of the property in question in Vested Property Tribunal Suit No. 247 of 2012 has been gifted in favour of the petitioner-school by registered deeds and as such the petitioner-school itself has filed Vested Property Case No. 6325 of 2013 before the same Tribunal for release of the said property from the vested property list in favour of the said school. Therefore, he submits that the petitioner was a necessary party in the said Vested Property Suit No. 247 of 2012 filed by the Opposite Party No. 1 for release of certain property including the property of the petitioner's school. Thus, he submits, the Tribunal as well as the learned District Judge have committed illegality in not allowing the petitioner to be added as party in the said vested tribunal case. 

3.2 On the question of maintainability of the civil revisional application against an interlocutory order of the tribunal, Mr. Razzak has referred to the said decision of a single bench of this Court in Surotunnessa and others vs. Government of Bangladesh, 68 DLR-463. He submits that in the said case a single bench has categorically held that civil revisional application is maintainable against an interlocutory order passed by the Tribunal. 

3.3 Mr. Razzak further argues that in the said case, this Court also has held that the petitioner therein is a necessary party in the suit concerned and as such should have been added as party in the said vested property suit. In this regard, learned advocate has drawn this Court's attention to Sections 25 and 31 as well as other relevant provisions of the Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001. According to him, if these provisions are read together, it will be clear that civil revisional application should be held to be maintainable against an interlocutory order passed by the Tribunal. 

3.4 Fortunately, in the middle of hearing, we have found Mr. Probir Neogi, learned senior counsel, being virtually present before this Court, and sought his opinion on the issue of maintainability of civil revisional application against interlocutory orders passed by the Tribunal. Mr. Neogi has then referred to various provisions of the Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 starting with the preamble of the said Ain. According to him, the properties listed in the gazette are no more vested properties after the amendment done in 2013 vide Act No. 46 of 2013, rather the properties have become returnable properties. Therefore, the Tribunals and the Appellate Tribunals' function is now to determine the prima-facie owner of the said property and, accordingly, release the property on the application of the said prima-facie owner. However, by referring to Section 12 of the said Ain, he submits that even if the property is released in favour of a particular claimant or applicant, such release will not in any way be deemed to have given title or possession in his favour as per law, he submits. Therefore, he opines that, if there is any dispute as regards title and/or possession of the property concerned, such dispute has to be resolved by the civil courts in accordance with law. 

3.5 As regards maintainability of the civil revisional application, Mr. Neogi has referred to the provisions under Sections 4 and 18 of the said Ain, and submits that as per Section 4 of the said Ain, only the provisions of Code of Civil Procedure which are mentioned to be made applicable as per the provisions of the said Ain are applicable and no other provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure can be made applicable in respect of proceedings before the Tribunal. Therefore, he submits that in view of the provisions under Sections 4 and 18 of the said Ain, the civil revisional application cannot be held to be maintainable against interlocutory order passed by the Tribunal. 

3.6 The Rule is not opposed by any one. 

4. Deliberations, Findings and Orders of the Court: 
4.1 Since we are confronted with a decision of this Court delivered by a single bench taking the view that civil revisional application is maintainable, we need to examine the issues afresh, particularly when we have heard contrary opinion from the Bar, in particular the submissions of Mr. Neogi. Therefore, in this matter, we will concentrate on the issue of maintainability of the civil revisional application first and then we will decide if the petitioner is required to be added as party in the Tribunal's case concerned, although that later issue will become immaterial if we take the view that civil revisional application is not maintainable. 

4.2 As submitted by Mr. Probir Neogi, learned senior counsel, it appears from the very preamble of the said Act, namely Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001, that this Act was in fact enacted by the Parliament in order for return of the properties, listed as vested properties, in favour of Bangladeshi original owners or their successors or successors in interest. Although some issues regarding vested property or returnable property are huge issues involving Constitution as well as our proclamation of independence, those issues may be dealt with in a proper case in future. For the purpose of this civil revisional application, it appears that the 'returnable properties,' or the `list of returnable properties' as defined by Clause-Ta' of Section 2 of the said Act, is the list which is published under Section 9 of the said Act.  Section 9 provides that the government shall publish a list of returnable properties through gazette in a particular way mentioned therein, and, according to Section 10, the owner of the said properties will be entitled to file application within certain period mentioned by law, or subsequent amendment to the law, before the Tribunal constituted by the said Act for release of the said properties. The Tribunal, thereupon, if satisfied that the claimant or the applicant has furnished enough supporting documents or evidences in support of his claim, will direct to release the said properties from the said list.
 
4.3 However, in deciding whether such properties should be released in favour of the said claimant or applicant, the Tribunal is required to determine whether the said claimant or applicant has established his prima-facie title in the said property, and this obligation of the Tribunal to determine prima-facie title becomes more relevant when we see sub-clause (Gha) of sub-section (8) of Section 10 of the said Act. However, if we read these provisions along with the provision of Section 12 of the said Act, it will become clear that such determination of ownership or title of a particular applicant or claimant is not the final decision as regards his title or possession. Section 12, clause (Kha) particularly, provides that any decision to release such property in favour of any person shall not be deemed to be a declaration of title or possession in his favour. This means that even after such release of the property in favour of a particular person treating him as prima-facie owner of the said property, anyone can challenge the title of that person in accordance with law before a competent civil court. 

4.4 Now the question is, in the process of such disposal of an application of a claimant or applicant, when the Tribunal passes various orders, which we call interlocutory orders, whether any party can challenge such order before the higher forum of judiciary under civil revisional jurisdiction in view of the provisions under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. To address this issue, it is pertinent to quote the provisions of Sections 4 and 18 of the Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 for our ready reference. 

“৪। এই আইনের অধীন কোন কার্ষধারায় দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধির নিম্নিবর্ণিত বিধানাবলী ব্যতীত জন্য কোন বিধান প্রযোজ্য হইবে না, যথাঃ-
(ক) এই আইনে বা বিধিতে কোন বিষয়ে দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধির কোন বিধান যতটুকু প্রযোজ্য মর্মে বিধান করা হয় ততটুকু; এবং
(খ) উক্ত কার্যবিধির ১১ ধারা।
১৮। (১) উপ-ধারা (২) এ উন্নিখিত ট্রাইব্যুনালের সিদ্ধান্তসমূহের বিরুদ্ধে শুধুমাত্র আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে আগীল দায়ের করা যাইবে; ট্রাইব্যুনালের অন্য কোন সিদ্ধান্তের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে বা অন্য কোন আদালতে বা কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট উক্ত সিদ্ধান্তের বৈধতা, যথার্থতা বা সঠিকতা সম্পর্কে কোন প্রশ্ন উথথাপন করা যাইবে না. এবং তাহা করা হইলে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা উক্ত অন্য আদালত বা কর্তৃপক্ষ সরাসরি নাকচ করিয়া দিবে।
(২) ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিয়বর্ণিত সিদ্ধান্তের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালে আবেদনকারী বা প্রতিপক্ষ আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেনঃ-
(ক) ধারা ১০ এর উপ-ধারা (১), (২) বা (8) এর অধীনে কোন আবেদন শুনানীর জন্য গ্রহণ না করিয়া সরাসরি নাকচের সিদ্ধান্ত;
(খ) একতরফা বা দোতরফা শুনানী অন্তে ধারা ১০ এর উপ-ধারা (১) বা
(২) এর অধীনে প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ বা ক্ষতিপূরণের টাকা পাওয়ার আবেদন মণ্ুর বা নামঞ্জুর করিয়া প্রদত্ত রায়;
(গ) একতরফা বা দোতরফা শুনানী অন্তে ধারা ১০৫৩) এর অধীনে উপস্থাপিত অবমুক্তকরণের আবেদন মঞ্ডুর বা নামঞ্জুর করিয়া প্রদত্ত রায়ঃ তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, এই উপ-ধারায় উল্লিখিত ট্রাইব্যুনালের সিদ্ধান্ত বা রায়ের পূর্বে প্রদর্ত এমন অন্তর্বতাঁ আদেশের ব্যাপারে আগীলে প্রশ্ন উত্থাপন করা যাইবে যাহার ভিত্তিতে ট্রাইব্যুনাল উক্ত সিদ্ধান্ত বা রায় প্রদান করিয়াছে।
(৩) ট্রাইব্যুনাল কোন আবেদন ধারা ২৩ (৩) এর অধীনে খারিজ করিলে সেই আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল করা যাইবে না।
(৪) উপ-ধারা (২) এ উল্লিখিত সিদ্ধান্ত বা রায় প্রদানের ৪৫ (পয়তাল্লিশ) দিনের মধ্যে আপীল দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং এই সময়সীমা বৃদ্ধি করার ক্ষেত্রে Limitation Act, 1908 (IX of 1908) এর Section 5 প্রযোজ্য হইবে না।
(৫) আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল উভয় পক্ষকে শুনানীর সুযোগ প্রদানপূর্বক আগীল দায়েরের ৩০০ (তিনশত) দিনের মধ্যে উহার রায় প্রদান করিবেঃ
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন অনিবার্য কারণে উক্ত মেয়াদের মধ্যে কোন আগীল নিষ্পত্তি করা সম্ভব না হইলে, আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল কারণ লিপিবদ্ধ করিয়া অতিরিক্ত ৬০ (ষাট) দিনের মধ্যে আপীল নিষ্পত্তি করতে পারিবেঃ
আরো শর্ত থাকে যে, উল্লিখিত বর্ধিত সময়ের মধ্যেও যদি যুক্তিসঙ্গত কোন কারণে কোন আপীল নিষ্পত্তি করা সম্ভব না হয়, তাহা হইলে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল উহার কারণ লিপিবদ্ধ করিয়া আবেদনটি নিষ্পত্তির জন্য সর্বশেষ আরো ৩০ (ত্রিশ) দিন সময় বর্ধিত করিতে পারিবে।
(৬) কোন পক্ষকে শুনানী অন্তে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল আপীল মঞ্জুর বা নামগ্তুর করিয়া সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিলে উহার ভিত্তিতে ৭(সাত) দিনের মধ্যে একটি ডি্রী প্রস্তুত করিবে এবং প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহনের উদ্দেশ্যে অবিলম্বে উক্ত রায় ও ডিক্রির অনুলিপি ট্রাইব্যুনাল ও জেলা প্রশাসকের নিকট প্রেরণ করিবে।”

4.5 It appears from the above quoted provisions of Section 4 of the said Act that the applicability of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure has been made very limited in that only the provisions of the Code mentioned in the said Act will be applicable and specifically the provisions under Section 11 of the Code regarding res-judicata will be applicable. Upon examination of the entire provisions of the said Act, we have not found any Section or provision which indicates that Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable in respect of a proceeding before the Tribunal under the said Act. 

4.6 Not only that, we have also not found any indication therein as regards applicability of Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding the provision of addition of parties. However that does not mean that if such application or any other reasonable application is made, Tribunal will be helpless. Section 25 of the said Act has given some latitude in favour of the Tribunal's power. According to this provision, if it is found during disposal of the application or appeal by the Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal, that there is not enough provision in the said Act or rules made there-under, they may take recourse to any appropriate procedure or decision for ends of justice. 

4.7 Therefore, even though Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been specifically mentioned in the said Act, we may safely hold that a party may be added in a proceeding before the Tribunal in a fit case by virtue of the application of the said provision under Section 25 if it is found by the Tribunal that such addition is necessary for ends of justice. On the other hand, it appears from the above quoted provisions under Section 18 of the said Act that according to this provision, the decisions of the Tribunal may only be challenged in appeal before the Appellate Tribunal. It provides that only the decisions mentioned under sub-section (2) of Section 18 are appealable to the Appellate Tribunal and the correctness, legality or appropriateness of any other decision of the Tribunal cannot be questioned before the Appellate Tribunal or any other Court or authority and if such other decisions are questioned either before the Appellate Tribunal or any other Court or authority, such application shall be rejected forthwith. Sub-section (2) of Section 18 refers in fact to the final decision of the Tribunal either accepting or rejecting an application at the initial stage or a judgment allowing or disallowing such application after hearing. However, the proviso to sub-section (2) provides that the issues involving such interlocutory orders of the Tribunal may be raised at the time of hearing of the appeal before the Appellate Tribunal. 

4.8 Therefore, upon careful examination of the above provisions under Section 4 and Section 18 and other provisions of the said Act, it appears that the applicability of the provisions of Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been clearly negated, which means civil revisional application cannot be maintained against interlocutory orders passed by the Tribunal. In this  regard, we have also examined the provisions under Section 31 of the said Ain, as this provision has been referred to in the said judgment of the single bench, namely in Surotunnessa’s Case. For our ready reference, this provision may also be reproduced. 
“৩১। এই আইনের অধীনে ট্রাইব্যুনাল ও আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনালের বা কেন্দ্রীয় কমিটির area Penal Code (XLV of 1860) এর Section 228 এ উল্লিখিত বিচারিক কার্যক্রম (Judicial Proceeding) ও Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act, V of 1898)- এর Section 480 তে উল্লিখিত Civil Court-এর কার্যক্রম বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।”

4.9. It appears from the above quoted provision that the proceedings before the Tribunal and Central Committee have been given a certain status by the Legislature, which is that such proceedings shall be deemed as judicial and civil Court proceedings. Thus, certain activities in such proceedings shall draw the provisions of Section 228 of the Penal Code, 1860 and Section 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Section 228 of the Penal Code penalizes any intentional insult or interruption to a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding. On the other hand, Section 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure empowers a Civil, Criminal or revenue Court to detain an offender during continuation of proceedings and take cognizance of offence and sentence the offender to certain amount of fine or simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to 1(one) month for commission of offence by him, during such proceedings, under Sections 175,178, 179, 180 or 228 of the Penal Code. Therefore, it appears that this provision under Section 31 has only given the proceedings of the Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal a status like the proceedings before a Court of law. Thus, under no circumstances, this provision has converted the proceedings before Tribunal and Appellate Tribunal constituted under Sections 16 and 19 of the said Act respectively into the proceedings of the Civil Court in order to make the interlocutory orders passed therein amenable to Civil Revisional Jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4.9. It has to be borne in mind that the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal constituted under the said Act have been constituted by the said Act only. Just because judicial officers have been assigned to be the presiding officers of such Tribunals or Appellate Tribunals does not epso-facto convert their proceedings into civil Court proceedings and does not also make the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure automatically applicable to the proceedings before such Tribunals. The law by which the Tribunal or Appellate Tribunal has been established has itself provided the scope of such Tribunals and the procedure to be adopted by such Tribunals in disposing of applications filed by the applicants in order for release of certain properties from the list of returnable properties published in the gazette. The extent to which the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure may be taken recourse to by such Tribunals in such proceedings has also been specifically provided by the said Act.
Therefore, as a Court of law, we cannot go beyond the specific provisions of the said Act as enacted by the Parliament.

4.10 Be it a lower judiciary or higher Court, it is the obligation of each and every Court to apply the law as it is as enacted by the Parliament, unless and until such law is declared unconstitutional by a competent Court. In this regard, we have also examined the decision of the said Surotunnessa Case, 68 DLR-463 as decided by a single bench of the High Court Division. It appears from the said decision, in particular paragraphs 8 and 9 of the reported case, that the said single bench has intended to treat the Tribunal as a civil Court by reading the provision of Section 31 of the said Act and, accordingly, held that “the proceedings of a tribunal under said Act shall be treated as the proceedings of the Civil Court. Further, a Judge of the Arpita Sampatti Pratyarpan Appeal Tribunal is presided over by an Additional District Judge. So, against an order of the Arpita Sampatti Pratyarpan Appeal Tribunal, a revision under Section 151(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is very much maintainable”. With all respect to the author Judge of the said decision, we have no option but to ignore this view in deciding the case in hand on the ground that the said view was not a correct view of law. Had it been a decision of a division bench, we would have referred to this matter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constitution of a larger bench. But, since the said decision was given by a single bench, we may simply ignore the same for the reasons stated above.

4.11 In view of the above facts and circumstances, we are of the view that civil revisional application as preferred by the petitioner before the learned District Judge was not maintainable. At same time, the instant civil revision as preferred by the petitioner against the judgment of the learned District Judge, who unfortunately did not consider the issue of maintainability of the civil revision, is not maintainable.

4.12 Although we can stop this judgment at this point without going into other issues, we are of the view that for the sake of ends of justice, we should address another issue which is that both the petitioner and opposite No. 1 have filed two Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Cases, namely Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Case Nos. 26325 of 2013 and 247 of 2012, which are still pending before the same Tribunal, namely the Second Senior Assistant Judge and Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Otirikto Tribunal, Narayangonj. Therefore, we hold that by application of the provision under Clause (Gha) of Section 17 of the said Act, both the cases should be heard by the same Tribunal analogously and, if necessary, the Tribunal should dispose of both the cases by one judgment.

4.13 In view of above, the Rule has no merit as the same is not maintainable. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged. The ad-interim order, if any, thus stands recalled and vacated. The Tribunal, namely the Second Senior Assistant Judge and Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Otirikto Tribunal, Narayangonj is directed to dispose of both the Arpito Shampatti Prottarpon Suit Nos. 26325 of 2013 and 247 of 2012 analogously and dispose of the same preferably within a period of 06 (six) months from receipt of the copy of this order. 

4.13. Before parting, we convey our gratitudes to Mr. Probir Neogi, learned senior counsel.

Communicate at once.

(Sheikh Hassan Arif, J)
| agree.
(Ahmed Sohel, J)

End.

full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated the 15th day of August, 2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.540 of 1999 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the present appellants as instituted Title Suit No.77 of 1979 in the 1St Court of Munsif, Goalandha, Rajbari (which was transferred later to the Court of the Assistant Judge, Pangsha, Rajbari and renumbered as Title Suit No.331 of 1983) for declaration of title in respect of 1.07 acres land and for confirmation of possession in the same in alternative to recovery of khas possession stating inter alia, that the land of RS Plot No.312 of RS Khatian No.255 corresponding to SA Khatian No.279 of Mouza-Maliyat originally belonged to Billada Sundari Saha and others. They are co-sharers in the suit land to the extent of 12 annas 5 gandas 1 kara 1 kranti and the rest 3 annas 14 gandas 2 kara 2 kranti belonged to Jagadish Chandra. Said Jagadish Chandra settled his share by an amalnama dated 8 Ashwin 1352BS to the plaintiff's predecessor and as such, they are in exclusive possession in 16 annas share in the suit land. It is further stated that SA record was wrongly prepared in the name of Jagadish Chandra along with the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Case No.XIII-68/77- 78 before the concerned Circle Officer (Revenue) who corrected the said Khatian. Defendant No.1 filed an appeal before the concerned Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) being Miscellaneous Appeal No.XX111/B-25/78- 79 which was allowed. Thereafter, the defendant threatened the plaintiff to dis-possess from the suit land and as such, the suit.

3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint and also denying the plaintiffs' right, title and possession in the suit land. The defendants' case was that the suit land was recorded in CS Khatian in the name of Kcdar Nath Bhoumik and others. The suit joie was sold in auction. Thereafter, Prosonya Kumar Saha and others got settlement of an area of 1.10 acres land in 1352BS fixing a rent of taka 4 only and since then, they are in possession. Prosonya Kumar Bhoumik was serving in the Railway and during his absence, RS Khatian No. 225 was wrongly recorded. Prosonya Kumar Bhournik settled the said land in favour of defendant No.1 who claimed the said settlement in his benami and in the name of Nirupma Dutta in 1356BS. The touji was sold in auction. Thereafter, by a registered patta deed dated 29.02.1956, the suit land was settled by Parma Chandra Dutta in favour of defendant No.1 and since then he had been in possession. The plaintiffs had neither title nor possession in the suit land.

4. The learned Assistant Judge, Pangsha, Rajbari upon consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 28.11.1989 holding that the claims of settlement as made by the plaintiffs were false and also holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their case and further held that the suit is bad for defect of parties.

5. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No.11 of 1990 and that appeal was heard by the learned District Judge, Rajbari who by the judgment and decree dated 17.01.1999 allowed the appeal, decreed the suit on setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the defendants filed the civil revision before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division sent the case back on remand to the learned District Judge, Rajbari for holding the bearing afresh who after hearing the appeal allowed the same after setting aside the judgment of the trial Court.

7. Against this judgment of the learned District Judge, The defendants again preferred a Civil Revision being No.540 of 1999 before the High Court Division and the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division again after hearing made the Rule absolute.

8. Against which the plaintiffs filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.30 of 2008 and leave was granted giving rise to this appeal.

9. Mr. Sasthi Sarker, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title to the extent of 3 annas 14 gandas 2 kara 2 kranti to the land by way of settlement and also to the other portion of the suit property and that they totally failed to prove their possession without considering that who had title in possession. He submits that the High Court Division committed an error mis-construing the evidence of PW1, Amarendra Nath Saha who has in his cross-examination stated that:-

“আমরা পূর্ববর্তীক্রমে মামলার জমি খায়। মামলার জমি পূর্ব-পশ্চিম লম্বা বর্তমান আমরা যাহারা বাদী আছি তাহারা ২৫/৩০ বৎসর এজমালি জমি খায় । ৮ বৎসর যাবৎ আমরা লাঙ্গল নাই এবং নিজ হাতে চাষ করি না। ৮ বৎসর পূর্বে আমার হালিয়া ওয়াছেল চাষ করতো। ইহার পূর্বে পরেত দিয়া চাষ করাইতাম। এ পরেতদের নাম বলতে পারিনা । মামলার জমির উত্তরে পরিতোষ কুমার সাহা ও মুল-ক চান, দক্ষিণে এবং পশ্চিমে দুলাল বিশ্বাস। PW2, Billal Hosscn, in his evidence stated that মামলার জমি আমি বাদীর অধীনে বর্গা চাষ করি। ৮ বৎসর যাবৎ এবং বর্গা ফসল অমরেন্দ্র সাহাকে দেই। আমি ফাগুন মাসে মামলার জমিতে দখলে যাই এবং ইহার পর ৭টি ফাগুন গিয়াছে। PW3, Hossain Al Mondal has said that মামলার জমি মিটু সাহা ভোগ দখল করে । মামলার জমির পূর্বে আমার উত্তরে মুলক চাদ আলী ও পরিবানুর মামলার জমি এক দাগ পশ্চিমে দুলাল শীল। পরে বলে কুয়েত আলী পূর্বে দুলাল শীল”

10. From the above view of the facts, it is clear that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their possession and as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. He lastly submits that the plaintiffs produced the rent receipts which are the evidence of possession and the lower appellate Court as the last Court of fact reassessed and reconsidered all the evidence of the parties and arrived at a conclusion that the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land, but the High Court Division made the Rule absolute without considering the evidence of the competent DWs and without considering the fact that the defendant did not derive any title.

11. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned Advocate, appearing for respondent Nos.1 and 1(c), made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submits that the plaintiffs were not able to prove their right, title and possession by adducing oral and documentary evidence on record and that the trial Court after elaborate discussion about evidence thereof rightly dismissed the suit, whereas the appellate Court below without reversing the valid and tenable findings of the trial Court illegally allowed the appeal and that the High Court Division rightly made the Rule absolute. He further submits that the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 20.01.1998 passed in Civil Revision No.651 of 1992 made the Rule absolute by sending back the case on remand before the appellate Court below directing the same to consider the evidence on record in respect of possession of the suit land and dispose of the appeal and cross-objection in accordance with law. But the lower appellate Court without complying with the direction of the High Court Division and without disposal of the matter in dispute in respect of possession illegally allowed the appeal. He further contends that the plaintiffs claimed the suit property by way of RS Khatian. PW 1 admitted in cross-examination that:-

“আর.এস. রেকর্ড সম্মন্ধে আমার ব্যক্তিগত জ্ঞান নাই । মামলার জমি সি.এস. খতিয়ান নম্বর, জমা ও উপারাস্ত মালিক ছিল কিছুই বলিতে পারি না। কি বুনিয়াদ আস.এস. রেকর্ড তৈরী হইয়াছে বলিয়া পারি না। মামলার জমিতে আমাদের ১৬ জন বাদীর মধ্যে আর.এস. রেকভীয় শরীকদের খাওয়া আমি দেখি নাই। মামলার জমির চৌহদ্দী, দাগ, খতিয়ান বলিতে পারি না। মামলার জমির পরগনা ও তৌজি বলিতে পারি না।”

12. The trial Court after perusing the above evidence on record rightly dis-missed the suit, but the appellate Court without any discussion about the aforesaid evidence illegally allowed the appeal holding that the plaintiffs proved their possession and that the High Court Division after considering the oral and documentary evidence and other materials on record rightly made the Rule absolute. He further submits that PW2, Billal Hossain, stated his examination-in-chief that: “বাদী-বিবাদী ও মামলার জমির দাগ খতিয়ান বলিতে পারি না এবং কত শতক জমি বলিতে পারি না। মামলার জমির প্রথম চিনিবার সন তারিখ বলিতে পারি PW3 stated examination-in-chief  আমি বাদী-বিবাদী ও মামলার জমি চিনি। মামলার জমি মিঠু সাহা ভযাগদখল করে । মামলার জমির পাশে আমার জমি আছে, but in cross-examination, he stated that  মামলার জমির দাগ নম্বর বলিতে পারি না। কত শতক জমি আছে বলিতে পারি না। এই মামলায় কতজন বাদী আছে কত জমি বিবাদীর আছে বলিতে পারি না, এবং সব বাদী-বিবাদীর নাম বলিতে পারি না। মামলা জমি মিঠু সাহা ছাড়া আর কোন বাদী খায় বলিতে পারি না এবং মামলার জমিতে কয়টি ভাগ আছে বলিতে পারি না। মামলার জমির এবং দাগ দক্ষিণে কার জমি বলিতে পারি না?”

13. The trial Court on the basis of the above evidence rightly dismissed the suit, but the appellate Court below illegally allowed the appeal without considering the deposition of above PWs and that the High Court Division after considering above deposition rightly made the Rule absolute. He further contends that the trial Court dismissed the suit holding that-

ৰাদীপক্ষ মামলার জমির রেকড়ীয় প্রজাগনের ওয়ারিশ ও ক্রমিক ওয়ারিশদের যে বিবরণ আরজিতে উল্লেখ করিয়াছে তাহা নিরপেক্ষ কোন সাক্ষী দ্বারা প্রমাণ করেন নাই এবং বাদীপ���্ষের সাক্ষীগণ সঙ্গতিপূর্ণ সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করিয়া নালিশী জমিতে তাহাদের দখল ও প্রমাণ করিতে সক্ষম হন নাই। ১নং বাদী জেরায় বলেন যে, মামলায় জমি আর. এস. রেকভীয় প্রজাগণের খাওয়া তিনি দেখেন নাই এবং ৮ বছর যাবৎ তাহার লাঙ্গল নাই এবং নিজ চাব করেন না। তিনি আরও বলেন যে, তাহার হালিয়া ওয়াছেল শেখ ৭-৮ বছর যাবৎ এই জমি চাষ করিয়াছে এবং ইহার পূর্ব পয়তে দিয়া চাষ করাতিন তবে এ পয়দদের নাম তিনি বলিতে পারেন না। তিনি আরও বলেন যে, ওয়াছেল শেখের পর জমি বেলালকে বর্গা দিয়াছেন এবং এঁ বছর তাহার অংশ ৪-৫ কাঠা ধান পাইয়াছেন। তিনি মামলার জমিতে ১৬ জন বাদীর মধ্যে কাহার কত শতক দাবী তাহা বলিতে পারেন না। বাদীর ৩নং সাক্ষী মোঃ হোসেন আলি মন্ডল তাহার জেরায় মামলার জমির দাগ নম্বর ও জমির পরিমাণ বলিতে পারেন না এবং মামলার জমি মিঠু সাহা ছাড়া আর কোন বাদী খায় তাহা বলিতে পারি না এবং মামলার জমিতে কয়টি বাগ আছে তাহা বলিতে পারেন না। সুতরাং মামলার জমি বাদীর ৩নং সাক্ষী চিনেন উহা আদৌ বিশ্বান হয় না। বাদীর ২নং সাক্ষী বেলাল হোসেন ৮ বছর যাবৎ মামলার জমি বর্গা চাষ করিয়াছেন বলিয়া জবানবন্দিতে উলে-খ করিলেও তিনি মামলার জমিতে দাগ খতিয়ান বলিতে পারেন না এবং নালিশী দাগ কত শতক জমি তাহা বলিতে পারেন না । মামলা দাখিলের সময় বা পূর্ব বাদীপক্ষ মামলার জমি দখল করিয়াছেন এমন কোন কিছু প্রমাণের জন্য বাদীপক্ষ আদালতে কোন সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করেন নাই । but the appellate Court without reversing the above findings of the trial Court illegally allowed the appeal which is violative of the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the High Court Division considering the above provision of law rightly made the Rule absolute and as such, the above appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submits that the trial Court held that-

জগদিশ ও বিল-াদা তারা শংকরকে ১৩৫২ সালের ৮ইং আশ্বিন তারিখে আমলনামা দাখিলা মূলে জমি প্রজাপন্তন করেন এইরূপ কোন দাৰী বাদীপক্ষ আরজিতে উল্লেখ করেন নাই এবং মর্মে বাদীর ৪নং সাক্ষীর বক্তব্য বিশ্বাসযণাগ্য নয়। বাদী পক্ষের প্রমানকৃত ১৩৫২ সালে ৮ইং আশ্বিন তারিখের তসদিক দৃষ্টেও প্রমানিত হয় যে, করিয়াছে এবং পুরাতন কাগজ পরবর্তীতে সৃজন করা হইয়াছে লেখাসমূহ কাগজের সহিত চুগসোইয়া গিয়াছে সুতরাং বাদীপক্ষের দাবীকৃত ১৩৫২ সালের ৮ইং আশ্বিন তারিখের পত্তন প্রমানিত হয় নাই এবং এ সংক্রান্ত বাদীপক্ষের ৪নং সাক্ষীর বক্তব্য শিখানো মতে প্রদত্ত বানোয়াট বলিয়া বিশ্বাস হয়। বাদীপক্ষ অন্য কোন সাক্ষী দ্বারা তাহাদের দাবীকৃত ১৩৫২ সালের ৮ইং আশ্বিন তারিখের পত্তন ও তদবলে মামলার কোন জমিতে তারা শংকর সাহার দখলপ্রাপ্ত হওয়া এবং দখল থাকা প্রমান Pastar ate, but the appellate Court below without reversing the above findings of the trial Court illegally allowed the appeal and as such, the above appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submits that the appellate settlement which took place on 8th Ashwin, 1352BS in support of his assertion, plaintiff No.16 filed a Dakhila dated 8tn Ashwin, 1352BS, the formed Dakhila has been marked as exhibit-1 and from the writing, it is seen that it has been created recently by using an old form and so the Assistant Judge disbelieved and discarded it and plaintiff No.16 did not appear before the trial Court to prove the alleged Dakhila and he did not file any Dakhila to prove that he paid rents in the subsequent years and his name was not recorded in SA Khatian." He adds that the appellate Court below passed the impugned judgment and decree contrary to his above own findings allowing the appeal on the full claim of the plaintiffs and as such, the appellate Court below erred in law occasioning failure of justice which cannot sustain in law.

14. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other materials on record.

15. The plaintiffs have come with an allegation that plaintiff. Nos.1-15 have acquired 12 annas 5 Gondas 1 Kora 1 Kranti share from disputed khatian by way of inheritance from R.S recorded tenant and plain-tiff No.16 acquired 3 annas 14 Gondas 2 Koras 2 Krantis share on basis of a settlement from Jagadish, one of the recorded tenants. The aforesaid RS Khatian has been prepared in the names of the plaintiffs which were marked as exhibit No.2 series and the same has been denied by the contesting defendants as per section 103-B of Bengal Tenancy Act, entries of the record have a unrebuttable presumptive value. The respondent failed to adduce any cogent evidence with a view to rebut the aforementioned presumption. From the plaint, it appears that Billuda Sundari Saha, Upendranath Saha, Jagadish Chandra Saha, Otul Chandra Saha, Boloram Saha, Lalon Chandra Saha, Derendrandra Nath Saha and Moindra Nath Saha were the owners of the suit land. The inheritance chart and sub-sequent devaluation as has furnished in the plaint has not been challenged by the defendant. Not only that, PW1, Amarandra Nath Saha deposed that Billuda Sundari died leaving behind two sons named Jagadish and Otul. He also deposed that Jagadish had 1 annas 1 Gonda 1 Kora 1 Kranti share and he inherited 2 annas 13 Gondas 1 Kora 1 Kranti share from his mother in the suit Khatian. There is no denial of the fact that plaintiff Nos.1-15 did not inherit the aforementioned share from the RS record tenant.

 

16. The material question that falls for determination is whether the revisional Court acted beyond its jurisdiction in set-ting aside the judgment of the learned District Judge, (the last Court of fact) on the basis of proper appreciation of evidence on record.

17. The case of the contesting defendants is that the suit land appertaining to 11/1, 11/2, 11/3, 11/4 numbers khabot under Khabot No.25 belongs to one Kader Nath Bhoumik which was put in auction and the interests of the tenancy were extinguished and one Puma Chandra Bhoumik took settlement of the same who stetted the suit land in the benami of mother's sister. It has been further alleged by the contesting defendant that Puma Chandra through patta 29.02.195.6 gave patta settlement in the benami of Nimpoma Datta and defendant No.1 claimed the suit and from his bemander and since then he has been pos-sessing the same. But the defendants failed to show any scrap of paper regarding such revenue sale or there was any assertion of such rent sale in the recital of such patta dated 29.02.1956.

18. Not only that, all rent receiving interest were acquired by Government under the provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, before 1956AD and as a result of which, no title had been acquired by Nerupoma Datta by dint of patta date 29.02.1956 since the patta has been registered after 13.12.1955. Nor the defendant has been able to prove the fact that Nirupoma was the Benamder of the defendant consequently Profullya Kumar Sarker (defendant No.1) acquired no title over the suit land from Nerupoma Datta. Over and above, the defendants failed to record his name in the rent role Ichatian. Thus, we find that defendant No.1 miser-ably failed to prove his case.

19. On the other hand, we find that plaintiff Nos.1 -15 have inherited 12 Annas 5 Gandas 1 Kara 1 Kranti share in the suit land by way of inheritance from the RS recorded tenant. Although plaintiff No.16 failed to prove his title in remaining 3 Annas 14 Gondas 2 Karas and 2 Krantis share since he failed to prove his statement of such land by adducing cogent evidence nor he get the said property recorded in his name during the SA operation.

20. Plaintiff No.16 has come with an alle-gation that he has taken oral settlement in respect of the share of Jagodish on 8th Ashwin, 1352BS and also filed a private dakhila. But on perusal of recital of such dakhila, it appears that the same has been created in recent past. The appellate Court as last Court of fact has observe on this issue that the writings of said dakhila shows that it has been created recently by using an old form and accordingly, the learned Assistant Judge of the trial Court disbelieved the same and discarded it. The learned appellate Court as the last Court of fact held the view that plaintiff No.16 did not appear before the trial Court with a view to prove such dakhila and there is no evidence on record to show that plaintiff No. 16 was able to record his name during SA operation and accordingly, plaintiff No.16 failed to prove his title over his claimed land. The appellate Court further observed regarding failure of proving the case of defendant No.1 in the following verbatim:-

"The defendant No.1 has failed to prove that the superior interest of the suit land was sold in revenue sale. There is no evidence that Ratikanta Saha again took settlement from the auction purchaser. There is no on record evidence that Ratikanta settled that suit land with Puma Chandra or his benamdar So, the title of Purnachandra has not been established by legal evidence. Defendant No.1 has stated that he took the suit land from Purnachandra by way of settlement by a register patta dated 29.02.1956 in the benami of his mother's sister Nirupama Datta. Alleged patta has marked Ext. Grha' settlement in the benami of Nirupama has not been proved by supporting evi-dence. All the rent-receiving interest were Acquisition and Tenancy Act before 1956AD. So, the alleged trans-fer by a registered patta dated 29.02.56 did not give any title to Nirupama Datta. If Nirupama Datta does not acquire title over the suit land by the said patta, how her sister's son Profulla Kumar Sarkar will acquire title over the suit land by way of inheritance. There is no description in the alleged patta that Purnachandra Saha or his predecessor purchased that land by auction. So, it has not been proved that the suit land was sold out by auction. According to law, no patta deed can be registered in the year, 1956AD and as such, no title can be passed by such a deed."

21. On perusal of the evidence and other materials on record, we find that there is no misreading and non-consideration and mis-appreciation of evidence on record so as to brush aside the above quoted finding of the appellate Court and in that end in view, the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division arrived at a wrong decision in controverting the finding and decision of the learned Judge of the appellate Court. In respect of pos-session, the learned District Judge found that the plaintiffs have filed a series of rent receipts granted by the Government (Ext No.4 series). He also scanned the evidence of PW1 who deposed that they have been possessing the suit land through BorgadeK Billal Hossain for 8 (eight) years and before such period, they used to possess the same through Washel Sheik. He also found that PW2, Billal Hossain who is the Borgader of the plaintiffs has corroborated the aforesaid testimony of PWI. The learned District Judge as the last Court of fact also found that the rent receipts though not document of title but arc important evidence of possession and possession may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession follows the title. He further opined that the trial Court has not considered and discussed the evidence of the plaintiffs in its true perspective and he found that the plaintiffs are in joint possession of the suit land. The learned Judge of the appellate Court also rejected the cross objection submitted by the defendant. In view of the evidence as has been laid in this case, we find that the learned appellate Court below after due consideration of evidence on record have arrived at a proper decision regarding title and possession of the plaintiffs over the suit land, but as a revisional Court (the High Court Division) have acted without jurisdiction and thereby reversed the judgment passed by the appellate Court below without adverting its cogent findings.

22. In the light of the facts and circumstances discussed above, we find that there is illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment, which in our view calls for interference.

23. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the appellate Court below is restored.

End.
