full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J. This appeal is directed against the decision dated 20.10.2004 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in A.A. T. Appeal No. 177 of 1999 reversing the decision dated 23.06.1999 passed by the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra in A.T. Case No. 114 of 1998. 

2. The short facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that appellant had been serving as Steno-Typist since 16.07.1988 in the Police Academy at Sardha. The then Vice-Principle of the Academy called him in his room on 30.01.1996 and abruptly abused him with filth language having had no such cases and also misbehaved with him. The appellant being shocked tendered his resignation letter in protest then and there. On the same date, the Principal of the Police Academy Sardha settled the matter expressing that the resignation letter submitted by the appellate would not be accepted. Few days thereafter, the appellant applied for sitting in the departmental examination and the authority allowed him to participate and the authority allowed him to participate in the said examination. The appellant obtained highest marks in the departmental examination. Result was published on 22.06.1996. Meanwhile, said Principal was transferred. As per advice of the Vice Principal, the appellant filed an application for withdrawal of his resignation letter on 30.10.1996. But unfortunately, the Superintendent of Police (Administration) respondent No. 3, with an ulterior motive, accepted the resignation letter on 18.11.1996 and removed the appellant from his service though he was not competent authority to accept the said resignation letter. On 19.11.1996, the appellant preferred appeal before the Principle, Police Training Academy against the order of his removal but he did not get any reply. Thereafter, the appellant preferred another appeal on 27.08.1997 before the Inspector - General of Police who dismissed the said appeal on 21.04.1998. Then the appellant filed aforesaid Administrative Tribunal case before the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra on 18.10.1998. 

3. The respondent Nos.3 and 5 Superintendent of Police (Administration) and Principal, Police Academy, Sardha contested the Administrative Tribunal Case by filing two separate sets of written objection contending that the service record and performance of the appellant was not at all fair and satisfactory. Even once warrant of arrest was issued against him in connection with a Criminal case from the Court of Magistrate. They further contended that on perusal of the materials on record, the authority rightly accepted the resignation letter as submitted by the appellant and, thereupon, rightly dismissed him from service. 

4. The Administrative Tribunal, by its decision dated 2306.1999, allowed the administrative case. The Government preferred Administrative Appellate Tribunal Appeal No. 177 of 1999 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal by its decision dated 20.10.2004 allowed the appeal upon setting aside the decision dated 23.06.1999 of the Administrative Tribunal. Thus, the appellant has preferred this appeal upon getting leave. 

5. Mr. Sikder Moqbul Haque, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that the appellant tendered his resignation on 30.01.1996 but, at the intervention of the Principal, the matter was settled and the appellant has been performing his duties accordingly and he was subsequently promoted and performed his functions till 30.10.1996. He also filed an application for withdrawal of his resignation let-ter. The resignation letter dated 30.01.1996 was accepted on 18.11.1996 by the Superintendent of Police (Administration) who was not his appointing authority. The learned Counsel further submits that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has misinterpreted the provision of second provision of sub-section (2) of Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 which came into force from 19th November, 1997, and erroneously observed that the instant A.T. Case was time barred. The learned Counsel, lastly, submits that the appellant preferred appeal on 19.11.1996 before the Principal, Police Training Academy for his reinstatement but he did not give any decision so the appellant preferred another appeal in 27.08.1997 before the respondent No.2, Inspector General of Police who dis-missed the said appeal on 21.04.1998, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal erred in law in holding that the A.T. Case was barred by limitation. 

6. Mr. Biswajit Debnath, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the respondents, submits that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal rightly held that the instant Administrative Tribunal Case was barred by limitation, and, thus, the appellant was not entitled to get any relief. 

7. It appears from the materials on record, that the appellant tendered his resignation from the service on 30.01.1996. After 9 (nine) months, on 30.10.1996, he filed an application for withdrawal of said prayer. The authority concerned accepted the resignation on 18.11.1996. The appellant preferred departmental appeal on 19.11.1996 but on decision was given by the authority concerned on the said departmental appeal. Thereafter, he preferred another departmental appeal on 27.08.1997 which was dismissed on 21.04.1998. 

8. Then, the appellant filed the instant Administrative Tribunal Case on 18.10.1998. Now, the prime question in this case was that whether the administrative case was barred by limitation or not. 

9. In this regard, this Division in Civil Review Petition No. 659 of 2017 (The Government V. S.M. Abdur Rauf and another) elaborately discussing the matters drew conclusion about the question of limitation in identical facts. Which was as follows: 
"To examine the point of limitation, decision of this Division in the case of Md. Sirajul Islam Khan Vs. Bangladesh Bank, Dhaka and others reported in XIII ADC 289 is relevant here. In the cited case 8 (eight) members bench f this Division has observed. 
It appears that a new second proviso has been inserted after proviso No. I in sub-Section (2) of Section 4 by the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Act 1997 (Act No. 24 of 1997). According to the said amended provision of Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act the appeal pending before the Higher Administrative Authority shall be deemed to have been disallowed by the authority after the expiry of two months from the date of submissions of the departmental appeal and accordingly the appellant ought to have filed the A.T. Case within six months after the expiry of said two months before the Administrative Tribunal but he did not do so and as such the case before the Administrative Tribunal was barred by limitation. 
In Civil Petition for leave to appeal No. 1454 of 2008, Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest- 2009, Volume- XII, Page.10 the fact was that the petitioner was dismissed from service on 24.01.1995. He preferred departmental appeal on 08.02.1995 and it was rejected on 14.01.2001. In the meantime the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Act, 1997 (Act No. XXIV of 1997) came into force on 19.11.1997 whereby new 2nd proviso to section 4(2) of the Act was introduced. This Division approved the view taken by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal that as the amending Act came into force on 19.11.1997 the appeal to the higher authority by the petitioner deemed to have been rejected on 19.01.1998 i.e. before 19.07.2001 long after the statutory period of limitation. Therefore, the Administrative Tribunal Case was hopelessly barred by limitation under section (42) of the A.T. Act, 1980. In Abul Bashar Vs. Investment Corporation of Bangladesh and another, 20 BLD (AD) 294 the fact was that the petitioner was an Assistant General Manager of the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh. In exercise of powers under Regulation 56(2) the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh (Officers and Employees) Service Regulations, 1993 the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh terminated the service of the petitioner, as Assistant General Manager of the Corporation on 23 April 1995. The petitioner challenged the order of termination in Writ Petition No. 921 of 1995. The petition was summarily rejected on 3 May 1995. The petitioner, thereafter, made a civil petition for leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division which was also summarily rejected on 13 December 1995. Being unsuccessful, the petitioner filed case No. 242 of 1995 before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka, on 31 December 1995 sought to have the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act on the ground that the time spent for prosecution of the writ petition and the civil petition for leave to appeal should be excluded in computation of the period of limitation prescribed under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980. This Division held that it is clear from the wording of the second proviso (Now that is third after the amendment of 1997) to subsection (2) of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act that the legislative intendment behind this provision is to exclude the proceedings governed by the Administrative Tribunals Act from the operation of the benefit conferred by sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and while computing the period of limitation in filing an application before the Administrative Tribunal a person cannot have the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908. This judgment justifies that limitation in regard to cases under Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 has to be calculated applying the procedures described in the Act itself and there is very little scope, if not no scope, to deviate from the strict rule of limitation embodied in the Act while dealing with Administrative Tribunals cases. From the above discussions and findings we are of the view that both the Tribunals below having considered the materials on record rightly arrived at a correct decision in the matter. Accordingly, we do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in affirming those passed by the Administrative Tribunals. 

10. In view of the decision referred above, it is apparent in the face of the record that the instant Administrative Case was hopelessly barred by limitation since the respondent filed the instant case before the Administrative Tribunal after about 7 years of arising its cause of action inasmuch as he was entitled to get 2 months+6 months time to file A.T. Case in view of the second proviso as added in Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act by the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Act, 1997 and the interpretation of this Division quoted above. The Administrative Tribunal relied upon the case of Jahangir Kabir (Md.) V. Bangladesh reported in 48 DLR (AD) 156 but the Said A.T. case was instituted in 1987 and Appeal was preferred in 1991 and C.A. was preferred and disposed of in 1995, that is, the same was decided by this Division before amendment of Section 4(2) of the Act by Act XXIV of 1997. This A.T. Case has been filed in 2011, that is, long after the said amendment. The Administrate Tribunal, ignoring the afore-said facts, most unfortunately, entertained the A.T. case referring Jahangir Kabir's case. 

11. The learned Attorney General submits that the Administrative Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the instant case since the same was hopelessly barred by limitation and that Tribunal was not authorized to condone the delay. The jurisdiction means the authority by which the Court/tribunal has to decide the matter that litigated before it, or to take cognizance of matters presented in a formal way for its decision. It is the authority to hear and determine cause, to adjudicate and exercise any judicial power in relation to it. The jurisdiction of the Court/ Tribunal may be qualified as restricted by variety of circumstances. The power of the tribunal may be exercised within the limitation of exercising power has been imposed by the Administrative Tribunal Act itself. The essence of the matter was whether the tribunal had power to entertain time barred case and to grant relief. Since the Tribunal was not authorized to entertain time barred case, the decision given by the tribunal was a nullity. The Administrative Tribunal cannot ignore the law declared by the highest Court of the Country and initiate proceeding ignoring the law so declared. The Administrative Tribunal also ignored the decision of 5 members Bench of this Division, that is, case of Abul Basher Vs. Investment Corporation of Bangladesh reported in 20 BLD(AD) 294 as quoted earlier." 

12. In this case, we have found that the appellant tendered his resignation on 30.01.1996. On 30.10.1996, he made a prayer for withdrawal of his application for resignation. The authority accepted his resignation on 18.11.1996. The appellant preferred departmental appeal on 19.11.1996. The amended provision of his application for resignation. The authority accepted his resignation on 18.11.1996. The appellant preferred departmental appeal on 19.11.1996. The amended provision of Administrative Tribunal Act came into force on 19.11.1997. Second appeal preferred by the appellant was redundant. The appellant filed A.T. case on 18.10.1998. In view of decision referred above it is apparent that the same was barred by limitation. 

13. Since the identical issue in similar circumstances has already been decided by this Division in the aforesaid manner, we do not find any force of submission of Mr. Sikder Moqbul Haque that the instant Administrative Case was not barred by limitation.

14. Thus, the appeal is dismissed. 

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-8 to show cause as to why the impugned Order dated 9-7-2019 passed by the learned Judge (Joint District and Sessions Judge) of Land Survey Tribunal, Khulna in Suit No. Land 580 of 2014 rejecting an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 read with section 145A/145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for rejection of plaint should not be set-aside and/or such other or further or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

	2. Facts in short are that the opposite party Nos. 1-8 as plaintiffs filed Land Tribunal Suit No.580 of 2014 under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for correction of record-of-right against the petitioners and opposite party Nos.9-11 who were defendants.

	3. In above suit defendants filed a petition under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure, 1908 for rejection of plaint. It was alleged that before the establishment of Land Survey Tribunal plaintiff filed Title Suit No.1105 of 2008 for the self same property praying and for same relief in which defendants are party and above suit is pending for trial in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Khulna. In violation of Section 145(5) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 plaintiffs have filed this second suit for the same property so the plaint is liable to be rejected.

	4. On consideration of submissions of the learned Advocates for both sides the learned Judge of the Tribunal rejected above petition.

	5. Being aggrieved by above order the defendants as petitioners moved to this Court and obtained this Rule.

	6. Mr Md Mamun Aleem, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that since the opposite parties filed a suit for correction of record-of-rights before establishment of the Land Survey Tribunal that suit could be brought to the tribunal under section 145A(5) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. A new and second suit for the same cause was barred by law.

	7. The learned Advocate further submits that since the Judge of the tribunal is appointed from among the Joint District Judge of the judicial service and the words “suit” “judgment” and “decree” have been used in section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the tribunal may be declared as a civil court and judgment, decree and order of the tribunal may be made subject to appeallate and revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. In support of above submissions the learned Advocate refers to the case laws reported in 17 BLC (AD) 50, 51 DLR (AD) 228, 10 DLR 527 and 68 DLR 463.

	8. Mrs. Shuchira Hossain, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos.1-8 submits that the learned Judge of the tribunal has rightly rejected the petition and the order of the Tribunal is not subject to revisional jurisdiction of this Court. As such, this Civil Revision is not tenable in law and the Rule is liable to be discharged.

	9. Considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties, perused the judgments and order of the courts below and other materials on record.

	10. At the outset it is to be mentioned that Chapter XVIIA of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was introduced in the above Act by Act No. IX of 2004 for establishment of land Survey Tribunal for entertaining only the suits arising out of final publication of the last revised record-of-rights. In 2004 the last revised record-of-right was the Bangladesh survey or BS khatian. The land survey tribunal has been vested with jurisdiction to determine the correction or falsity of BS khatians. The tribunal has no jurisdiction to determine or declare right to property or right to office which a Civil Court has.

	11. It turns out from record that Title Suit No.1105 of 2008 was filed for two reliefs. Firstly, declaration of title and secondly for further declaration that RS khatian prepared for above land is erroneous and not binding upon the plaintiffs. Since Title Suit No.1105 of 2008 was not filed challenging the correctness of BS khatian above suit was beyond the jurisdiction of the Land Survey Tribunal.

	12. Since the Land Survey Tribunal is authorized only to determine the correctness of latest survey record-of-rights and not other suits or cases and the tribunal is not a civil court the filing of a petition under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the tribunal is misconceived.

	13. The right to appeal or revision are creations for statute. Section 145B and 145C provides a special procedure and forum for challenging the judgments and orders passed by the Land Survey Tribunal. The tribunal is not a Civil Court and the statute creating the Tribunal does not provide for appeal or revision to the High Court Division.

14. As mentioned above a Tribunal is empowered only to give decision as to correctness or falsity of the BS khatian and not on any other subject. A record-of-right or khatian is not a deed of title. A khatian merely provides a presumption as to possession which is rebuttable by legal evidence. It is well settled that none is required to resort to remedial measures for correction of erroneously prepared record-of-rights unless someone threatens or interested to threaten his title on the basis of wrong record-of-rights. A dispute as to title as to any immovable property can be adjudicated by a Civil Court. Now the question is would it be feasible and useful to make the judgments and orders of the Tribunal subject to the appellate and orders of the Tribunal subject to the appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division? In my opinion the answer should be negative. If a suit is dismissed by the competent Civil Court with an appropriate civil suit for declaration of his title or declaration of title and recovery of possession for the disputed property.

	15. As such this civil revision from an order of the Land Survey Tribunal is not tenable in law. The case laws referred to above by the learned Advocate for the petitioners have no relevance with the facts and circumstances of this case.

	16. In above view of the matter I am unable to find any substance in this civil revision and the Rule issued in this connection is liable to be discharged.

	17. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

	18. The interim order passed at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

	Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted down at once.

	End.

full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, J: The instant reference to a larger Bench has been made seeking a correct interpretation of section 194 of the Customs Act, 1969. Since all the writ petitions involve similar questions of law and fact, they were heard together and this single judgment will govern each of the twelve writ petitions. 

2. A brief statement with regard to the factual aspect of each of the case is called for.

3. In Writ Petition No. 12424 of 2017, the facts are as follows : 
The petitioner company is engaged in manufacturing of garments accessories, which is supplied to 100% export oriented readymade garments industries. Whilst the petitioner was carrying on his business, the officials of respondent No. 2 carried out an inspection at the petitioner's bonded warehouse on 16-11-2015 and found shortage 4,07,688.02 Kg and an excess amount of 29,477.93 Kg of different raw materials as per the Bond Register, valued at Taka 2,09,24,784.17, with a duty payable thereon amounting to Taka 1,02,86,435.19. 

4. On the basis of the report submitted by the Inspection team, respondent No. 2 issued a demand-cum-show cause notice dated 3-4-2016 asking the petitioner why it should not be held liable for punishment under section 156(1), Table Clauses 1, 51, 51A, 61 and 90 for violation of sections 86, 97, 144 and section 13(1) of the Customs Act, 1969. On receipt of the said notice, the petitioner submitted a objection on 12-5-2016 refuting the allegations made in the said show cause notice. Upon conclusion of hearing, respondent No. 2 passed the Adjudication Order No. 242/Bond Circle-06/2017 dated 11-6-2017, imposing a penalty of Taka 1,00,000 in addition to the customs duty and taxes amounting to Taka 1,02,86,435.19, thereby totaling Taka 1,03,86,435.19. 

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Adjudication Order dated 11-6-2016, the petitioner preferred an appeal on 18-6-2017 before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka (briefly, the Tribunal) vide CEVT/Case(Cus)-413/2017. On the very same date, the petitioner also filed an application under the 2nd proviso of section 194(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) seeking exemption from depositing the demanded amount on the ground of hardship. After hearing the petitioner, respondent No. 1, by order dated 17-7-2017, directed the petitioner to deposit 10% cash and furnish a Bank Guarantee for 10% of the demanded amount within 1-8-2017. However, on that date, the petitioner filed an application praying for waiver of the deposit, as stated in the order dated 17-7-2017 and prayed for accepting the appeal without the deposit. However, by order dated 13-8-2017, as evidenced by Annexure D, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal on the ground of non-compliance with the order dated 17-7-2017. It is this very order of rejection of the appeal that the petitioner has sought to challenge by filing the instant writ petition. 

6. In Writ Petition No. 13416 of 2017, the petitioner, a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, is engaged in the business of manufacturing garments accessories, zipper and plastic and is duly registered with the VAT Authorities. 

7. On 11-2-2015, the petitioner filed an application before respondent No. 2 for adjustment of the export proceeds without issuing the Utilization Permission (UP) following which an inspection was carried out on 4-3-2015 at the petitioner's bonded warehouse. During the said inspection, the respondent found a shortage of 157.59 MT of raw materials as per the Bond Register, having a dutiable value of Taka 1,23,66,341.19. On the basis of the said Inspection report, respondent No. 2 issued a demand-cum-show cause notice, to which the petitioner submitted a written objection on 27-10-2015 denying the allegations made in the said show cause notice and further stating that the petitioner exported/supplied garments accessories by using the imported raw materials, without, however, obtaining any Utilization Permission, due to lack of knowledge. After concluding the hearing, respondent No. 2 passed Adjudication Order No. 19 of 2017 dated 2-3-2017, imposing a penalty of Taka 2,00,00,000 in addition to the customs duty and taxes amounting to Taka 1,23,66,341.19, thereby totaling Taka 3,23,66,341.19. 

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Adjudication order dated 2-3-2017, the petitioner preferred an appeal before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka for accepting the appeal without any deposit. However, by order dated 19-6-2017, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved thereby, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

9. In Writ Petition No. 13761 of 2017, the petitioner, a 100% export oriented company, is duly registered with the VAT Authorities. The petitioner filed an application before respondent No. 4 under section 196A of the Customs Act, 1969 (briefly, the Act) for setting aside the Order No. 38/EPZ Sodar/2017 dated 1-8-2017 directing the petitioner company to pay additional customs duty amounting to Taka 2,38,88,259.17 along with an amount of Taka 5,00,000 on account of the petitioners alleged failure to produce documentary evidence in support of the export of 6,588.10 Kg of imported duplex board and 4,67,560 Kg of liner paper. At the same time, the petitioner also made a prayer for dispensing with the statutory deposit, required to be paid at the time of filing the appeal on the ground of hardship. By order dated 28-9-2017, respondent No. 4 rejected the application and directed the petitioner to deposit 10% of the demanded amount in cash and 10% in Bank Guarantee, amounting to Taka 47,77,651.82 by 4-10-2017, failing which the appeal was to stand dismissed. Being aggrieved thereby, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule along with the order of stay of the proceeding of CEVT Case No. 607 of 2017. 

10. In Writ Petition No. 13987 of 2017, the petitioner is a 100% export oriented manufacturer of garments accessories. On 8-12-2016, on the basis of secret information, a team from the Customs Bond Commissionrate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's factory and found a shortage of 1) 8613 Kg of PP to 1550 of duplex board, with a total dutiable value of Taka 15,01,178. Respondent No. 1 issued a showcause notice on 2-2-2017 upon the petitioner 2-2-2017, directing the petitioner to file a reply with 15 days thereof. By Order No. 35 of 2017 dated 28-5-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-parte, imposing a penalty of Taka 15,00,000 and also imposed of a duty of Taka 6,55,117.20 and directed the petitioner to deposit the same through Treasury chalan within 15 days. Challenging the order dated 28-5-2018, the petitioner filed an appeal 4-6-2017, being No. CEVT/Case/Cus 383/2017 on before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. At the same time, the petitioner also filed an application for accepting the appeal without any deposit on the ground of hardship. By order dated 18-7-2017, respondent No. 1 dismissed the appeal on account of the petitioner's failure to make the statutory deposit. Being aggrieved thereby, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

11. In Writ Petition No. 13989 of 2017, the petitioner is engaged in the business of manufacturing and export of garments accessories. It is a 100% export oriented industries. On 16-2-2016, a Preventive Team of the Customs. Bond Commissionarate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's industry and allegedly found shortage of 14,248 MT of Art Card, having total payable duty of Taka 8,26,668.96. On 23-10-2016, respondent No. 1 issued show cause notice upon the petitioner directing him to file a reply within 15 days as to why penal action should not be taken against him under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act. 

12. Vide Order No. 34/2017 dated 4-5-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-parte, imposing a penalty of Taka 10,00,000 for the alleged shortage of the goods and also imposed a duty of Taka 4,85,134.85, directing the petitioner to deposit the same within 15 days. Challenging the aforesaid order dated 4-5-2017, the petitioner filed an appeal on 4-6-2010 being No. CEVT/ Case (Cus) 375/2017 under section 196A of the Customs Act before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. At the same time, the petitioner also filed an application seeking waiver on the deposit on account of hardship. However, by order dated 18-7-2017, respondent No. 1 dismissed the appeal on account of the petitioner's failure to make the statutory deposit. 

13. In Writ Petition No. 13990 of 2017, the petitioner is engaged in the business of manufacturing and exporting garments accessories. It is a 100% export oriented industries. On 2-4-2016, a Preventive Team of the Customs Bond Commissionarate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's industry and allegedly found 1) 12,899 Kg. of paper, 2) 471.716 Kg of paper and 3) 95.750 Kg of polyethylene, having payable duty amounting to Taka 2,16,51,176. On 26-4-2016, respondent No. 1 issued show cause notice upon the petitioner directing him to file a reply within 15 days as to why penal action should not be taken against him under the relevant provision of the Customs Act. 

14. Vide Order No. 30/2017 dated 24-4-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-. parte, imposing a penalty of Taka 5,00,00,000 for the alleged shortage of the goods and also imposed a duty of Taka 7,16,51,176.167, directing the petitioner to deposit the same within 15 days. Challenging the aforesaid order dated 24-4-2017, the petitioner filed CEVT/Case/(Cus)-380/2017 under section 196 A of the Customs Act before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. At the same time, the petitioner also filed an application seeking waver on the deposit on account of hardship. However, by order dated 18-7-2017, respondent No. 1 dismissed the appeal on account of the petitioner's failure to make the statutory deposit. 

15. In Writ Petition No. 13991 of 2017, the petitioner is engaged in the business of manufacturing and exporting garments accessories. It is a 100% export oriented industries. On 22-12-2016 a Preventive Team of the Customs Bond Commissionarate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's industry and allegedly found 1) 12,899 Kg. of Paper Line, 2) 83,708 Kg of LLDPE and 3) 2,27,811 Kg of P.P. Film having total payable duty amounting to Taka 2,73,64,994.53. On 29-12-2016, respondent No. I issued show cause notice upon the petitioner directing him to file a reply within 15 days as to why penal action should not be taken against him under the relevant provision of the Customs Act. 

16. Vide Order No. 33/2017 dated 24-4-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-parte, imposing a penalty of Taka 2,01,79,185.59 for the alleged shortage of the goods and also imposed a duty of Taka 2,85,31,357.79, directing the petitioner to deposit the same within 15 days. Challenging the aforesaid order dated 24-4-2017, the petitioner filed CEVT/Case/(Cus)-376/2017 under section 196 A of the Customs Act before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. At the same time the petitioner also filed an application seeking waiver of the deposit required for the purpose of filing the appeal on account of hardship. However, by order dated 18-7-2017, respondent No. 1 dismissed the appeal on account of the petitioner's failure to make the statutory deposit. 

17. In Writ Petition No. 13992 of 2017, the petitioner is engaged in the business of manufacturing and export of garments accessories. It is a 100% export oriented industries. On 19-2-2017, a Preventive Team of the Customs Bond Commissionarate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's industry and allegedly found excess of 1) 9678 Kg. of Craft Liner Paper, 2) 3750 Kg of LLDPE and 3) 9678 Kg of PP Film, having payable duty amounting to Taka 9,50,291.17. On 22-2-2017, respondent No. 1 issued show cause notice upon the petitioner directing him to file a reply within 15 days as to why penal action should not be taken against him under the relevant provision of the Customs Act. 

18. Vide Order No. 111/2017 dated 27-4-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-parte imposing a penalty of Taka 15,00,000 for the alleged shortage of the goods and also imposed a duty of Taka 9,50,291.17, directing the petitioner to deposit the same within 15 days. On 19-2-2017, an Intelligence Team of the Customs Bond Commissionarate, Chittagong inspected the petitioner's industry and allegedly found shortage of 1) 3,00,785 Kg of PP Film, 2) 33,020 Kg of HIPS 3) 1,60,216 Kg of LLDPE, 4) 32,114 Kg of Duplex Board 300 GSM and 5) 7,511 Kg of Duplex Board 350 GSM, having total payable duty of Taka 1,44,22,470.20. On 22-2-2017, respondent No. 1 issued show cause notice upon the petitioner directing him to file a reply within 15 days as to why penal action should not be taken against him under the relevant provision of the Customs Act. 

26. Vide Order No. 31/2017 dated 24-7-2017, respondent No. 1 adjudicated the matter ex-parte, imposing a penalty of Taka 50,00,000 for the alleged shortage of the goods and also imposed a duty of Taka 1,44,22,470.20, directing the petitioner to deposit the same within 15 days. Challenging the aforesaid order dated 24-4-2017, the petitioner filed an appeal on 4-6-2017, being No. CEVT/Case/(Cus)-382/2017 under section 196 A of the Customs Act before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. At the same time, the petitioner also filed an application seeking waiver on the deposit for the purpose of filing the appeal on account of hardship. However, by order dated 18-7-2017, respondent No. 1 dismissed the appeal on account of the petitioner's failure to make the statutory deposit. 

27. Mr Tanjib-ul Alam, the learned Advocate appears along Mr MA Hannan, Mr M. Ataul Gani, Mr Bahadur Shah, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioners in all the writ petitions, while the Rule is being opposed by Ms. Israt Jahan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appears along with Ms. Most. Khairun Nessa, Mr Swarup Kanti Deb and Mr Abul Kalam Khan, the learned Assistant Attorney Generals on behalf of respondent No. 1. 

28. The common submission advanced by the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners is that the Tribunal passed the impugned orders without application of mind. It has further been contended that the respective petitioners filed applications seeking waiver from making the statutory deposit on the ground of hardship. However, without taking into account this particular aspect of the case, i.e. the hardship of the petitioners, the Tribunal passed the orders in a mechanical and arbitrary manner. Referring to various orders passed by the Tribunal in respect of other appeals, the learned Advocates have argued strenously that while granting exemption, the Tribunal acted in an arbitrary manner and applied a "pick and choose" policy in as much as, in some cases, the appeals were allowed to be filed with a deposit of only 5%, while in other cases, the appeals were directed to be filed upon payment of 25% on the demanded amount. The learned Advocates have submitted in a uniform voice that the gross variation in respect of the percentage of the deposit ranging from 5% to 25% indicates clearly that the Tribunal was not consistent and even handed in considering the applications of hardship filed by the respective petitioners. 

29. Referring to various judgments passed by this Division, the learned Advocates have also tried to impress upon us that while dealing with similar matters, the petitioners were directed to pay varying amounts of deposit, starting from 0% and going upto 25%. 

30. Referring to section 194 of the Customs Act, 1969 (briefly the Act), it has been argued at the Bar that the second proviso to section 194 of the Act provides for granting waiver/exemption from making the deposit of duty demanded by the Customs Authority. However, while passing the impugned orders, the Tribunal failed to make a proper assessment of each individual case and applied a pick and choose policy in granting exemptions, which is manifested in the respective orders. 

31. Appearing in opposition to all the Rules, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the Tribunal has been vested with the power to decide the issue of hardship, which is essentially a question of fact that has to be determined upon consideration of the facts and circumstances of each individual case. The learned DAG submits forcefully that this Court, in exercise of the writ jurisdiction, is precluded from undertaking an exercise which involves ascertainment of the factual aspect of a case. She submits that since the issue of hardship is essentially a question of fact, which varies from case to case, the Tribunal has been vested with the sole authority to decide the issue of granting exemptions in appropriate cases. 

32. At the very outset of the discussion, it would be pertinent to refer to section 194 of the Act, which reads as under : 
"194. Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied—(1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196A against decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer the duty demanded or the penalty levied; 
Provided that such person may, instead of deposing as aforesaid the entire amount of the penalty, deposit only fifty per cent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance; 
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. 
(2) If, upon an appeal, it is decided that the whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty or penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be." 

33. In this reference before us, we are primarily concerned with the 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Act. 

34. A careful and close reading of the 2nd proviso of section 194 leaves no room for doubt that the power to dispense with the deposit, either unconditionally or upon imposition of conditions, has been left to the "sole discretion of the Tribunal." 

35. It is the cardinal rule of interpretation that the words used in a Statute are to be interpreted as it is, and not what they ought to be. The Legislature, in their wisdom, and in our view quiet correctly, stipulated that the discretion to allow dispensation with the deposit is vested only with the Tribunal. This is apparent from the very last sentence, which reads, "it may dispensed with such deposit, either unconditionally or submit to such conditions as it may deem fit and proper." (emphasis added on the word "it") By using the word "it", the Legislatures have very clearly expressed their intention that it is the Tribunal and the Tribunal alone which is vested with the sole authority to dispense with the deposit or otherwise accept an appeal upon such conditions as it deems fit to impose with regard to such deposit. The use of the word "it", in our view, implies that the jurisdiction or authority of this Court to interfere in matters of granting exemption on the ground of hardship has been excluded. I am fortified in any view by a decision which dates back to more than half a century in the case of Pandyan Insurance Company Limited vs KJ Khambatta and others, reported in AIR 1955 (Bombay) 241. While delivering the judgment, Chagla, CJ observed as under : 
"If the law confers discretion upon an office or upon a tribunal it is for that officer or that tribunal to exercise its discretion. It is not for the High Court to exercise this discretion for him. In the case of discretion it is very rarely and under great limitations that the High Court interferes." 

36. While dealing with the issue of the Tribunals jurisdiction/authority to deal with the factual aspect of a case, the Supreme Court of India, in the case of State of Andhra Pradesh and others vs Chitra Venkata Rao, reported in AIR 1975 (SC) 2151, held: 
"The findings of fact reached by an inferior court or Tribunal as a result of the appreciation of evidence are not re-opened or questioned in writ proceedings." 

37. In that case, the Court further held: 
"A finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal cannot be challenged on the ground that the relevant and material evidence adduced before the Tribunal is insufficient or inadequate to sustain a finding. The adequacy or sufficiency of evidence led on a point and the inference of fact to be drawn from the said finding are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Tribunal." 

38. In the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. and another, Tutelor Oil Service Pvt Co Ltd. and another, National Warehouse and another vs Assistant Controller of Customs, reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 227, relied on by the petitioners, the Apex Court, while allowing the appeal, held as under : 
"Payment of the demanded sum, as a condition precedent as required under Section 194 of the Act for filing an appeal, would have surely caused a great hardship to the appellants. The appellants' prayer for exemption from depositing the demanded sum was rather arbitrarily rejected by the appellate authority." 

39. In our view, the aforesaid decision of the Apex Court is distinguishable from the present case before us for the simple reason that in the decision referred to above, no exemption was granted and the appellant's application of hardship was rejected summarily. In the present writ petitions, the petitioners were granted exemptions, albeit of varying degrees. It is the non-deposit of the exempted amount which led to the rejection of the appeals by the Tribunal. 

40. When a Tribunal is set up under an Act for adjudicating the disputes between the contending sides relating to the rights and priviledges conferred under the Act, unless otherwise provided by law, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal is exclusive. However, this should not be inferred as a total ouster of the Court's jurisdiction. Where the Tribunal exceeds its authority or where if fails to exercise its power in accordance with law or where it has acted malafide, in such cases, this Court can and should interfere. 

41. In our view, this Court does not have the jurisdiction to substitute its own decision for that of the Tribunal in granting exemption in respect of the applications for hardship filed by the respective petitioners. In other words, the 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Act vests absolute and total authority upon the Tribunal to decide the question of hardship, giving due consideration to each and every case on merit. Therefore, the logical inference from our discussion leads us to the conclusion that the instant reference be answered in the negative and accordingly, it is so answered. Consequently, the Rules issued in all the writ petitions are liable to be discharged. 

42. Accordingly, the Rules issued in all the writ petitions stand discharged. 

43. The interim orders, granted at the time of issuance of the Rules, are hereby recalled and vacated. 

44. Before parting with the case, we wish to make certain observations with regard to the issue that we are being called upon to decide. 

45. It is apparent that while disposing of the hardship applications filed on behalf of the respective petitioners, the Tribunal did not act in a uniform manner and did not apply a uniform percentage while granting exemptions. Regrettably, this Court did likewise. This certainly cannot be the purport and intent of the law. 

46. We, therefore, direct the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs to take proper and effective steps to incorporate necessary amendments in the Customs Act, 1969 so as to bring a uniformity in the application of the law with regard to granting of waiver by the Tribunal while deciding applications seeking exemption from making the statutory deposit on the ground of hardship. 

47. There will be no order as to cost. 

The office is directed to communicate the order. 

End.

full_judgment:
Borhanuddin, J: In this application under Article 102(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Constitution the petitioner Md Sarwar Hossain challenged the order dated 21-1-2008 passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal in CEVT/CASE (CUS)-65/2007 dismissing the appeal for default on the ground of not taking step by the appellant at the time of hearing of the appeal. 

2. Petitioner's case in brief is that the petitioner, a citizen of Bangladesh, in course of his business opened a Letter of Credit being No. 094105010025 dated 20-3-2005 for importing Synthetic Sharees from India under HS Code No.6204.43.00; After arrival of the goods at Benapole Land Station, the petitioner through C&F agent submitted Bill of Entry No. C-9837 dated 29-3-2005 alongwith necessary documents for assessment of the goods; Though the Customs Authority conducted 100% physical examination of the goods and found the same as per declaration but the customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of previous CRP value which is four times higher than the declared value and also imposed a fine for importing the goods without pre-shipment inspection; Under compelling circumstances, the petitioner released the goods on payment of entire amount of duties and taxes including fine and Customs Authority issued release order; After releasing the goods the petitioner loaded the Sharees in the covered van; While the covered vans came out from the gate of the customs house then the intelligence of the customs authority stopped the vans on the plea that there might be excess sharees in the vans; After re-cheking in the customs house premises they found the goods as per declaration; Inspite of that the customs authority arbitrarily detained the goods; Finding no other way the petitioner filed writ petition No. 2393 of 2005 before the High Court Division and obtained a Rule; After contested hearing a Division Bench of this court made the rule absolute with an observation that: 
"The action of the respondent No.3 in taking back the released imported goods as contained in covered vans Nos. Dhaka Metro Ta 11-3208 and Dhaka Metro Ta 11-2593 in the Customs House premises at Benapole and the subsequent action of the respondent in withholding the said goods of the petitioner as per Bill of Entry No.C-9837 dated 29-3-2005 are declared to have been done without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to release the goods of the petitioner as mentioned above forthwith on production of the certified copy of this judgment keeping one piece of sharee as sample from each of the five categories as mentioned in the Atak Pratebedan vide Annexure-T to the Writ petition. We make it very clear that if so advised the customs authority may proceed against the petitioner under section 83A of the Customs Act, but they must follow the law very strictly". 

3. After receiving a copy of the judgment the customs authority released the goods keeping five pieces of Sharees and thereafter on 16-5-2005 issued a notice under section 83A of the Customs Act upon the petitioner demanding Taka 68,15,770.85 as short levied duties and taxes; The petitioner filed application for supply the basis of the re-assessment and after about one year the petitioner supplied an attested copy relating to basis of re-assessment stating that a team of the Customs House, Benapole inspected Khulna New Market and on the basis of the information gathered from the market reassessed value of the goods following deductive method as per Valuation Rules, 2000. 

4. Being aggrieved by the notice, the petitioner filed appeal being No.65 of 2007 before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal on 22-1-2007 under Rule 13 of the Valuation Rules, 2000. Tribunal vide notice dated 14-1-2008 directed the petitioner to comply with the provisions of section 194 of the Customs Act directing to deposit fine through Bank Guarantee and cash. After receiving the notice the petitioner filed an application on 23-1-2008 before the Tribunal stating that the petitioner filed appeal against the fixation of value under Rule 13 of the Valuation Rules and no fine was imposed upon the petitioner as such section 194 of the Customs Act is not applicable in this case and also requested the Tribunal to admit the case for hearing without direction to deposit fine amount. The Tribunal fixed 24-1-2008 for hearing on the point of limitation and depositing money under section 194 of the Customs Act. Though the Tribunal fixed hearing at 10-00 am and the learned advocate for the petitioner waited till 1-30 pm but the Tribunal did not resume and, as such, learned lawyer filed an application for adjournment but the Tribunal without considering the bonafide cause stated in the application rejected the application and also dismissed the appeal for not taking step vide impugned order dated 24-1-2008 which is reproduced below:
ট্রাইব্যুনালের আদেশ
মামলাটি অদ্য তামাদি ও টাকা জমার বিষয়ে শুনানীর জন্য দিন ধার্য আছে। আপীলকারী সময়ের আবেদন জানান। তাছাড়া ইতিপূর্বেও বহুবার বিভিন্ন অজুহাতে সময়ের আবেদন দাখিল করেন। আবেদন নামঞ্জুর। আপীলকারীকে প্রতিকার নেওয়ার জন্য নির্দেশ দেয়া হলো । কিন্তু আপীলকারী কোনরুপ প্রতিকার নেয়নি । অতএব,
আদেশ হইর যে,
অত্র আপীল মোকদ্দমাটি প্রতিকারের অভাবে খারিজ করা হইল ।

5. Thereafter, the respondent again issued notice on 24-3-2008 upon the petitioner demanding the amount under section 83A of the Customs Act. 

6. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order passed by the Tribunal as well as subsequent demand, the petitioner moved this writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present rule alongwith an order of stay relating to demand dated 24-3-2008. 

7. Mr ARM Qayyum Khan, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the impugned order passed by the Tribunal is ex facie illegal inasmuch as pursuant to section 196B of the Customs Act, 1969 the Tribunal has no power to dismiss the appeal for default on the ground of non appearance of the petitioner as such the order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. He also submits that the Tribunal under section 196B of the Customs Act cannot dismiss the appeal without touching merit of the appeal as such order passed by the Tribunal is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of the Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras vs Chenniappa Mudaliar, reported in AIR (SC) 1068 and an unreported judgment passed by the Gujrat High Court in the case of Viral Laminates Pvt. Ltd. vs Union of India. 

8. On the other hand, Mr Md Humayun Kabir learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.2 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition submits that the Tribunal has given ample opportunity to the appellant-petitioner but the appellant did not take any step and, as such, the Tribunal justly and legally passed the order. 

9. Heard learned advocate for the petitioner and learned Assistant Attorney-General for the respondent No.2. Perused the writ petition and the annexures appended thereof alongwith affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.2 and also the decisions cited by the learned advocate for the petitioner. 

10. The moot question is to be decided in this case whether Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal can pass an order dismissing the appeal for default for non appearance of the appellant without touching merit of the appeal. Power to pass orders by the Customs Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal provides in section 196B of the Customs Act, 1969, which is as follows: 
196B. Orders of Appellate Tribunal:- (1) The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving the parties to the appeal an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders thereon as it think fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or order appealed against or may refer the case back to the authority which passed such decision or order with such directions as the Appellate Tribunal may think fit, for a fresh adjudication or decision, as the case may be, after taking additional evidence, if necessary. 

11. It appears from the impugned order as quoted above that the Appellate Tribunal did not give any decision regarding the issue whether reassessment under section 83A was legally done in the light of the judgment passed in writ petition No. 2393 of 2005, Although it appears even from the plain reading of section 196B of the Customs Act, the Tribunal ought to have given decision after giving the parties to the appeal an opportunity of being heard. Appellate Tribunal under section 196B is not empowered to dismiss the appeal pending before it for default simpliciter for the reason of non appearance. The law requires that a decision will have to be given on the issue and having not been given in the instant case the impugned order passed by the Tribunal is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

12. In the case of The Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras vs Chenniappa Mudaliar, reported in AIR (SC) 1068, Indian Supreme Court arrived at a finding: "The scheme of the provisions of the Act relating to the Appellate Tribunal apparently is that it has to dispose of an appeal by making such orders as it thinks fit on the merits." 

13. Though the above case arose out of Income Tax Act where rules framed under the Act and Rule 24 of the Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1946 enables the Tribunal to dismiss the appeal for default of non appearance and the same is challenged in the case as ultra virus of the provisions of section 33 of the Income Tax Act, 1992. 

14. Section 33(4) of the Income Tax Act empowers the Tribunal to dispose of the appeal on its merits, whether there being an appearance of the party before it or not and thereafter rule in its present form amended in the year 1948, in so far as it enables the dismissal of an appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal for default of appearance of the appellant will. Therefore, be ultra-virus as being in conflict with the provisions of section 33(4) of the act. Brief facts of the case are that the assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. After some adjournments the appeal was finally fixed for hearing on August. On that date no one was present on behalf of the assessee nor was there any application for adjournment. 

15. After thorough discussions Indian Supreme Court arrived at a finding: "Assuming that for the aforesaid reasons the Appellate Tribunal is competent to set-aside an order dismissing an appeal for default in exercise of its inherent power there are serious difficulties in upholding the validity of Rule 24. It clearly comes into conflict with sub-section (4) of Section 33 and in the event of repugnancy between the substantive provisions of the Act and a rule it is the rule which must give way to the provision of the Act." 

16. In our Customs Act, it is provided in section 196C(6) that subject to the provisions of this Act, the Appellate Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure and the procedure of the Benches thereof in all matters arising out of the exercise of its powers or of the discharge of its functions, including the places at which the Benches shall hold their sittings. But unfortunately this provision of law is not complied with till date. 

17. In the case of Viral Laminates Pvt. Ltd. vs Union of India, the Gujrat High Court after discussing section 129B(1) of the Customs Act, which runs as follows: "129B(1)—The Appellate Tribunal may after giving the parties to the appeal, an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or order appealed against or may refer the case back to the authority which passed such decision or order with such direction as the Appellate Tribunal may think fit, for a fresh adjudication or decision, as the case may be, after taking additional evidence, if necessary." 
Arrived at a finding: 
"129B (1) of the Customs Act and in particular use of the word "thereon" that the Tribunal has to go into the correctness or otherwise of the points decided by the departmental authority in the light of the submissions made by the appellant. This can only be done by giving a decision on the merits on questions of fact and law and not by merely disposing of the appeal on the ground that the party concerned has failed to appear." 
Further observed that: 
"The use of expression "thereon" means that the appellate tribunal has to pass order on the subject matter of the appeal and on the issue in controversy. The expression "thereon" does not mean that the Appellate Tribunal can pass an order of dismissal for default of appearance, since such an order has nothing to do with the matter in controversy. Having regard to the scheme of the Excise Act as well as the Customs Act, there is no manner of doubt that the appeal filed before the Appellate Tribunal has got to be disposed of on merits and not for default of appearance of the appellant. Thus the Appellate Tribunal has to decide the issue ex-parte, but dismissing appeal for non appearance does not seem to be legally or even on equity grounds, correct." 

18. The language of section 196B of our Customs Act and the language of section 129B(1) of the Indian Customs Act are almost similar. When section 196B mandates that the Appellate Tribunal confirm, modify and annul the decision or order appealed against or may refer the case back on remand after giving the parties an opportunity of hearing, Tribunal cannot dismiss the appeal for default on the ground of non-appearance or not taking step. 

19. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case as well as provisions of law and the decisions referred above we are of the view that the order passed by the Tribunal in dismissing the appeal for default without touching merit of the appeal is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

20. Accordingly, subsequent demand dated 24-3-2008 by the respondent No.3 Joint Commissioner of Customs is also illegal and without lawful authority. 

21. The rule is made Absolute. 

22. Order dated 24-1-2008 passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. As such demand dated 24-3-2008 is also declared illegal and beyond jurisdiction. 

23. No order as to cost. 

24. The respondent No.1 Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, is hereby directed to hear and dispose of the appeal under nothi No. CEVT/CASE (CUS)-65/2007 on merit by giving an opportunity of hearing to the parties and also producing additional evidence, if necessary, in accordance with law, within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt copy of this judgment. 

25. The respondent No. 3 is directed not to take further steps before order passed by the Tribunal on merit. 

Communicate a copy of this judgment at once. 

End.
