The petitioner in reply is dismissive of the approach taken by the Respondent No. 3, Commissioner as being "misleading" inasmuch as there is an admission of the existence of 1109 EXPs on the one hand placed incongruously with an allegation that 31,52,741.53 kg chemicals (being the total imported quantity during 2015-2017) have been used against only 4,42,707.53 kg finished goods, thereby, raising concern about the status of exports under 281 EXPs. In reply it is stated that during the 2015-2017 period the petitioner imported a total of 31,52,741.53 Kg chemicals which have been used to manufacture goods exported under 1066 EXPs. It is suggested that if the customs authority had taken care to "spread over" the said quantity of chemicals on the total number of 1066 EXPs it would readily be found that the chemicals in their entirety have been properly utilized in the exported manufactured products during 2015-2017 making the allegation of evasion of duty and taxes for that period unfounded and baseless.
15. It is against this factual milieu playing out in the form of a highly contentions case that this Court has now to consider the extent to which the Tribunal had a legal duty imposed on it to ensure the petitioner's unhindered access to the statutory appellate forum and to what extent the Tribunal's order of appeal rejection constitutes a violation of such duty.
16. This Court notes at the outset that the discretionary power to dispose of hardship applications of an appellant is statutorily left solely to the Tribunal under section 194 of the Act free of interference by this Court should of course such authority have been lawfully discharged in accordance with law. That in our view can be the only true interpretation of the larger bench's finding in the above quoted judgment in Writ Petition No. 12424 of 2017 that the Tribunal nevertheless must "decide the question of hardship, giving due consideration to each and every case on merit." Conversely, if the Tribunal fails to properly exercise its discretionary power in disposing of a hardship application, this Court can, of course, scrutinize such failure in judicial review.
17. It is to be noted too in this context that section 194 neither prescribes any procedural formalities nor authorizes the government to make necessary rules governing the exercise of discretionary authority thereunder. Consequentially, the fear is that such provision may become an obvious vehicle for arbitrariness. It cannot be gainsaid that the notion of procedural fairness as part of the common law tradition is deeply rooted in our law and lies at the heart of the judicial function and conditions and qualifies the exercise of a large array of administrative powers affecting the rights, duties, privileges and immunities of individuals and organizations.
18. Contextualizing the petitioner's case as above, the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Md Yousuf Ali submits that since the application for dispensation of pre-deposit pending appeal before the Tribunal is an interim application, the same has to be considered and disposed of by applying a fair procedure like the disposal of any other interim application in any suit or proceeding pending before any court or tribunal. In doing so therefore, considering the prima facie merit of the pending appeal emerges too as an essential ingredient for the rule of fairness to prevail.
19. This Court notes that in our jurisdiction there exists no judicial precedent shedding light on the term "hardship" or "undue hardship", thereby, leading this Court in this regard to explore judicial pronouncements in other jurisdictions with comparable legislative history or common legislative standards. It is here that Mr Yousuf Ali .has highlighted the Indian experience necessitating a comparative analysis of section 194 of the Act with the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Central Excise Act, 1944 applicable in India coupled with an analysis too of the trajectory of the metamorphosis of the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 (hereinafter referred to as necessary as the "Indian Customs Act" for ease of reference) and other relevant statutes in India.
20. In reiteration, section 194 of the Act reads as follows:
"194. Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied : (1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196A against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer fifty per cent of the duty demanded or fifty per cent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be:
Provided that such person may, instead of depositing the amount of the penalty as aforesaid, deposit only fifty percent thereof and furnish' a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance:
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty imposed will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may  dispense with such deposit either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose.
(2) lf, upon an appeal it is decided that the whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty or penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be."
21. Section 194 significantly represents almost verbatim as its highlighted proviso above that of section 129 of the Indian Customs Act, 1962 as it existed prior to eventual amendments as later noted:
"129(1) Where the decision or order appealed against related to any duty demanded in respect of goods which are not under the control of customs authorities or any penalty levied under this Act, any person desirous of appealing against such decision or order shall, pending the appeal, deposit with the proper officer the duty demanded or the penalty levied;
Provided that where in any particular case the appellate authority is of opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may in its discretion dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit.
(2) If upon any such appeal it is decided that the whole or any portion of such duty or penalty was not leviable, the proper officer shall return to the appellant such amount of duty or penalty as was not leviabie.”
22. In 1980 the above provisions of the  Customs Act, 1962 were amended with a view to balancing the element of an applicant's “undue hardship” with that of safeguarding the “interests of revenue”:
“129E. DEPOSIT, PENDING APPEAL, OF DUTY AND INTEREST DEMANDED OR PENALTY LEVIED.—
Where in any appeal under this Chapter, the decision or order appealed against relates to any duty and interest demanded  “in respect of goods which are not under the control of the customs authorities or any penalty levied under this Act, the person desirous of appealing against such decision or order shall, pending the appeal, deposit with the proper officer the duty and interest demanded or the penalty levied.
Provided that where in any particular case, the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal is of opinion that the deposit of duty and interest demanded or penalty levied would cause undue hardship to such person, the Commissioner (Appeals) or, as the case may be, the Appeilate Tribunal may dispense with such deposit subject to such conditions as he or it may deem fit to impose so as to safeguard the interests of revenue.”
23. Finally, in 2014 section 129E was completely overhauled in favour of an absolute requirement for a pre-deposit at a fixed rate injecting simultaneously the notion of a conditional appeal into the law as follows:
“129E.—Deposit of certain percentage of duty demanded or penalty imposed before filing appeal—The Tribunal or the Commissioner (Appeals), as the case may be, shall not entertain any appeal,—
(i) under sub-section (1) of section 128, unless the appellant has deposited seven and a half per cent. of the duty, in case where duty or duty and penalty are in dispute, or penalty, where such penalty is in dispute, in pursuance of a decision or an order passed by an officer of customs lower in rank than the Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs;
ii) against the decision or order referred to in clause (a) of sub- section (1) of section 129A, unless the appellant has deposited seven and a half per cent. of the duty, in case where duty or duty and penalty are in dispute, or penalty, where such penalty is in dispute, in pursuance of the decision or order appealed against;
iii) against the decision or order seterred to in clause (b) of sub- section (1) of section 129A, unless the appellant has deposited ten per cent. of the duty, in case where duty or duty and penalty are in dispute, or penalty, where such penalty is in dispute, in pursuance of the decision or order appealed against:
Provided that the amount required to be deposited under this section shall net exceed rupees ten crores:
Provided further that the provisions of this section shall not apply to the stay applications and appeals pending before any appellate authority prior to the commencement of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 (25 of 2014).”
24. Likewise, prior to a contemporaneous overhauling of the Central Excise Act, 1944 of India in 2014 on similar lines, section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 provided as under in the same vain as section 194 of the Act:
35F—Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied—Where in any appeal under this Chapter, the decision or order appealed against relates to any duty demanded in respect of goods which are not under the control of Central Excise authorities or any penalty levied under this ' Act, the person desirous of appealing against such decision or order shall, pending the appeal, deposit with the adjudicating authority the duty demanded  or the penalty levied:
Provided that where in any particular case the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal is of opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty  levied would cause undue hardship to such  person, the Commissioner (Appeals) or, as  the case may be, the Appellate Tribunal,  may dispense with such deposit subject to  such conditions as he or it may deem fit to  impose so as to safeguard the interest of revenue:
Provided further that where an  _ application is filed before the  Commissioner (Appeals) for dispensing  with the deposit of duty demanded or  penalty levied under the first proviso, the  Commissioner (Appeals) shall, where it is  possible to do so, decide such application  within thirty days from the date of its filing.
25. No wonder, therefore, and given the similarities of the above provisions, the Supreme Court of India has given a clear observation in Indu Nissan Oxo Chemicals Ind. Ltd. vs Union of India (UOI) and others [MANU/ 5C/4581/2007} that the parameters of deciding the issue of undue hardship under the Central Excise Act, 1944 and the Customs Act, 1962 remain the same.
26. A comparative analysis further of legislative enactments and their subsequent metamorphosis in the Bangladesh and Indian jurisdiction reveals that although the Indian statutes have been amended several times touching on the issue of the undue hardship of the appellant in making a pre-deposit, our law has been amended only once in 2004 and that too only with regard to the quantum of the required deposit, i.e., before amendment of the Act in 2004, subject to the proviso, an appellant was required to deposit 100% of demanded duty or penalty levied. By the amendment in 2004 the quantum of deposit has been decreased to 50% keeping the second proviso to section 194(1) intact otherwise.
27. It is evident, therefore, that prior to 2014, in both the Bangladesh and Indian jurisdictions, the Tribunal had the authority to dispense with the entire pre-deposit requirement upon consideration of the undue hardship of an appellant. While the Indian Tribunal could grant an entire waiver of the pre-deposit requirement subject to safe- guarding the interest of the revenue, a tribunal in Bangladesh remains empowered to grant a total waiver unconditionally if a case of undue hardship is made out. The question now is how the Tribunal should determine whether a case of undue hardship has been duly and satisfactorily established by an appellant.
28. Normally, the term “hardship” refers to financial hardship. In the English jurisdiction, the Upper Tribunal Tax and Chancery Chamber in The Commissioner for her Majesty's Revenue and Customs vs Elbrook (Cash & Carry) Ltd and Totel Ltd. R vs The First Tier Tribunal [MANU/UKWA/ 0831/2012] explained the term “hardship” only with regard to financial hardship. Attaching the term “sindue” to “hardship” the laws in both our and Indian jurisdictions, therefore, use the term “undue hardship” as connotes a greater degree of deprivation relative to mere “hardship”. In this context Mr Ali submits satisfactorily that for a financial hardship to be undue, it has to be shown that the facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant or justify the burden of pre- deposit requirement to be foisted on an appellant.
29. It is seen that historically the Indian ‘Supreme Court analysed the severity of hardship or undue hardship in terms of the prima facie merit of the pending appeal before the tribunal considering the hardship application. According to the Indian Supreme Court, it will always be an undue hardship to an appellant to make the pre-deposit when he has a good prima facie case before the tribunal. Accordingly, the existence of a strong prima facie case cancels out or provides good reason against requiring an appellant to make a prior deposit. In Bongaigaon Refinery and Petrochem. Lid. vs Collr. of C. Ex. [MANU/WB/0300/1992] the High Court of Calcutta held—
“ the phrase “undue hardship” would cover a case where the appellant has a strong prima facie case. The phrase also in my view covers a situation where there is an arguable case in the appeal...”
30. It was further held by the High Court of Allahabad in ITC Ltd. vs CC (Appeals) and CE [MANU/UP/0515/2003] that—
“...While considering the application for stay/waiver of a pre-deposit, as required under the law, the Court must apply its mind as to whether the appellant has a strong prima facie case on merit. In case it is covered by the judgment of a Court/Tribunal binding upon the Appellate Authority, it should apply its mind as to whether in view of the said judgment, the appellant is likely to succeed on merit. If an appellant having strong prima facie case, is asked to deposit the amount of assessment so made or penalty so levied, it would cause undue hardship to him, though there may be no financial restrain on the appellant running in a good financial condition.”
31. The Supreme Court of India has taken the similar view in Benara Valves Ltd. vs CCE and others [(2006) 13 SCC 347] where it was held inter alia-
“...if on a cursory glance it appears that the demand raised has no leg to stand, it would be undesirable to require the assessee to pay full or substantive part of the demand. Petitions for stay should not be disposed of in a routine matter unmindful of the consequences flowing from the order requiring the assessee to deposit full or part of the demand. There can be no rule of universal application in such matters and the order has to be passed keeping in view the factual scenario involved...”
32. A similar observation has also been made by the Supreme Court of India in Indu Nissan Oxo Chemicals Ind. Ltd. vs Union of India (UOI) and others.
33. In Sony India Limited vs Union of India and others [MANU/DE/0953/2000} the High Court of Delhi held as follows:
“In our view the above factors make out a strong prima facie case in favor of the petitioners. Accordingly, we direct that the appeal filed by the petitioners before the CEGAT be heard on merits without insisting on any amount being deposited by the petitioners by way of pre-deposit. The impugned order dated 17th September, 1999 passed by the Tribunal directing the petitioners to make a pre-deposit of Rs. 20 crores is hereby set-aside. The petitioners will be entitled to have the appeal heard without making any pre-deposit. Petition stands disposed of. No costs.”
34. The High Court of Delhi in arriving at the above decision followed the precedent in Union of India and others vs Sony India Ltd. [(2002) 10 SCC 757] in which the Supreme Court of India observed—
“When a Writ Petition is disposed of, we would expect, however briefly, some discussion of what the “facts and circumstances of the case” are, a reference to the circulars that are made the basis of the decision and some explanation how the terms of these circulars apply to the facts and circumstances of the case. An order of the kind under challenge disposing of the writ petition cannot be sustained.”
35. The Supreme Court of India also held in Mehsana Dist. Co-op. Milk P.U. Ltd. vs Union of India (UOD [MANU/SC/0423/2003} as follows—
“The Appellate Authority should have addressed its mind to the prima facie merits of the appellants’ case and upon being satisfied of the same determined the quantum of deposit taking into consideration the financial hardship and other such relevant factors...”
36. It is to be noted too that due to the injudiciousness and arbitrariness of the appellate authority in deciding the hardship applications without considering the prima facie case, the Indian legislature has amended the relevant provisions of both the Customs Act, 1962 and Central Excise Act, 1944 in 2014 requiring an appellant to pre-deposit a fixed rate of seven and a half percent of the duty, in case where duty or duty and penalty are in dispute, or penalty. But in that process, this Court is of the opinion that the right of appeal under section 129E of the Indian Customs Act has become a conditional one. ,
37. Turning to the impugned order of the Tribunal in the instant case, it appears that the Tribunal passed that order in response to the hardship application in a mechanical and slipshod manner as tantamounts to unreasonably and injudiciously penalizing the petitioner without adequate reasons given. The learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Ali submits that although in the facts the Tribunal has scaled down the pre-deposit requirement, such partial waiver does not mean that it has effectively considered the hardship application in accordance with law given that the law  requires the consideration of the prima facie merits of the petitioner’s case. In the instant case, the petitioner contends that depositing 30% of the amount of taxes and duties imposed results still in a huge burden on the petitioner and that upon consideration of the petitioner's strong prima facie case the Tribunal would have hesitated to insist upon an even 1% pre-deposit. The submission now is that since the petitioner has a strong prima facie case it is entitled to get the unconditional waiver to secure the ends of justice.
38. The prima facie case of the petitioner is that during the relevant period of 2015-2017, a total 1109 EXPs were issued by the petitioner (as admitted by the Respondents) out of which 43 EXPs were subsequently cancelled. Accordingly, the petitioner realized export proceeds only against 1066 EXPs. It follows that the lien Bank provided PRCs for an amount of $45,276,589 only in favour of the petitioner against those 1066 EXPs. We are told that for making the finished goods exported under the 1066 EXPs, the petitioner imported a total of 31,52,741.53 kg chemicals during the 2015-2017 period and duly used these in_ its manufacturing process. All that the Respondent No. 3 needed to do was to spread over the said quantity of chemicals on the total 1066 EXPs to support a finding that the entire amount of chemicals imported had been properly utilized in manufacturing the exported products during the period of 2015-2017, thereby, negating any question of evasion of duty and taxes for that period.
39. The question that also looms large in this case is whether a partial waiver of pre- deposit signifies compliance of fair procedure. In that regard the decision of the Upper Tribunal Tax and Chancery in The Commissioners for HM Revenue and Customs vs Elbrook (Cash & Carry) Ltd. [2017] UKUT 0181 (TCC) illuminates us in the following terms by declaring that a partial waiver is no waiver at all:
“Finally, we should note that the test for financial hardship is an “all or nothing” one. The only question is whether payment or deposit of the whole of the disputed tax would cause financial hardship. It is of no relevance that payment of some lesser amount might be capable of being achieved without hardship.”
40. This line of reasoning is based on a judicial appreciation that fundamentally the “test is one of capacity to pay without financial hardship, not just capacity to pay.”(Sintra Global Inc. us HMRC [2016] UKFTT 726 (TC).
<u>41. This takes us to the Chapter XIX provisions on appeals in the Act as bear a significance both procedural and substantive. It is to be remembered at the outset that the basic nature of an appeal is to secure to an appellant an unhindered access to the appellate process to its fullest statutorily sanctioned extent that may not come to be unhinged unduly on one pretext or the other. The Chapter XIX appeals provisions straddling sections 193 to 196G must, accordingly, collectively be treated as a singular process through which the appellant shall at all material times have the prospects open to ultimately address an appeal to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court as per the stipulations in sections 196D, 196F and 196G. It is in this context that the deposit requirement under section 194 attains considerable significance in this Court's view. In safeguarding both the interests of the customs authority and guarding against frivolous claims being brought before the Appellate Tribunal under section 196A the pre- deposit requirement in the scheme of Chapter XIX is not intended in this Court’s opinion to put a brake as such on the appellate process midway, thereby, negating due access to the next higher appellate stage. The Tribunal must not lose sight of due substantive disposal of appeals that of their own permit of consideration by the next higher appellate authority. The section 194 pre-deposit requirement demands, in this Court's view, the fullest and effective consideration of the relaxation and waiver privileges as a matter of norm and not by exception and as facilitators and determinants in equal measure of the continued mobility of the appeal process up to the High Court Division stage. It would, therefore, be highly presumptuous of any customs appellate authority to wield power under section 194 in a manner that abruptly halts the procedure of redress leaving the appellant with no avenue to pursue the statutory right of appeal potentially to the ultimate statutorily contemplated end. In this regard, due attention is to be given to the pre- deposit relaxation and waiver provisions of section 194 that aim in the ultimate analysis to operate as facilitators of appeal and not the vehicles of outright and perfunctory elimination and ouster from the appellate process. There is not envisaged in Chapter XIX any concept of the “first point of elimination”. Rather, Chapter XIX, according to this Court, is to be read as incorporating a seamless transition of appeal potentially from one stage to the next higher level of which the section 194 pre-deposit requirement is but secondary to the ultimate objective of securing the right of appeal to the fullest.</u>
42. Such, therefore, is the cautionary note as appears as a constant refrain in several judicial pronouncements as reproduced herein below:
The Supreme Court of India observed in Bhavya Apparels Private Limited and others vs Union of India (Uol) and others [MANU/ SC/3753/2007] as follows:
“A right of appeal is not a fundamental right. It is a statutory right. As a right of appeal is a statutory right, it may also be hedged by conditions. It is, however, trite that conditions imposed may not be such which may for all intent and purport take away a vested right of appeal.”
43. In ITC Limited vs CCE (A) {MANU/TN/ 0700/2000} the High Court of Madras held as follows:
“this court has no hesitation in holding that the powers exercised by the Commissioner of Appeals while considering the application under section 35F, being quasi- judicial powers, which in the very nature of things is required to be exercised fairly, judiciously and objectively and at any rate without arbitrariness and subject to the rules of natural justice including hearing of the application to grant and to record reasons for the conclusions ultimately arrived at as rejection of an application for exemption or waiver or stay leads to rejection of the very appeal itself and denial of a remedy of appeal which violates  Article 14 and also renders the very remedy of appeal nugatory. The view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) cannot be sustained.”
44. High Court of Calcutta held in JN Chemical (Put.) Ltd. vs CEGAT [MANU/WB/ 0378/1989] that—
“These judicial pronouncements of high authority show that even where enabling or discretionary power is conferred on a public authority, the words which are permissive in character may be construed as involving a duty to exercise the power, if some legal right or entitlement is conferred or enjoyed and, for the purpose of effectuating such right or entitlement, the exercise of such power is essential. If there is failure on the part of the donee to exercise such power accordingly, the court will require it to be exercised.” —
45. The petitioner’s learned Advocate, Mr Md Yousuf Ali submits that given in our jurisdiction no such principle has yet been established by any judicial pronouncement governing scenarios where the Tribunal disposes of hardship applications perfunctorily, peremptorily, mechanically and_ arbitrarily without considering a strong prima facie case, and thereby, depriving one of a right to appeal, this Court may be pleased to consider expounding the applicable course of conduct and issue consequential directions upon the Tribunal to secure the ends of justice. That is precisely what this Court has undertaken to do as is evident from our considered opinion as above already expressed.
46. There is the other dimension to statutory conditionalities seemingly impairing the exercise of rights akin to the right of appeal. Indeed, as highlighted by the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr Pratikar Chakma representing the Respondent No. 3, Commissioner of Customs (Bond), Chapter XIX of the Act through the avenue of section 194 endorses the concept of a “conditional appeal”. Mr Chakma finds authority for that view in Vijay Prakash D. Mehta and others vs Collector of Customs (Preventive), Bombay, AIR 1988 SC 2010; MANU/SC/05070/1988. There the Supreme Court of India was seized with the issue of the legislative intent behind section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962 (corresponding to section 194 of the Act) and found thus on the “obligatory” nature of the pre-deposit requirement even when section 129E retained its permissive character as was lost by dint of the recasting of the section and its ethos in 2014 as already above noted:
“The aforesaid section provides a conditional right of appeal in respect of an appeal against the duty demanded or penalty levied. Although the section does not expressly provide for rejection of the appeal for non-deposit of duty or penalty, yet it makes it obligatory on the appellant to deposit the duty or penalty, pending the appeal, failing which the Appellate Tribunal is fully competent to reject the appeal.
Right to appeal is neither an absolute right nor an ingredient of natural justice the principles of which must be followed in all judicial and quasi-judicial adjudications.  The right to appeal is a statutory right and it can be circumscribed by the conditions in the grant.
The purpos of the section is to act in terrorem to make the people comply with the provisions of law.”
47. This Court finds itself to be in disagreement with the reasoning above as is abundantly made clear in this Court’s own views as above recorded. But it suffices to note here that the pronouncement in the Vijay Prakash D. Mehta case, was in many ways the harbinger of the drastic amendment to section 129E expressly incorporating the notion of a conditional right of appeal.
48. The law may “terrorize” (as per Sabyasachi Mukhaerjee, J in Vijay Prakash D. Mehta Case) but the better jurisprudential view, this Court finds, is that the law as an inherently moral construct also strives to grant reprieves or reliefs within reason. The law’s aspirational value to strike an essential balance between legal strictures and sanctions on the one hand and the availing of legal rights on the other is witnessed best in section 194 of the Act which, unlike section 129E of the Indian Customs Act, 1962 is still possessed of its permissive character intact. That balance is best exemplified in the law’s consideration of “undue hardship’ and that too “unconditionally” to entertain applications for deposit waiver. On the other hand, and as we have already noted above, section 129E of the Indian Customs Act, 1962 has through a series of amendments shed much of its permissive character in favour of the revenue’s interests taking centrestage and ultimately the statutory right of appeal being whittled down to a mere conditional one. But that has not been our legislative experience in this jurisdiction, at least not yet. This Court finds, therefore, that in its present formulation section 194 of the Act is weighed heavily in favour of exercise of discretionary power in relation to the reduction or waiver of pre- deposit requirements and that so long as the element of discretion remains so written into the statute it must be one that has to be exercised in favour of preserving the right of appeal and not ousting it peremptorily and arbitrarily. And in engaging in such act of preservation a prima facie satisfaction of the facts becomes unavoidable.
49. The test of sufficiency of the discretion granted under section 194 in this regard is indeed that of acting “judiciously”. Faced with the ratio decidendi as in Vijay Prakash D. Mehta Case that the right of appeal may indeed be whittled down, the argument and indeed this Court’s finding instead is for the Customs Authority or rather the appellate authority to be seen to be doing justice in its judicial capacity as opposed to acting merely mechanically and not judicially. The starting point, therefore, for evaluating the infirmity or sufficiency of the impugned order, in this Court’s opinion, must be the observation of the Supreme Court of India in L. Hirday Narain vs ITO, Bareilly {Law (SC) 1970-7-7):
“The High Court observed that under section 35 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the jurisdiction of the Income-tax Officer is discretionary. If thereby it is intended that the Income-tax Officer has discretion to exercise or not to exercise the power to rectify, the view is in our judgment erroneous. Section 35 enacts that the Commissioner or Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Income-tax Officer may rectify any mistake apparent from the record. If a statute invests a public Officer with authority to do an act in a specified set of circumstances, it is imperative upon him to exercise his authority in a manner appropriate to the case when a party interested and having a right to apply moves in that behalf and circumstances for exercise of authority are shown to exist. Even if the words used in the statute are prima facie enabling the Courts will readily infer a duty to exercise power which is invested in aid of enforcement of a right— public or private—of a citizen.”
50. Predicated on the above discussion, expanding on this Court’s opinions already above expressed, a perusal of the pleadings revealing highly contentious perspectives of underlying facts canvassed by both parties, consideration of the submissions made and identification of the resulting issues determinable on appeal, this Court is led resultantly to deduce that the petitioner has a strong prima facie appealable case the strength of which is to be gauged substantively and with finality by the statutorily assigned appellate forum. In this regard we note that in Bongaigaon Refinery and Petrochem. Ltd. vs Collr. Of C. Ex.(A) reported in 1994(46)ECC87; MANLI/WB/0300/ 1992 Ruma Pal, J. with her eyes on the underlying facts pertinently observed thus:
“As already seen the phrase “undue hardship” would cover a case where the appellant has a strong prima facie case. The phrase also in my view covers a situation where there is an arguable case in the appeal. In the former case the Appellate Authority should dispense with the pre- deposit altogether on the basis of the authorities referred to earlier. In the latter case the authority would have to safeguard the interest of the revenue. The Collector has not applied his mind to this aspect of the matter at all. He had to consider whether, if the deposit were waived, the interest of the revenue would be jeopardized. There was no suggestion or even allegation that there would be any jeopardy to the revenue if the pre-deposit were waived in the petitioner’s case. Keeping in view the mandate that a discretionary power must be exercised in favour of the assessee unless there was good reasons to the contrary, no reason has been disclosed by the Collector for refusing to exercise his discretion in favour of the petitioner particularly when the revenue’s interest was not said to be un-safeguarded. It is to be remembered that this Court, while remanding the matter back to the Collector had directed the petitioner to give an undertaking to this court that it would not deal with or dispose of any of its assets except in the usual course of business or with the leave of the court. This under- taking is still subsisting. The Collector did not reject this safeguard as inadequate. The demand relates to a period for the clearance had already been made. There is no question of the petitioner recovering the amount from its customers.”
51. Paving the way in the present instance for such an eventuality in which the question of undue hardship inextricably merges with an initial satisfaction of the prima facie merits of the petitioner’s case, it is this Court’s belief that the impugned order relaxing albeit partially the exacting pre-conditions for filing an appeal, but without reason for such relaxation and as also being devoid of citation of grounds that in the appellate authority’s view militate against the granting an unconditional and total waiver in the alternative, is found to be inherently bad in law and must be set-aside. It is also this Court's view that an inexact order as this must not be permitted to operate to take away the vested statutory right of appeal entrenched through the very scheme of the Act.
52. Accordingly, the two impugned orders of 9-8-2021 and of 12-10-2021 are, hereby, set- aside on grounds of the legal infirmities as cited above and the finding that both have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.
53. The Respondents No. 2, Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal is, hereby, directed to reconsider any hardship application which the petitioner shall now be at liberty to place before the Tribunal and to decide on that application in accordance of law. In this regard, we are convinced too of the persuasiveness and rationality of the outcome of two noted cases in the Indian jurisdiction i.e., Bongaigaon Refinery and Petrochem. Ltd. vs Collector of Customs, Excise [MANU/WB/0300/1992] by the High Court of Calcutta and Sony India Limited vs Union of India and Others decided by the High Court of Dethi [MANU/DE/0953/2000] and as later upheld by the Supreme Court of India in Union of India and others us Sony India Limited reported in (2002)10 Supreme Court Cases 757 to the effect that the Customs appellate authority is always vested with the jurisdiction and authority to consider the admission of the appeal in the facts and circumstances without requiring the payment of any statutory deposit per se. We see no bar in section 194 of the Act to accommodate any appellant so. This Court, accordingly, recognizes the petitioner’s entitlement to pursue its right of appeal upon being granted a complete waiver of making a pre-appeal deposit in keeping with such dispensation incorporated in the second proviso to section 194, and unconditionally so, and the Appellate Tribunal’s attention is particularly drawn to such recognition given.
54. Accordingly, this Court finds merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued.
55. Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute with the findings, observations and directions above.
There is no Order as to costs.
Communicate this Judgment and Order at once.
End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29.03.2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.9988 of 2015, 9987 of 2015, 6628 of 2016 & 10946 of 2013)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, C. J: These Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal are directed against the judgment and order dated 29.03.2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 9988 of 2015 heard analogously with Writ Petition Nos. 9987 of 20015, 6628 of 2016 and 10946 of 2013 making all the Rules absolute, declaring the decisions, given by the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra in A.T. Case No.126 of 2011 heard analogously with A.T. Case Nos.117 of 2011, 122 of 2011 and 124 of 2011, were without lawful authority and in an unlawful manner.
2. The relevant facts, for disposal of these petitions, in short, are that the writ petitioners of the above mentioned writ petitions were appointed as Surveyors in the service of the Land, Record and Survey Department under the Ministry of Land after being selected through a competitive selection process. The writ petitioner No.1 in writ petition NO. 9988 of 2015 had joined on 15.09.2005 as Surveyor in the Upazilla Land Office, Nagarkanda, Faridpuir. The writ petitioner No.2 had joined on 14.11.2013 as Surveyor in the Upazilla Settlement Office, Kalia, Narail. The writ petitioner No.1 in writ petition No.6628 of 2016 Md. Nurul Islam had joined on 27.12.1993 as surveyor in the Upazilla Land Office, Barisal Sadar, Barisal in the scale of taka 1200/-. The writ respondent No.2 in all the writ petitions filed the aforesaid A.T. Cases before the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra for a direction upon the Government to promote them to the post of Kanungo/ Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer upon inclusion of those posts in the Kanungo Recruitment Rules, 1984 with retrospective effect from 2003 as some Surveyors had been promoted in the said post. The Administrative Tribunal, Bogra, by the impugned judgment, allowed the cases and directed the Government to promote them in the posts of Kanungo/ Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer upon making necessary amendment of the Service Rules. It has been stated that the filing of the Administrative Tribunal Cases were barred by law under the provision of Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”). No case can be filed before the Administrative Tribunal without preferring departmental appeal before the Appellate authority of the impugned order. The cases were filed in the nature of mandamus and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain such case wherein no final order was impugned. The impugned decisions of the Administrative Tribunal, which had been originated from the cases filed in violation of the specific provisions of the Act, were liable to be declared illegal, without lawful authority and those were void ab initio. It has been further stated that the impugned decisions have been obtained by way of suppression of very important decision of the Apex Court. With the similar and identical claims earlier some employees filed writ petition No.6006 of 2002 and writ petition No.4264 of 2004, wherein both the Rules were discharged by a single judgment and order dated 15.06.2005 on the finding that the writ petitioners, who were the Mutation Assistant, Copyist cum-Bench Clerks, Record Keepers, and Peskars, could not make out a case for inclusion of their posts in the schedule of the Kanungo Recruitment Rules, 1984 as feeder posts of Kanungo. Some employees, who have been holding the post of Copyist-cum- Bench Assistant (Now Bench Clerks), had filed the case for their upgradation from category II to category I as under the Kanungo Recruitment Rules, 1984 the posts of category I has been given preferential consideration for promotion as Kanungo. The writ respondent No.2 was the petitioner No.09 in writ petition No.4264 of 2004 with almost similar and identical prayer one Record Keeper named Md. Mohibur Rahman and 6 others Copyist-cum-Bench Assistant filed Writ Petition No.8217 of 2013 and some other employees standing on the same footing to the writ respondent No.2 filed another writ petition being No.2353 of 2013 in this Court. Those were disposed of analogously by a judgment and order dated 17.06.2014. In the said judgment, the High Court Division has categorically observed that a person interested for promotion is to enter into the zone of feeder post for making them eligible to be included in the list and unless and until the posts of the prospective promotee are included in the list of feeder posts they cannot enter into the zone of promotion. However against the said judgment and order dated 17.06.2014 passed by those writ petitions, the writ petitioners preferred in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2479 of 2014 in the Appellate Division which was dismissed for default on 08.03.2015.
3. The present writ petitioners when awaiting for promotion for long time, they have been deprived of getting their promotion due to the impugned decisions. The writ petitioners requested to the concerned Ministry to challenge the impugned decisions but it kept silent inexplicably and, therefore, the writ petitioners moved this Court and obtained the Rules as stated above.
4. The Rules were contested by the writ respondent No.2 contending that an employee could not seek promotion in the next higher post unless the post is included in the schedule of the feeder post. The post of the writ petitioners had not been included in the feeder post of Kanungo, Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer. As the post of Surveyor had not been included existing of Kanungo Recruitment Rules, the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order, made all the Rules absolute declaring that the decisions given by the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra in A.T. Case Nos.117 of 2011, 122 of 2011, 124 of 2011 and 126 of 2011 have been passed without lawful authority and in an unlawful manner. Against which, the leave petitioners have filed the instant leave petitions.
5. Mr. Pankaj Kumar Kunda and Mr. S.M. Atiqur Rahman, learned Counsel, instructed by Mr. Joynal Abedin, learned Advocate-on-Record, appeared on behalf of the petitioners and Mr. Salahuddin Dolon, learned Senior Counsel, instructed by Md. Jahurul Islam, learned Advocate-on-Record, appeared for the respondents.
6. The learned Counsel for petitioners, submits that against the decisions of Administrative Tribunal, the writ petitions were not at all maintainable, the High Court Division erred in law in declaring the decisions of Administrative Tribunal void and unlawful. He further submits, that the specific provision provided in the said statute that against the decision of Administrative Tribunal, the aggrieved persons are entitled to prefer appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, the High Court Division erred in law in interfering the decisions of the Administrative Tribunal. On the other hand, Mr. Salauddin Dolan, submits that the High Court Division upon proper appreciation of the facts and law involved in the instant writ petitions rightly made the Rule absolute declaring the decisions of the Administrative Tribunal unlawful.
7. It appears from the decisions of Administrative Tribunal, Bogra in A.T. Cases Nos. 126 of 2011, 117 of 2011, 122 of 2011 and 124 of 2011 that the petitioners of those A.T. cases have been serving in different posts of Land Records and Survey Directorate. They prayed before the Administrative Tribunal for getting promotion in the posts of Kanungo/ Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer with retrospective effect. The Tribunal, by the impugned decisions passed the identical order with the following words, “অত্র মামলাটি পুতিদ্বন্দিতাকারী পুতিপরে বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা সূত্রে এবং অন্যান্য পুতিপগণের বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা সূত্রে বিনা খরচায় মঞ্জুর করা হইল। প্রার্থীর পদের নাম তাহার সমপর্যায়ের পদের (ইতোপূর্বে পদোন্নতি প্রাপ্ত কর্মচারীদের পদের ন্যায়) কর্মচারীদের ন্যায় “কানুনগো/উপ-সহকারী সেটেলমেন্ট অফিসার” নিয়োগ বিধিমালাতে অন্তভূক্ত করতঃ উল্লেখিত পদে পদোন্নতি প্রদানের প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের জন্য এতদ্বারা প্রতিপক্ষগণকে নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেল।” Against those identical decisions , the writ petitioners filed the aforesaid writ petitions.
8. The learned Advocate for the leave petitioners, at first, submits that the instant writ petitions were not at all maintainable since there is specific provision of preferring appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal against the decisions of the Administrative Tribunal, the High Court Division exceed its jurisdiction in entertaining the instant writ petitions. Since the statute provides specific provision of preferring appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, against the decisions given by the Administrative Tribunal, the instant writ petitions filed by the writ petitioner- respondents in the High Court Division were not at all maintainable, the High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction in setting aside the impugned decisions of the Administrative Tribunal. Part VI, Chapter III of the Constitution containing Article 117 provides,
“117.(1) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of –
(a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishments;
(b) the acquisition, administration, management and disposal of any property vested in or managed by the Government by or under any law, including the operation and management of, and service in any nationalised enterprise or statutory public authority;
1[(c) any law to which clause (3) of article 102 applies.]
(2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal:
Provided that Parliament may, by law, provide for appeals from, or the review of, decisions of any such tribunal.”
<u>9. The aforesaid provisions empower the Parliament to enact law providing for the adjudication of the service disputes. Article 117(1) clearly contemplates that the Administrative Tribunals shall be constituted by the law enacted by the Parliament to exercise jurisdiction for all the matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic. Proviso of Article 117(2) provides specific provision of preferring appeal against the decision of the Administrative Tribunal and law enacted by the parliament provided the provision of preferring such appeal. That the decision of the Administrative Tribunal will be subject to scrutiny before Administrative Appellate Tribunal within its jurisdiction. It is true that under our constitutional scheme, only the constitutional Court has been vested with the power of judicial review but in the instant case the writ petitioners have challenged the appealable decisions of the Administrative Tribunal.</u>
<u>10. It appears from words used in the order of the High Court Division that the Administrative Tribunal by its decision directed the concerned authority to take steps by amending respective “Bidhimala” for giving promotion of the writ petitioners in the post of Kanungo/ Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer. In fact, by the impugned order, the Administrative Tribunal directed to amend the law in giving positive relief of the writ petitioners which can not be allowed. The Administrative Tribunal cannot direct the Government to amend the law as well as it cannot direct the Government to give promotion of the writ petitioners in the post of Kanungo/ Sub- Assistant Settlement Officer because the promotion is not a right.</u>
11. However, the writ respondents may consider the case of writ petitioners following the provisions of law, if they are at all entitled.
12. With observation made above, this civil petition for leave to appeal is disposed of. The judgment and order dated 29.03.2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ petition Nos.9988 of 2015, 9987 of 2015, 6628 of 2016 and 10946 of 2013 are hereby set aside.
End.
