full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam, J: This civil appeal by leave is directed against the order dated 7-4-2008 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 2008 disallowing the miscellaneous case.
2. Short facts are that the respondent herein as petitioner filed Administrative Tribunal Case No. 256 of 1994 under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 against the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Forest and two others for declaration that the order dated 27-6-1992 passed, by the opposite party No.3, the Deputy Chief Conservator, Dhaka removing him from service and the order dated 10-3-1994 issued by the opposite party No. 2, the Chief Conservator of Forest, Dhaka rejecting his departmental appeal are illegal, void, without jurisdiction and of no legal effect and to direct the opposite parties to reinstate him in service with arrear salary and other attending benefits.
3. It is stated that the petitioner joined in the service on 25-11-1992 as Forest Ranger. While he was serving in the office of the Divisional Forest Office, Chittagong, the opposite party No.3 framed charge against him for desertion and asked him to show cause as to why he would not be dismissed from service. The petitioner submitted his written statement of defence denying all the allegations. The authority without considering his explanation appointed Inquiry Officer to inquire into the matter. The Inquiry Officer without holding the inquiry submitted a perverse report against the petitioner.
4. The opposite party No.3 therefore, issued notice upon the petitioner asking him to show cause as to why he would not be dismissed from the service. The petitioner submitted his second written statement of defence pleading innocence. But the authority without considering his reply passed the impugned order removing the petitioner from service. He preferred depart-mental appeal to the opposite party No.2 which was rejected on 10-3-1994 and hence the case was filed on 28-8-1994.
5. The opposite parties contested the case by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the petition stating, inter alia, that the petition is not maintainable and the petitioner has no cause of action.
6. The defence case, in a nutshell, is that the charge of desertion has been proved against the petitioner in the departmental inquiry and, as such, he was removed from service. There was no illegality or irregularity in the departmental proceeding. The impugned order is quite perfect and legal. It does not deserve interference by the Tribunal. The petition is totally misconceived and, as such, it is liable to be dismissed with cost.
7. The Administrative Tribunal allowed the case. Against which the present appellants preferred appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The appeal was dismissed for default on 26-2-2008. The appellants preferred an application for restoration of the said appeal which was also rejected.
8. Beine aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the decisions of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal the present appellants filed the civil petition for leave to appeal and obtained leave giving rise to this appeal.
9. Mr AM Aminuddin, the learned Attorney-General for the appellants submits that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal erred in law in rejecting the application for restoration in view of the fact that no steps could be taken on 26-2-2008 when the appeal was fixed for hearing as the learned lawyer of the appellants could not appear as the appeal was not listed in his personal list.
10. He further submits that the appellants not being at fault and responsible of their own for not appearing through the lawyer at the time of hearing of appeal and the appeal having been dismissed for default due to mistake of the lawyer, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal erred in law in rejecting the application for restoration and allowing the appellants a chance of being heard.
11. On the other hand Mr Md Asrarul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the respondent supporting the impugned order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal as well as the Administrative Tribunal contends that the appointment of the Inquiry Officer by the Opposite Party No. 3 in the Charge-sheet in violation of the Rule 7(2)(c) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 shows the pre-determination of the Appellant No.3 to impose major penalty of removal from Service and the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka considering such aspect allowed the case, thus the appeal is liable to be dismissed.
12. He further submits that the appellant No.3 is not the appointing authority of the respondent and passing the order of removal from service by the appellant No.3 in violation of Rule 4(6) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 read with Article 135(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is absolutely without jurisdiction and void ab-initio and the appeal is liable to be dismissed.
13. We have heard the learned Advocate of both sides. We have also perused the judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and Administrative Tribunal and other documents on record.
14. On appreciation of the argument of the parties it is felt by us that the core question that has to be addressed in this Civil Appeal is that whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal could disallow the Miscellaneous application for restoration of an appeal filed under rule 6(7) of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 for setting aside the order dated 26-2-2008 dismissing the appeal for default.
15. Let us now see what has been prescribed in the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (the Act, 1980) and the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 regarding the issue before us.
16. Rule 11 of the Rules, 1982, has provided that the provisions of the Rules, 1982 shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to an appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.
17. Rule 11 of the Rules, 1982 states:
"Appeals—Save as otherwise provided in the Act, the provisions of these rules shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to an appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 6."
18. And rule 6 of the Rules, 1982 has clearly provided the procedure for disposal of an application. And as per sub-rules (4), (5) and (6) of rule 6 of the Rules, 1982, an application (here the appeal) can be dismissed for default only if on the date fixed for hearing, the applicant does not appear. Rule 6 provides:
"Procedure for disposal of application.—
(1) ................
(2) ..................
(3) .................
(4) Where on the day so fixed neither party appear and it is found that the notices to appear have been served upon the parties to the dispute, Tribunal may make an order dismissing the application.
(5) Where on the day so fixed the applicant appears and the opposite party does not appear, Tribunal may if it is found that the notice to appear has been served, hear the application ex-parte.
(6) Where on the day so fixed the opposite party appears and the applicant does not appear, the Tribunal may make an order dismissing the application: Provided that where the opposite party admits the claim of the applicant or from the materials on record it is found that the relief claimed by the applicant should be allowed, the Tribunal shall make an order granting the relief to such extent as it deems fit.
(7) Any party to the dispute aggrieved by an order made under sub-rules (4), (5) and (6) may apply to the Tribunal for an order to set-aside the dismissal or the order made ex-parte and, if the Tribunal is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the non-appearance of the party, the Tribunal shall make an order setting aside the dismissal or the order made ex-parte on such conditions as it deems fit."
19. Further section 7(8) of the Act, 1980 stipulates:
"Subject to the other provisions of this Act, a Tribunal shall, for the purpose of hearing an application or appeal, as the case may be, follow such procedure as may be prescribed:
Provided that where, in respect of any matter no procedure has been prescribed by this Act or by rules made thereunder, a Tribunal shall follow the procedure in respect thereof as may be laid down by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal."
20. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Nurul Alam: 65 DLR (AD) 77 it has been observed:
"The point at issue was considered in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 43 of 2010. In the said case after considering the relevant provisions of the Act, 1980, namely: sections 5, 6 and 12 and rules, 6 and II of the Rules, 1982, this Division held that:—
From a close study of the above mentioned provisions of the Act as well as the Rules, it appears to us that no period has been prescribed for filing an application for setting-aside an order of dismissal of an appeal, so the question of rejection of an application on the ground of limitation does not arise at all. But, unfortunately the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case in passing the impugned order. The Appellate Tribunal has also not stated the provisions of law under which the appellant was required to file an application for restoration within a specified time when it mentioned that the application was filed out of time by 7 (seven) days. What appears to us is that an Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, may reject an application for setting-aside an order of dismissal or an ex-parte order even if the same is filed within the shortest possible period, if the applicant or the appellant fails to give sufficient cause to the satisfaction of the concerned Tribunal for failure to appear when the case or appeal was taken up for hearing.
We find no reason to take a different view in this case other than the view taken in the said decided case."
<u>21. It is true that proviso to sub-section (8) of section 7 of the Act has provided that where, in respect of any matter, no procedure has been prescribed by the Act or by the Rules made thereunder, a Tribunal shall follow the procedure in respect thereof as may be laid down by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal but in the Rules, 1982 it has been clearly stated that an application (here the appeal) may be dismissed only when the applicant (here the appellant) does not appear on the date of hearing.</u>
<u>22. In the present case we found that the appeal was filed back in the year 2003 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. But after long laps of time when the matter was fixed for hearing on 26-2-2008 none appeared for appellants. So, it is apparent that the appellant had lost his interest to proceed with the appeal. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed for default. Subsequently, on an application for restoration of the appeal the same was also disallowed as the Administrative Appellate Tribunal did not believe the plea of the learned Counsel of the appellant to have lost his personal case diary to be an acceptable extenuating circumstance.</u>
<u>23. To have the restoration Miscellaneous application sustained the learned counsel of the appellant ought to have shown sufficient cause by furnishing supporting documents (here the personal case diary) to satisfy the appellate Court below.</u>
24. In view of the above discussions it is abundantly clear that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal rightly disallowed the said application for restoration following the provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act and Rules.
Therefore, we do not find any legal infirmity in the impugned order passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. Accordingly, this civil appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
End.

full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed, J. : Both these matters were taken up for analogous hearing and are being disposed of by this common judgment. The determination below of common facts and law proceeds on the pleadings and submissions in both cases. The reasoning and decision of this Court shall be deemed applicable to both cases until otherwise specifically and expressly indicated.
2. The Petitioner obtained a Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017 (‘1st Writ Petition’) challenging the legality of the Assessment Order and Notice of Demand both dated 27-4-2017 issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Taxes Circle 164, Taxes Zone-8 (‘the DCT’) for the Assessment Year 2016-2017. Rule Nisi was issued on 8-6-2017 in the following terms:
‘Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the Assessment Order dated 27-4-2017 for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 and Notice of Demand dated 27-4-2017 both issued by the respondent No. 4 as evidenced by Annexure-A & A(1) shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and also, as to why the respondents shall not be directed to re-assess the petitioner's Income Tax for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 by treated him as a non-resident and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper’
3. At the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi, the High Court Division passed an interim order in the following terms:
‘Pending disposal of the Rule, let the operation of the Assessment Order dated 27-4-2017 for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 and Notice of Demand dated 27-4-2017, both issued by the respondent No. 4, in relation to the petitioner, as evidenced by Annexure-A &A(1), be stayed for a period of 6 (six) months from date’.
4. In Writ Petition No. 8229 of 2017 (`2nd Writ Petition'), the Petitioner obtained a Rule Nisi challenging the legality of the Assessment Order and Notice of Demand both dated 27-12-2016 issued by the DCT for the Assessment Year 2015-2016. Rule Nisi was issued on 8-6-2017 in the following terms:
‘Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the Assessment Order dated 27-12-2016 for the Assessment Year 2015-2016 and Notice of Demand dated 27-12-2016 both issued by the Respondent No. 4 as evidenced by Annexure-A &A(1) shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect……’
5. At the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi, the High Court Division passed an interim order in the following terms:
‘Pending disposal of the Rule, let the operation of the Assessment Order dated 27-12-2016 for the Assessment Year 2015-2016 and Notice of Demand dated 27-12-2016 in relation to the petitioner, both issued by the respondent no 4, as evidenced by Annexure-A &A(1), be stayed for a period of 6 (six) months from date’.
6. Thereafter, the Chairman, National Board of Revenue filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 2494 and 2519 of 2017 challenging the interim orders of stay dated 8-6-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 8228-8229 of 2017. Both Civil Petitions were dismissed by the Appellate Division on 9-7-2017.
7. In both Writ Petitions, it has been asserted by the Petitioner that he left Dhaka for London on 17-12-2013, and that he had not returned to Bangladesh since his departure, which is evident from the departure seal on the Petitioner's Bangladesh Passport No. F0585646. The departure of the Petitioner was also widely reported in various newspapers and online news websites. By a letter dated 23-1-2014, the Petitioner informed the DCT of his departure which was duly received by the office of the DCT on 4-2-2014. It has been further averred in the Writ Petitions that upon filing the tax returns for the relevant Assessment Years, the DCT fixed a date for hearing, which was duly attended by the Petitioner's representatives. During the hearing, it was submitted that the Petitioner was not resident in Bangladesh. As such, the Petitioner was required to be treated as a non-resident for the purpose of assessment of his income and tax for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017.
8. In Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017, i.e., the 1st Writ Petition, it is averred by the Petitioner that in May 2017, his representative received a copy of the impugned assessment order issued by the DCT for the Assessment Year 2016-2017, and was surprised to note that he had been described as a 'resident' in the said assessment order. The DCT had determined that the Petitioner had a total income of Taka 1,69,08,371 (Taka One Crore Sixty nine lacs eight thousand three hundred and seventy one) against which, the DCT imposed a tax of Taka 1,21,08,371 (Taka One Crore Twenty One lacs eight thousand three hundred and seventy one), i.e., income tax was imposed at the rate of 71.61%. Furthermore, in the 1st Writ Petition, it has been averred that by treating the Petitioner as a resident, the DCT held that the Petitioner earned Taka 2,00,00,000 (Two Crores) from the legal profession in Bangladesh in the relevant assessment year, which is without any basis. The Petitioner also contended that the appeals process is not equally efficacious as the impugned assessment order has been passed completely without jurisdiction.
9. In Writ Petition No. 8229 of 2017, i.e., the 2nd Writ Petition, it has been averred that that Petitioner, upon making enquiries with the office of the DCT regarding the Assessment Year 2015-2016, obtained a certified copy of the impugned assessment order on 28-5-2017. The Petitioner's representative was surprised to note that the Petitioner had been described as a 'resident' in the said assessment order, The DCT had determined that the Petitioner had a total income of Taka 1,59,32,346 (Taka One crore fifty nine lacs thirty two thousand three hundred and forty six) against which the DCT imposed income tax of Taka 43,39,704. It has been further averred that by treating the Petitioner as a resident, the DCT held that the Petitioner earned Taka 1,80,00,000 (Taka One crore eighty lacs) from the legal profession in Bangladesh in the relevant assessment year, which is without any basis.
10. Based on such averments in the two Writ Petitions, the Petitioner challenged the legality of the Assessment Orders and Notice of Demand issued by the DCT for the Assessment Yeas 2015-2016 and 2016-2017.
11. The Respondent No. 2, DCT as represented by the learned Assistant Attorney-General Ms Tahmina Polly filed Affidavits-in-Opposition and Supplementary Affidavits-in-Opposition in both Writ Petitions, contending, inter alia, as follows:
(i) The impugned assessment order dated 24-4-2017 issued in respect of Assessment Year 2016-2017 has been revised under section 173 of the Income Tax Ordinance by an order dated 8-5-2017, i.e., prior to issuance of the Rule in Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017 on 8-6-2017. As such, the Rule in the aforesaid Writ Petition, being infructuous, is liable to be discharged.
(ii) The letter dated 23-1-2014 issued by the Petitioner was not served upon the DCT. The DCT had no knowledge of the letter dated 23-1-2014, and, as such, there was no scope to treat the Petitioner as a 'non-resident' for the relevant Assessment Years. Until 2017, the assessee or his representative did not inform the Respondents orally or in writing that he had left the country or that he was not resident in Bangladesh.
(iii) The Writ Petitions were maintainable as the Petitioner had the opportunity of filing an appeal before the relevant authority, and accordingly, the Rules are liable to be discharged.
(iv) There was no illegality or arbitrariness or latches on the part of the Respondents as the assessee-himself submitted the tax returns as 'resident' and did not inform the respondents about the residency status of the assessee, and, as such, the respondents rightly determined the income of the assessee as resident
12. The Petitioner filed Affidavits-in-Reply in both Writ Petitions. In the Affidavit-in-Reply in Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017 the Petitioner contended inter-alia that the certified copies of the order sheet of the DCT in respect of the Assessment Year 2016-2017 clearly showed that the purported order of revision bearing the date 8-5-2107 was in fact passed in 2018 (i.e., after the issuance of the Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017) and that the order sheet had been tampered with to make it appear that the purported order of revision was passed prior to issuance of the Rule Nisi. Details of the fraud committed by the then concerned officer have been set out in paragraphs 6-21 of the Affidavit-in-Reply in Writ Petition No. 8228 of 2017. The then concerned officer had served as DCT for Taxes Zone- 8, Taxes Circle-164 from 19-3-2017 to 25-9-2018.
13. Furthermore, the Petitioner annexed a copy of the letter dated 23-1-2014 to both the Affidavits-in-Reply showing that the same was received on 4-2-2014 bearing the seal of the office of the DCT and the signature of an identifiable member of the staff. As such, the Petitioner contended that the said letter had been duly served upon the Respondent No. 2.
14. Heard the learned Advocates for the not parties in both Writ Petitions, perused the Applications, Supplementary Affidavits, Affidavits-in-Opposition, Affidavits-in-Reply and the annexures annexed thereto in both cases.
15. The core argument of the Petitioner is that although he was not resident in Bangladesh during the relevant Assessment Years, his income has been assessed as if he is a resident. The Petitioner contends that the fact of his non-residency in Bangladesh for the relevant Assessment Years is apparent from the following documents:
(i) Receipts and Expenditure Accounts (which form part of the tax returns);
(ii) Letter dated 23-1-2014; and
(iii) Petitioner's passport.
16. A perusal by this Court of the aforesaid documents, taken as a whole, clearly indicate to this Court that the Petitioner was required to be treated as a non-resident for the purposes of the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017. This Court's findings in this regard are enumerated hereinbelow:
(i) Receipts and Expenditure Accounts: In the tax returns for the Assessment Year 2015-2016 submitted by the Petitioner Annexure-H, Pg 21, Supplementary-Affidavit of 1st Writ Petition), the 'Resident' box has been ticked by the Petitioner's tax advisor. The fact that this was done inadvertently is borne out by the Receipts and Expenditure Account for the Year ended 30-6-2015 (annexed to the returns for the Assessment Year 2015-2016) which, however, shows that the Petitioner has been described as 'living abroad'. Similarly, in the tax returns for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 submitted by the Petitioner (Annexure-H(1), Pg 70, Supplementary Affidavit of 1st Writ Petition), the 'Resident' box has been inadvertently ticked by the Petitioner's tax advisor. However, the Receipts and Expenditure Account for the Year ended 30-6-2016 (annexed to the returns for the Assessment Year 2016-2017) shows that the Petitioner has been described as 'living abroad'.
(i) 	Letter to the DCT dated 23-1-2014:
The Petitioner's letter to the DCT dated 23-1-2014 as received by a member of the DCT's staff on 4-2-2014 (Annexure-D, Pg 80, 1st Writ Petition) clearly shows that the DCT was put on notice of the fact that the Petitioner had departed Dhaka for London on 17-12-2013. The Petitioner has annexed as Annexure-I (Pg 76, Affidavit-in-reply in 1st Writ Petition) a colour photocopy of the said letter containing the official blue seal of the office of the DCT and the signature of an identifiable member of the staff. The signature of the recipient as affixed to the letter dated 23-1-2014 is identical to that of the Head Clerk as appears in the certified copy of the order sheet. Predicated on the above, it is this Court's finding that the letter dated 23-1-2014 was duly served upon the Respondent No. 2, DCT.
It is further noted in this regard, that the Respondent No. 2 contends that the letter dated 23-1-2014 was issued for the purpose of the Assessment Year 2014-2015 and not for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017, and that as such, the DCT could not be expected to take into consideration such letter at the time of issuance of the impugned assessment orders. The Petitioner's response to such argument is that in assessing the income/tax of an assesseee, the DCT necessarily has to examine the records of the previous assessment years (and in fact he has done so, which is apparent from the impugned assessment orders which refer to income/expenses of previous assessment years). Finding such response to be satisfactorily adequate, this Court hold in this regard that the DCT should in such circumstances be presumed to have notice of the letter dated 23-1-2014 while assessing the tax payable for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017.
The Court's finding in this regard and elaborated hereinbelow:
(a) Firstly, in assessing the income/tax of an assesseee, the DCT necessarily has to examine the records of the previous assessment year (and in fact he has done so). As such, he should be presumed to have notice of the letter dated 23-1-2014 while assessing the tax payable for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017. This is evident from a close reading of the impugned assessment orders:
(i) In the impugned assessment order dated 27-12-2016 and 27-4-2017 for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017, the DCT has estimated the Petitioner's agricultural income on the basis of past records.
(ii) Under the heading `Professional Income' in the impugned assessment orders, the DCT refers to expenses of the previous assessment year incurred in the form of salaries.
(iii) In the DCT's conclusions as recorded in the impugned assessment orders for both Assessment Years, the DCT clearly refers to the contents of the previous assessment year in estimating the Petitioner's income.
(iv) In the impugned assessment orders, the DCT refers to FDR earnings of the previous assessment years.
(v) In the impugned assessment order, the DCT refers to details of the Petitioner's wealth and liabilities of the previous assessment year.
(vi) In the impugned assessment orders, the DCT refers to contents of the records of the previous assessment year in the computation of the Petitioner's family expenses.
(vii) In the table on depreciation at Pg 45, 1st WP, the DCT refers to the previous year's value of the Petitioner's assets indicating reference to the contents of the records of previous assessment year.
(b) Secondly, it will be seen from the tax returns submitted by the Petitioner for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 that the Petitioner has stated 'as before' in describing the details of wealth and liabilities in respect of (i) non-agricultural assets, (ii) agricultural assets and (iii) jewelleries, (iv) furniture, and (v) electronic goods. This is a standard practice which is followed whilst filling out tax returns. This indicates that at the time of considering an assessee's tax returns, the DCT is required to consult and consider his tax file for previous assessment years.
(c) Finally, it will be seen from section 93(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 ("the Ordinance") that the DCT is entitled to issue notice in respect of concealed income within 5 years from the end of the assessment year for which the assessment is made. As such, the DCT consults and considers the relevant materials and information in the Petitioner's tax records for previous assessment years.
(iii) Petitioner's passport:
The Petitioner further argues that the departure seal on his passport (Pg 56, 1st Writ Petition) clearly shows that he left the country on 17-12-2013. This has in fact not been disputed or denied by the Respondent No. 2, DCT in the multiple affidavits filed by him before this Court. Indeed, at no point in time has the Respondent No. 2 disputed the authenticity or validity of the departure seals on the Petitioner's passports. Nor have they made any positive assertion that the Petitioner had not departed Dhaka for London on 17-12-2013. As such, it is the admitted position of the parties before this Court that the Petitioner has not been resident in Bangladesh since December 2013. Consequently, it stands to reason in this Court's opinion and as aptly argued by the Petitioner, that by operation of section 2(55) of the Ordinance the Petitioner was required to be treated as a non-resident for the purpose of the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017.
17. The Petitioner has next drawn this Court's attention to the fact that although it is beyond doubt that he is a non-resident, his income has been assessed for the relevant Assessment Years as if he was present in Bangladesh and earning a local professional income. This is reflected in both the impugned assessment orders in which the DCT has uniformly noted as follows:
‘নথি পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় করদাতা একজন স্বনামধন্য ব্যারিস্টার ও সিনিয়র আইনজীবি । তিনি আইনী পরামর্শ দিয়ে এবং মামলা পরিচলনা করে পেশাগত আয় প্রাপ্ত হয়ে থাকেন।’
18. Here the Petitioner has argued that the DCT failed to appreciate that as a practising Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court, the Petitioner earned his professional income from fees received from his clients. Personal endeavour and demonstration of skill on the part of the Petitioner in arguing and moving cases whilst in Bangladesh is a core element of his professional income. This in turn required the Petitioner to be physically present within the territory of Bangladesh in order to enable him to exercise his professional skills and represent his clients by arguing cases before the Bangladesh courts. The Petitioner emphasizes in this regard that personal endeavour and the exercise of professional skill within the territory of Bangladesh are inextricably linked to his local professional earnings. In other words, the physical presence of the Petitioner employing his personal skill before the relevant judicial forum in Bangladesh is a sine qua non for generation of his income. Thus, as the Petitioner's learned Advocate, Mr AF Hassan Ariff has rightly impressed upon this Court, prior to undertaking assessment of the Petitioner's professional earnings, it was incumbent upon the DCT to ascertain whether the condition precedent for earning a professional income as a lawyer in Bangladesh was satisfied, i.e., whether the Petitioner was "resident in Bangladesh during the relevant period and in a position to exercise his professional skill and earn a professional income as a lawyer. This, the Court finds, was clearly not done by the DCT. The question of residence of the Petitioner, this Court notes, being a jurisdictional fact, the same was required to be resolved prior to the DCT making an assessment of the Petitioner's professional income. Failure to determine such jurisdictional fact by the DCT has, therefore, rendered the impugned assessment orders wholly without: jurisdiction. Such a finding by this Court finds substantiation in various judgments as cited before this Court by the Petitioner's learned Advocates Mr AF Hassan Ariff and Mr Imran Siddiq. Of these cases the following merit specific reference with their rationes decidendi specifically extrapolated in support of this Court's ultimate findings:
(i) Mohammad Jamil Asghar vs Improvement Trust Rawalpindi reported in 17 DLR (SC) 520
6. ‘...A purely administrative officer who is empowered to pass an order if certain circumstances exist has no jurisdiction to determine those circumstances, and the objective existence of those circumstances is an essential condition of the validity of his order. In respect of every order passed by him, the Court can make an enquiry and if it finds that all the circumstances needed for passing the order were not present it will declare the other void. Of course, although the officer has been granted no jurisdiction to determine any facts, he will have to ascertain whether the requisite circumstances exist for otherwise he cannot pass the order, but his conclusion as to the existence of those circumstances binds no body and it is open to any person affected to challenge his act on the ground that those circumstances do not in fact exist....’
(ii) Arun Kumar and others vs Union of India (UOI) and others reported in (2006) Sapp (6) SCR 290
41. ‘...A "jurisdictional fact" is a fact which must exist before a Court, a Tribunal or an Authority assumes jurisdiction over a particular matter. A jurisdictional fact is one on existence of non-existence of which depends jurisdiction of a court, tribunal or an authority. It is the fact upon which an administrative agency's power to act depends. If the jurisdictional fact does not exist, the court, authority or officer cannot act. If a Court or authority wrongly assumes the existence of such fact, the order can be questioned by a writ of certiorari. The underlying principle is that by erroneously assuming existence of such jurisdictional fact, no authority can confer upon itself jurisdiction which it otherwise does not possess.
42. ‘...The existence of a jurisdictional fact is thus sine qua non or condition precedent for the exercise of power by a court of limited jurisdiction.'
(iii) Mian Jamal Shah vs Election Commission reported in 18 DLR (SC) 1.
45. ‘...It is a distinction attaching only to judicial tribunals that their acts with in their jurisdiction though illegal are not null and void. So far as administrative officer and authorities are conceived there is no distinction between illegality and want of jurisdiction. When an administrative officer acts illegally he acts without jurisdiction. An administrative officer has authority to pass order or to take action if certain facts exist. If those essential facts do not exist his order or action is void.
(iv) Reza Textiles vs ITO, Rampur reported in AIR 1973 SC 1362
3. ‘...No authority, much less a quasi-judicial authority, can confer jurisdiction on itself by deciding a jurisdictional fact wrongly. The question whether the jurisdictional fact has been rightly decided or not is a question that is open for examination by the High Court in an application for a writ of certiorari. if the High Court comes to the conclusion, as the learned single Judge has done in this case, that the Income-tax Officer had clutched at the jurisdiction by deciding a jurisdictional fact erroneously, then the assesses was entitled for the writ of certiorari prayed for by him'.
19. The jurisdictional fact wholly lost sight of by the DCT is that pursuit of a profession or vocation dependent on 'personal skill'. The Petitioner's learned Advocate have adverted to the following precedents as propound that view:
(i) Commissioner of Income Tax vs Ms Bhagwan Broker Agency reported in RLW 1993 (1) Raj 610
8. ‘….Scrutton, LI in Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Maxse (supra) observed.: -‘….it seems to me, as at present advised, that a 'profession' in the present case of language involves the idea of an occupation requiring either purely intellectual skill, or if any manual skill, as in painting and sculpture or surgery, skill controlled by the intellectual skill of the operator, as distinguished from an occupation which is substantially the production, or sale or arrangements for the production or sale of commodities. ...’
11. ‘...The term profession involves the idea of an occupation requiring either purely intellectual skill or of manual skill controlled as in painting and sculpture, or surgery, by the intellectual skill of the operator, as distinguished from an operation which is substantially the production or sale or arrangements for the production or sale of commodities.’
13. ‘...I think that everybody would agree that, before one can say that a man is carrying on a profession, one must see that he has some special skill or ability or some special qualification derived from training or experience.’
(ii) P. Stanwill & Co. Auctioneers, Cawnpore vs Commissioner of Income Tax, UP & Ajmer-Merwara, Lucknow reported in AIR 1953 All 88
6. ‘...the main difference between ordinary commercial business and profession lies in the amount of knowledge or skill employed in carrying it on though that may not be sole criterion....’
(iii) Commissioner of Income Tax vs Lallubhai Nagardas and Sons reported in [1993] 204 ITR 93- (Bom)
11. ‘...The word 'profession' implies professed attainments in 'special knowledge as distinguished from mere' skill   A profession involves labour, skill, education and special knowledge and implies a vocation requiring higher education and learning, intellectual skill as distinguished from that used in an occupation for the production or sale of commodities...’
(iv) DP Dunderdele vs GP Mukhojee reported in AIR 1958 (Cal) 465
12. ‘...The distinctive work of a solicitor is not the work of bookkeeping and of actual typing. His skill is the skill of law. It is true that in communications and in keeping of books of accounts, help is needed and for that purpose a staff is employed. But I cannot see how employment of typists and correspondence clerks or accountants can convert a profession which remains by its nature the personal work depending on the individual corporate and professional skills of the solicitor or solicitors concerned into an industry, so long of course, the solicitors and their firm carry on the work of solicitors.'
(v) Mason (Inspector of Taxes) vs Innes reported in [1967] 2 WLR 479
‘... I turn accordingly to consider what is involved in the professional activities of an author during his life ... It is only by exploiting the work of his brain and his pen that he can make any professional income'.
20. Relying upon the rationes decidendi of the above judgments, this Court finds that personal endeavour is a crucial element of earning a professional income. Since the Petitioner was not present in the territory of Bangladesh from 17-12-2013, there is a clear absence of personal physical endeavour on the part of the Petitioner to exercise his personal skill and effort and earn a local professional income. In the circumstances, the impugned Assessment Orders, which are predicated on the assumption that the Petitioner is resident in Bangladesh, are found by this Court to be without jurisdiction and liable to be set-aside as prayed for in these two Writ Petitions.
21. Crucially, therefore, the DCT may only assume jurisdiction to compute income when the income is generated within territorial limits. Activities generating income within the territory must exist to confer jurisdiction upon the DCT to compute and assess. Existence of such an income (professional) is the foundation of and confers a legal competency to compute and assess. As such before proceeding with computation and assessment of professional income, the DCT is required to examine whether the facts provide it with the necessary jurisdiction to compute and assess. The DCT's actions therefore suffers from want of jurisdiction, that is, non-existence of income (within the territory) to compute and assess. The question of residence of the Petitioner, being a jurisdictional fact, the same was required to be resolved prior to .the DCT making an assessment of the Petitioner's professional income. Failure to determine such jurisdictional fact by the DCT has rendered the impugned assessment orders wholly without jurisdiction.
22. The Petitioner also argues that the facts of these two cases raise the spectre of impugned Assessment Orders being issued mala fide. In this regard, it is pointed out that the Petitioner's income for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 has been shown by the DCT to be Taka 1,69,08,371 whereas tax has been assessed as Taka 1,21,083,871, i.e., tax has been charged at 71.61% although the highest tax bracket is 30%. It is submitted, therefore, that the DCT imposed tax at an arbitrary rate which is beyond the provisions of the Ordinance or any other law. As such, he acted mala .fide and wholly without jurisdiction. Moreover, it is contended, such an arbitrary and astronomical figure has been assessed as the tax payable by the Petitioner so as to harass him by making it impossible for him to appeal, which is ex-facie mala fide.
23. It is further argued by the Petitioner by reference to an egregiously aggravated set of circumstances that evidence of the mala fide actions of the DCT was apparent from the manner in which the DCT tampered with the order sheet of the Petitioner's tax file for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 (details of which are stated in paragraphs 6-21 of the Affidavit-in-Reply in the 1st WP). In this regard, upon a due consideration of all relevant facts and circumstances this Court has arrived at the finding that the DCT, despite being fully aware of the order of this Court dated 8-6-2017 staying operation of the impugned assessment order dated 27-4-2017, resorted to elaborate forgery in an attempt to revise the impugned assessment with effect from a date prior to issuance of the Rule Nisi in the 1st Writ Petition.
24. It has not escaped this Court's attention that the DCT has at no point in time denied that the Petitioner was not resident in Bangladesh during the relevant period. This Court finds in this regard that the Petitioner having taken due care with noticeable promptitude and foresight to make the DCT aware of the Petitioner's non-resident status by a letter dated 23-1-2014 as admittedly received by a member of the DCT's staff on 4-2-2014, and the DCT, accordingly, being fully aware of the non-resident status of the Petitioner at all material time, nevertheless for reasons inexplicable treated him as a resident and taxed him accordingly merely because the Petitioner inadvertently ticked the wrong box. This Court cannot but help conclude in this regard that the DCT has taken undue and unreasonable advantage of an inadvertent mistake of the Petitioner to burden him with a tax liability that the DCT had knowledge was not lawful or justifiable, which is malafide.
25. It follows, therefore, that as a result of the aforesaid matt fide actions of the DCT, the impugned assessment orders are to be regarded as a nullity in the eye of the law. The entire assessment process having been vitiated by rnala fide on the part of the DCT, we are now inclined to accept the submissions made by Mr AF Hassan Ariff that the Petitioner's income be re-assessed as a non-resident. In this regard, this Court has duly considered the judgments as are cited hereinbelow:
(i) Jayanti Lal Patel and others vs Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax and others reported in [1998] 233 ITR 588 (Raj)
73. 'It is proved beyond doubt that the taxation authority has framed assessment orders purely out of malice both in fact and in law. The petitioner's case is a proved case of malice in fact and malice in law. The appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the present case is neither efficacious nor effective remedy. In these circumstances, it can be said that this court has jurisdiction to interfere in the mala fide orders passed by the Assessing Officer.
(ii) Abdul Rauf vs Abdul Hainid Khan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515:
7. 'The decision of the question whether the civil court had jurisdiction in the present case would depend on whether the impugned orders and proceedings were without jurisdiction. There is in this case an attack on the proceeding on the ground of mala fide too. A mala fide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction. A mala fide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a mala fide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment...'
(iii) Nur Mohammad vs Mvi Mainaddin Ahmed reported in 39 DL R (AD) 1
38. , The mala fide act is an act without jurisdiction. No legislature grants power for mala fide exercise of it, and when such mala fide is alleged in fact, the civil courts have the power to investigate and give decisions thereon, '
(iv) Sharnsur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 15 BLC 482
28. ...It is well-settled that mala fide goes to the root of jurisdiction and if the impugned action is mala fide, the alternative remedy provided by statute need not be availed of.
(v) Kamala Devi vs State of UP reported in 2015 (III) ALR 633
12. ‘...Fraud and justice never dwell together. ... Lord Denning observed in a language without equivocation that 'no judgment of a Court, no order of a Minister can be allowed to stand if it has been obtained by fraud, for fraud unravels everything.’
26. It is also evident to this Court from a cursory reading of the impugned assessment orders that the same are based on conjecture and surmise. In proceeding under section 83(2) of the Ordinance, the DCT has to make an assessment on the basis of sufficient materials. It cannot be done arbitrarily or subjectively. In the instant case, the DCT assessed the Petitioner's income for the Assessment Year 2015-2016 and the Assessment Year 2016-2017 to be Taka 1.80 crores and Taka 2 crores respectively without any materials to support such a conclusion. Such finding was made by DCT purportedly on the basis of the seniority and reputation of the Petitioner, although there is no objective indicator of quantifying one's reputation and seniority. As such, and by reference to judgments cited hereinbelow, the DCT's conclusion, not being based on any objective considerations or yardstick, the issuance of the impugned Assessment Orders in either case is found by this Court to be illegal and void:
(i) Mark Builders Ltd. vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 59 DLR 463
16. ‘...Discretion of statutory authority in the exercise of statutory power, particularly in taxation matter, if thought to be unlimited, then exercise of such discretion may result in arbitrariness and selectivity.'
(ii) Ashrafil Kamal vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 21 BLC 594.
12. ‘…..order to deal with the instant Assessee-Applicant, who is an Advocate of the Supreme Court, the exact way to estimate the income lies in the consultation of his professional diary he maintains, and if he fails to furnish the said diary, upon notice under the provisions of section 83(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance, then only the estimation on the basis of other documents can be resorted to but (not) (sic) on whim and caprice of the DCT concerned...'
(iii) Abdul I amid Chy is Commissioner of Taxes reported in 53 DLR 234.
8. ‘….it appears that the Tribunal, in fact, without any basis whatsoever affirmed the estimate of the professional income as well as the family expenses of the assessee applicant.'
(iv) Ali Azam, Advocate vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 53 DLR 92.
4. ... the Assistant Commissioner of Taxes arbitrarily and without material basis subjectively and without giving any opportunity to the applicant assessed the family expenses at Taka 50,000 simply saying that the figure is in keeping with the standard of living of the applicant...'
(v) State of Orissa vs BP Singh Deo reported in AIR 1970 (SC) 670
4. ‘... assessment must be based on some relevant material. It is not a power that can be exercised under the sweet will and pleasure of the concerned authorities..,.'
(vi) Dhirajlal Birdharilal vs Bombay reported in AIR 1955 (SC) 271
9.'.. It is apparent from the judgment of the Tribunal that not only was its approach to the question raised before it tainted with suspicion, but it took into consideration a number of circumstances based purely on conjectures and surmises for which there was not a scintilla of evidence on the record....'
10. ‘.. It is well established that when a court of fact acts on material, partly relevant and partly irrelevant, it is impossible to say to what extent the mind of the court was affected by the irrelevant material used by it in arriving at its finding. Such a finding of fact is vitiated because of the use of inadmissible material, and thereby an issue of law arises.'
(vii) In Re Ram Khelawan and Sahu Thakur This reported in [1939] 7 ITR 607 (All).
Now "local reputation" can hardly be said to be a judicial basis or legal basis under section 13 of the Act and it is contended on behalf of the assessee that the entire assessment is vitiated because it is based on local reputation which is not admissible evidence... (Pg 194, 2nd column) `
‘...and in the present case we find that the Income Tax Officer acted only on local reputation and the conditions of the business during the year and the Assistant Commissioner who heard the appeal against the decision of the Income Tax Officer did not look at least nowhere says that he did — at the previous records.' (Pg 195, 1st column)
(viii) Seth Nathuram Munnalal vs CIT reported in [19541 25 ITR 216 (Nag)
4. ' ...The order is appealable and must stand scrutiny by an appellate court. It must therefore be a speaking order. If the basis and manner of computation are not disclosed in the order, the assessee's right of appeal may be illusory unless the appellate authority refers the matter back to the Income-tax Officer to disclose the basis and manner of his computation...' (Pg 197, 2nd column).
(ix) Dhakeswari Cottton Mills Ltd. vs CIT, West Bengal reported in AIR 1955 (SC) 65
14. ‘... We think that both the Income-tax Officer and the Tribunal in estimating the gross profit rate on sales did not act on any material but acted on pure guess and suspicion....'
15. 'In the result we allow this appeal, set-aside the order of the Tribunal and remand the case to it with directions that in arriving at its estimate of gross profits and sales it should give full opportunity to the assessee to place any relevant material on the point that it has before the Tribunal, whether it is found in the books of account or elsewhere and it should also disclose to the assessee the material on which the Tribunal is going to found it estimate and then afford him full opportunity to meet the substance of any private inquiries made by the Income-tax Officer if it is intended to make the estimate on the foot of those enquiries. ...'
27. Given our findings above that the impugned Assessment Orders are tainted by mala fide and are completely without jurisdiction, the instant Writ Petitions are, consequentially, found to be maintainable even without invoking the appeals forum in the Ordinance. Our finding in this regard is arrived at by full subscription to the rationes decidendi of the following judgments:
(i) Nagin Silk Mill vs Income Tax Officers reported in 15 DLR (SC) 181
7 ' At the same time, it was held that in cases of absence or excess of jurisdiction or where the impugned order suffers from illegality on the face of the record, a certiorari may be granted, even though the right of statutory appeal had not been availed
(ii) Mis Usinania Glass Sheet vs Sales Tax reported in 22 DLR (SC) 443
13. ‘... where it can be said that the impugned order is being challenged on the ground that it suffers from an illegality on the face of the record, and in such cases, an order in the nature of a certioarari could always issue, even though a right of statutory appeal had not been availed of.’
(iii) Calcutta Discount Co. vs ITO reported in AIR 1961 (SC) 372
27....Where such action of an executive authority acting without jurisdiction subjects or is likely to subject a person to lengthy proceedings and unnecessary harassment, the High Courts, it is well-settled, will issue appropriate orders or directions to prevent such consequences.’
(iv) L. Hriday Narirnan vs ITO reported in 78 ITR 26 (SC)
‘Supreme Court set-aside the order of the High Court dismissing the writ petition of the asseseee for mandamus. The Court concluded in the following terms:
‘The appeals must therefore be allowed, and the order passed by the High Court set-aside. Writs will issue directing that the assessment ... for the years 1951-52 and 1952-53 be rectified...’
(v) Ajanta Pharma Ltd. vs Asst. CIT (Born) reported in 267 ITR 200(Bombay).
‘...At the same time it is also well-settled and the decision of the Constitution Bench of the apex Court ... is very clear on the point that mere availability of an alternative relief can be no bar for an exercise of writ jurisdiction when the authorities seek to assume jurisdiction which they do not possess or act in an arbitrary manner.' (last para, middle part)
(vi) JS Parkar vs VB Palekar reported in 94 ITR 616(Bom)
‘... it is by now settled law that existence of an alternative remedy by itself does not amount to an absolute bar to entertainment of the petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. Citizens are entitled to come to this Court and invoke its extraordinary jurisdiction where the impugned orders involve a question of patent lack of jurisdiction, or the question of gross violation of the principles of natural justice, or the question of deciding the vires of the Act or the Rules, or where the impugned order seeks to levy or collect some amount from the citizens without the authority of any law'. (1st Column, 1st para)
vii) Snit Jamila Ansari vs Income Tax Department reported in 225 ITR 490
‘It is true that the Petitioner has such an alternative remedy, but the existence of an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar to the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India -by a High Court.... (2nd Column, last para)
(viii) Saradbhai M Lakhani vs ITO reported in 231 ITR 779 (Guj)
`...Where the action of an executive authority is without jurisdiction, and is likely to subject one to lengthy proceedings and unnecessary harassment, it is well-settled, the High Courts are to issue appropriate orders to prevent such consequences.... (1st column, last para) (ix) Ajit fain vs U01 reported in 242 ITR 302 (Del) The availability of an alternative remedy is not an absolute bar to the entertainment of a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution, though on account of availability of statutory remedies, courts normally do not entertain writ petitions, but where an action is wholly without jurisdiction, and results in infringement of any fundamental right, the plea of alternative remedy is of no avail.' (2nd column, 2nd last para)
(x) Gujarat Gas Co. Ltd. vs Joint CIT reported in 245 ITR 84(Guj)
`Thus, it is clear that ordinarily when an alternative remedy is provided, the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction, but it does not mean that when the order passed by the authority is bad and illegal, the court cannot exercise the jurisdiction. ... (1st column, 2nd para)
(xi) Foramer vs ClT reported in 2471TR 436
‘As regards alternative remedy, we are of the opinion since the notice under section 148 is without jurisdiction, the petitioner should not be relegated to his alternative remedy ...' (1st column, 2nd last para)
(xii) Mercury Travels Ltd. vs Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax reported in 258 ITR 533 (Cal)
‘... It has been observed by the apex court ... that the High Courts have ample powers under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, and are in duty bound thereunder, to issue such appropriate orders or directions as are necessary in order to prevent persons from being subjected to lengthy proceedings and unnecessary harassment by an executive authority acting without jurisdiction. The alternative remedies that are provided by the Income Tax Act, 1961 cannot always be a sufficient reason for refusing relief in a fit and proper case.' (1st column, 1st para)
(xiii) Bangladesh Bank vs Zafar Ahmed reported in 56 DLR (AD) 175
7. 'The principle of law laid down ... is the principle in which the aggrieved person instead of availing the appellate forum could avail the writ jurisdiction in spite of alternative remedy by way of appeal which is not likely to be equally efficacious and effective in the facts and circumstances of the case...' (1st column, 2nd para)
(iv) Assessing Officer, Narayanganj Range vs BE Officer reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 450
25. 'As we have found the impugned action without jurisdiction, the question of availing statutory alternative remedy does not arise. ...'(last column, 2nd last para)
28. It cannot be gainsaid that the order of the DCT is a nullity in the eye of the law in view of the fact that the Petitioner, being a non-resident, the DCT had no lawful authority to treat him as a resident and to compute subjective income for assessment. As such, the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution may be invoked to impugn an order of assessment which is of no legal effect, i.e., a nullity in the eye of the law. In order to substantiate the above proposition of law, the Petitioner begs to quote the following paragraphs from Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed's 'Certiorari: An Administrative Law Remedy':
‘7.25. The jurisdiction for issuance of writ of certiorari in the public law domain could not have been the same as the jurisdiction under section 115 of the CPC of our country in the domain of private law. Yet, Kaikaus, J has the analogy of section 115 before him and justified the view by saying that the language in paragraph (ii) of Article 98(2)(a) is "without lawful authority and is of no legal effect". According to him, if the language was only "without lawful authority" there would have been no difficulty. But those words do not stand by themselves but is followed by the words "is of no legal effect" which mean a "nullity" and further according to him, a determination of a Tribunal acting within its jurisdiction cannot be said "to be of no legal effect" but it is only an act "without jurisdiction" or "excess of jurisdiction" which can be said to be "of no legal effect".
7.26. It is submitted that this said nothing new but followed precedents established by English Courts without being mindful of the fact that there were specific historical and casuistic reasons for making this difference in England in the exercise of the non-entrenched power of the judicial review beset by ouster "no-certiorari" clauses. These were not the right precedents to support the codified language of Article 98. Firstly, the word `jurisdiction' nowhere appears in that Article and secondly, why an action "without lawful authority" of itself should not be a nullity. An action "without lawful authority" whether within or without jurisdiction is a nullity. Any cowcary view can be possible only when one admits of degrees of nullity, when in law there can be no degree of nullity.
……………………………………………..
7.28. In Bangladesh, the same codified language is used in Article 102 as in Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962. However, the language has not been interpreted, and it is submitted that it was about time that it was done in light of the developments in England, now that English courts have freed themselves from jurisdictional and non-jurisdictional fetters which they put around them. Our courts exercising in this field an entrenched constitutional jurisdiction should no longer hesitate to hold that any illegality whether within or without jurisdiction substantially affecting a decision is a 'nullity'. The High Court Division and the Appellate Division should no longer be haunted by older English precedents, established in exercise of a much lesser non-entrenched jurisdiction of judicial review. Also our superior courts should cast aside the fetters out around them by pre-liberation Pakistan precedents begun with lamal Shah.
7.29. In the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs Court of Settlement, it was held that so long as the Court of Settlement acts within jurisdiction and does not commit any excess of jurisdiction, the High Court Division will not interfere. In the case of Ayesha Salauddin vs Chairman, 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka which was a case of no evidence, and could have been disposed of on that ground, the Appellate Division observed as follows:
`The jurisdiction in the nature of certiorari is exercised by the High Court Division to issue such writs where the subordinate Tribunals act wholly without jurisdiction or in the excess of it or in violation of the principles of natural justice or refuse to exercise jurisdiction vested in them or where there is an error apparent on the face of the record.'
7.30. We have seen that the doctrine as to the error of law on the face of the record is definitely obsolete and after 1991 (R vs Hull University Visitor exp Page), the distinction between jurisdictional and non-jurisdictional errors is also obsolete as all errors of law substantially affecting a decision are nullity.
7.31. The ground is well prepared now as it always was but lost by us. Let the great judicial power entrusted to our judges by entrenchment of the jurisdiction of judicial review of administrative and legislative acts be used by them to usher in a new era of a liberal and progressive constitutional order. At the break of the dawn of this order, we will have made the greatest achievement of our life time at the Bar and by our judges in their judicial life time from the Bench. Our citizens shall be assured of effective protection of their guaranteed rights and we all will prosper in freedom."
29. Furthermore, in this Court's view the Petitioner's statements regarding fraud and forgery against the then concerned tax officer do not involve disputed questions of fact. In this regard, it is found that the Petitioner is relying on the documents of the DCT (i.e., (i) Certified copies of the order sheet of the Petitioner's tax records for the Assessment Year 2016-2017 provided by the office of the DCT and (ii) Monthly Tax Assessment Register (Register-4) for the Assessment Years 2016-2017 and 2017-2018 available at the office of the DCT) to demonstrate the commission of fraud by the then concerned officer. There is no scope for the Respondent No. 2 to deny the authenticity/validity of its own documents. Since the Petitioner is not relying on any documents prepared/drawn up by him but is relying entirely on the documents prepared by the office of the DCT, the aforesaid Writ Petitions do not in this Court's view involve any disputed questions of facts. The Appellate Division in the case of Government of Bangladesh & others vs Md Ghularn Mustafa and others reported in 65 DLR (AD) 85, para 20 held as follows:
‘A fact involved in a writ petition does not become disputed simply because the same is denied or disputed by a contending party, unless the veracity of the same is put under challenge or is put under doubt by filing any counter document/paper which, prima facie, renders a fact emerging from a document/ paper annexed to the writ petition relied upon by the writ-petitioner(s) doubtful or questionable,'
30. As such, the aforesaid Writ Petitions are maintainable.
31. Before parting, this Court deems it prudent, and indeed necessary, to address an issue deliberated upon at length on behalf of the Petitioner and considered by this Court to have profound implications on the scope and nature of judicial review of decisions of the income tax authority. This was to do with the nature of assessment after hearing under section 83(2) of the Ordinance.
32. The impugned assessment orders have been passed by the DCT under section 83(2) of the Ordinance (`Assessment after hearing'). `Assessment after hearing' is one of several modes of assessment which have been set out in Chapter IX of the Ordinance (`Assessment').
<u>33. It suffices to note at the outset that of the various modes of assessment set out in Chapter IX, 'assessment after hearing' under section 83(2) is the only form of assessment which expressly calls for giving the assessee a 'hearing' prior to passing an assessment order. As such, a meaningful interpretation has to be given to the term 'hearing', as used in section 83(2).</u>
<u>34. The Petitioner has contended, and aptly so, that the word 'hearing' has deep-rooted implications in the context of an adjudicatory process. In particular, where the obligation of a `hearing' has a statutory basis (as in s. 83(2) of the Ordinance, the process of hearing has to be a meaningful one and must necessarily involve an interaction and exchange of information between the aggrieved individual and the adjudicator. Moreover, a meaningful pre-adjudication hearing presupposes that the aggrieved individual will impart information and/or advance arguments in support of his case during the course of the hearing before the adjudicating authority. Material brought on record attest to the fact that the Petitioner's representative, during the course of the section 83(2) hearing, emphasized on the non-resident status of the Petitioner for the relevant Assessment Years and in consonance with the scope of 'hearing' duly placed supporting facts and materials relating to the Petitioner's non-residency were before the DCT. This Court notes that the DCT, however, did not consider the same without assigning any reason and without recording the submissions of the Petitioner. In this regard, this Court emphasizes that it is well settled that the obligation to hear includes the obligation to consider. Proceeding on that all- important point of reference, this Court now finds that in the instant case there is nothing in the impugned assessment orders to show that the DCT has in fact considered the contentions/statements/ arguments of the Petitioner's representative regarding the fact of the Petitioner's non-residence for the relevant Assessment Years. As such, a proper hearing within the meaning of the law not having been conducted by the DCT, the impugned assessment orders are unavoidably found to be ultra vires section 83(2) of the Ordinance and are struck down as void on this ground as well.</u>
35. It serves all well in this regard to bear in mind certain basic tenets on both the parameters and perimeter of the notion of 'hearing' considered in its true substantive sense. Accordingly, and in support of the aforesaid finding, this Court enumerates below certain analyses of the substantive meaning to- be accorded to the notion of hearing as adverted to in particular by the learned Senior Advocate Mr AF Hassan Ariff appearing for the Petitioner in both Writ Petitions. The Petitioner relies on the following cases and materials:
(i) Black's Law Dictionary
Hearing: .’..it consists of any confrontation, oral or otherwise, between an affected individual and an agency decision maker sufficient to allow the individual to present his case in a meaningful manner'. (Pg 207, 2nd column (top part).
(ii) Aiyar's Advanced Law Lexicon
‘The words 'Hear the Argument' does not mean that the justices shall literally hear the argument, but means that the argument shall be considered by the Court'. (Pg 211, 1st column, top part) `A provision that certain matters shall be `heard and finally determined' by an inferior court does not oust the jurisdiction of the High Court. (Pg 211,1st column, 4th paragraph) `Authority to hear and determine a cause is jurisdiction to try and decide all the questions involved in the controversy.' (Pg 211, 1st column, 6th para).
(iii) Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases
See for meaning of 'Heard and finally determined' (Pg 215, last para) which is the same as in (ii) above.
(iv) Sham Lai (Dead) vs Atme Nand Jain Sabha, Dal Bazar reported in AIR 1987 (SC) 197
'15. The principles that can be deduced from the plethora of case law on the point, including the authorities referred to above, are consistent with the literal meaning of word 'hearing' which in its Dictionary sense means 'the listening of evidence and pleading in Court of law, the trial of a cause'.
(v) Sohan Singh Ram Singh vs Hans Raj repotted in AIR 1960 (P&II) 34
5. 'Now, what is the meaning of the expression "hearing" in its application to the particular facts and circumstances of this case? To "hear" implies that there is someone before the Court to speak, In a broad general sense the expression "hearing" is applied to the consideration of a case before a person clothed with judicial or quasi-judicial powers at the several stages of its progress, subsequent to its inception,'
(vi) Mehjabeen Simon vs Fayaz Ahmad Simon reported in AIR 2006 (J&K) 105
36. On the question further of what the word `hearing' means, the following reference material bear particular significance in this Court's view:
(a) 'In Black's Law Dictionary, the meaning of word 'hearing' is given as under: hearing. A judicial session, usu., open to the public, held for the purpose of deciding issues of fact or of law, sometimes with witnesses testifying.'
(b) 'In New Webster's Dictionary, the meaning of word 'hearing' is given as under: hearing an opportunity to be heard — Law, preliminary investigation of a case to determine its validity; a judicial investigation before a Court'.
(c) 'In Oxford Dictionary, the meaning of word 'hearing' is given as under: hearing an opportunity to state one's case (give them a fair hearing), the listening to evidence and pleadings in a law Court'.
(e) 'The "hearing" means a positive hearing i.e. parties are to be heard or listened but when a party has no notice of posting of the case then how it can be said that case was adjourned and posted for hearing'.
(f) 'The hearing means recording of evidence, taking steps for taking the case to its logical conclusion, examination of questions involved in the suit, considering the arguments.'
37. In view of the above, the Rules Nisi in both Writ Petitions are found to merit a favourable consideration by this Court given that the impugned Assessment Orders dated 27-12-2016 and 27-4-2017 in the Writ Petitions are found to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Consequentially the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Taxes Circle-164, Tax Zone-8 is, hereby, directed to reassess the Petitioner's tax for the Assessment Years 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 as a non-resident,
38. In light of the above, and upon finding merit in the two Writ Petitions and substance in the Rules Nisi, both these Rules Nisi are, hereby, made absolute subject to the direction above.
There is no Order as to costs.
Communicate this Judgment and Order at once.
End.

Secretary, Ministry of Land and others………………….   Respondents
full_judgment:
SM Masud Hossain Dolon, J: By filing this writ petition, under article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the petitioner challenged the legality of the judgment and decree dated 28-9-2022 passed by the learned Judge, Land Survey Tribunal, (Joint District Judge) Madaripur in Land Survey Suit No.309 of 2020.
2. The main contention of the writ petition is that as the appellate forum of the said judgment and decree i.e. the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal has not been established, therefore the petitioner has/have no other alternative forum but to file this writ petition.
3. Heard the learned Advocate for the Respondent, perused the writ petition along with its annexures, and other materials on record placed before us.
<u>4. It appears that some factual aspects are involved with the impugned judgment and decree and the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal is the proper forum to adjudicate the same. It also appears that till filing this writ petition no Land Survey Appellate Tribunal was established, but during the pendency of the Rule the Government has established the same.</u>
5. In view of the aforesaid, we are of the view that justice would be best served if without entering into the merit of the case the Rule is disposed of with directions.
6. Accordingly, the Rule is disposed of with the following directions:
(i) The petitioner is at liberty to file an appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal as established by the Government;
(ii) If the petitioner intends to prefer an appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal having jurisdiction, the petitioners are directed to file such appeal within 90 (ninety) days from date;
(iii) The impugned judgment shall remain stayed till filing of appeal by the instant petitioner within the period set out in direction No, (ii); and
(iv)The parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of possession of the land in question till filing of the appeal.
7. However, there shall be no order as to costs.
Communicate the judgment and order at once.
End.
