Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Legislative Drafting Division and others --------- Respondents [In both the writ petitions]
full_judgment:
Naima Haider, J: A Larger Bench was constituted to hear and dispose of the instant writ petitions given the important questions of law involved. Since similar questions of facts and law are involved, these writ petitions are taken up together for hearing and disposed of by this single Judgment.
2. The writ petitioners challenged the legality of sections 9, 13 and 14 of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ (hereinafter referred to as the "2001 Act"). They also challenged the legality of the inclusion of the petitioners' respective property in the schedule of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি. Compensation for wrongful inclusion is also sought for in these writ petitions.
3. In Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2012, Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms:
Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to as to why the provisions of sections 13 and 14 of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ (Act XVI of 2001) as amended till date should not be declared to be void and as to why inclusion of the petitioner's land measuring 0.1350 acres in plot No. 3364 of SA Khatian No. 1290 (corresponding to RS Khatian No. 10342 as evident from Annexure-A to the writ petition) under Mouza Bainakhamar, Police Station and District Khulna in the Ka Schedule of vested property published in Bangladesh Gazette Extra ordinary dated 2-5-2012 at page 34942 against serial No. 8 should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
4. In Writ Petition No. 17187 of 2012, Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms: Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why section 9, 13 and 14 of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ should not be declared void and inclusion of house of the petitioner on BS Plot No. 6069 of Mauza Dahshin Kattoli under police station-Double Mooring within District-Chittagong in the "Ka" schedule of প্রত্যর্পণ যোগ্য অর্পিত সম্পত্তি at serial No. 252 at page No. 9236 of the Bangladesh Gazette published on 8-4-2012 and taking over possession of the house on 20-11-2012 should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and as to why the respondents should not be directed to restore possession of the house to the petitioner with adequate compensation and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
5. The disposal of these writ petitions depend primarily on interpretation of law and therefore, detailed facts are discussed, only to the extent needed.
6. The facts which are relevant is that the petitioners' respective property have been treated as vested property under the 2001 Act; the petitioners claim that the properties in question are not vested properties and the inclusion in the list prepared under the 2001 Act was illegal and therefore the properties should be released from the list. For the wrongful inclusion in the list, the petitioners claim compensation.
7. Mr Qumrul Hoque Siddique, Senior Advocate, appearing for the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No. 10614 of 2012 takes us through the writ petition and the documents annexed therein. He also takes us through the provisions of the 2001 Act. Mr Hoque submits that sections 2, 7, 8, 9, 13 and 14 of the 2001 Act are inconsistent with Article 31 of the Constitution and consequentially void. Mr Hoque, having placed emphasis on section 9 and section 2 of the 2001 Act, submits that the cumulative effect of the said provisions is that unfettered power is placed upon low profile public officials to include any property in the K or L schedule of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি list; this is according to Mr Hoque inconsistent with the spirit of the rule of law as enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution. With regard to section 13 of the 2001 Act, Mr Hoque submits that the said provision, so far it relates to "abetment of pending proceeding or suits" tantamount to forfeiture of rights acquired on property thorough legal proceeding and, as such, the provision is unconstitutional. Mr Hoque also submits that operation of section 14 of the 2001 Act tantamount to confiscation of property which is unconstitutional. Mr Hoque also referring to the scheme of the 2001 Act argues that the legislation only permits the "owners" to take steps to release property; others with interest in the listed property are not permitted to take steps for release, despite their interest. According to Mr Hoque, such limited right results in violation of the rights of others, who may have proprietary interest in the property listed as vested property.
8. Mr Hoque submits that if section 9 of the 2001 Act, which deals with publication of list of returnable vested property is declared unconstitutional then petitioner's property which was included in the list will automatically be released and the issue of referring disputes before the Tribunal constituted under the 2001 Act will not arise. Primarily on these counts, the learned Counsel submits that the Rule should be made absolute and that the property in question pertaining to Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2012 should be released from the list of vested property.
9. The learned Counsel appearing in Writ Petition No. 17187 of 2012 adopts the submissions of Mr Hoque. However, he adds that section 14 of the 2001 Act provides wide powers to the Deputy Commissioner to lease out any property as soon as the property is listed ক or খ schedule; such power, according to the learned Counsel is violative of Article 42 of the Constitution. He also submits that though alternative forum has been provided in the 2001 Act for adjudication of dispute, through section 13 of the said legislation, right to seek justice before any civil Court has been taken away which is violative of the fundamental rights as guaranteed by the Constitution. In respect of his case, the learned Counsel submits that eviction of the petitioner from his house/property subsequent to the inclusion is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. On these counts, the learned Counsel submits that the Rule should be made absolute.
10. The Rules are opposed. In Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2012, the respondent Nos.2 and 3 filed two separate Affidavits in Opposition. In Writ Petition No. 17187 of 2012, the respondent No.2 filed an Affidavit-in-Opposition and Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition.
11. Mr Sk. Md Morshed, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the Act 16 of 2001 being an ordinary piece of legislation cannot take away the jurisdiction of the High Court Division or Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh devolved upon it under the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
12. He next submits that the case of Bangladesh & another vs Md Salimullah, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 1 is not applicable for adjudicating the present issue as because the issue considered in the said reported case is regarding the proclamation of March, 24 of 1982 whereby the power and jurisdiction of the High Court Division and Appellate Division was suspended, but in the instant matter, the constitutional provision is in operation and the Supreme Court has been exercising its jurisdiction under the constitution.
13. He further submits that the Act No. 16 of 2001 being an ordinary piece of legislation cannot take away the jurisdiction of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh, High Court Division as well as of the Appellate Division enshrined/devolved upon it by the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ ( Act No. 16 of 2001) since an ordinary piece of legislation and simultaneously a "beneficial piece of legislation" the pending proceedings in the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh, High Court Division as well as in the Appellate Division will not be abated under section 13(1) of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১. To substantiate the prayer against section 14 of the Act, 2001, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that this is also not legally tenable as because until and unless the প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি is released/delisted in accordance with law from the list of vested properties, government as the custodian of the প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি has the lawful authority and under an obligation to control/manage the same. The said authority of the government is absolute and exercisable till the property is within the list of প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি as published under section 9 of the Act, 2001.
14. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents vehemently opposes the Rules issued. Taking us through the 2001 Act and also the scheme of the legislation, he submits that the 2001 Act is clear and unambiguous and the provisions therein are not unconstitutional. He also points out that the 2001 Act is a special legislation; on this count he questions whether this Division can or should interfere in any provisions of such special legislation. Taking us through the factual background leading to filing of the writ petitions, he submits that disputed questions of facts are involved in both the writ petitions and this Division, in exercise of powers under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot intervene. Primarily on these arguments, he submits that the Rules should be discharged.
15. We have perused the writ petitions, the Affidavits in Opposition and the documents annexed in the petitions. We have also taken note of the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels for the petitioners and the respondents.
16. To begin with, we shall first address the issue of the scope or whether there is limited scope for interference by this Division.
17. It is our view that a law is special when it is different from others of the same general kind or designed for a particular purpose, or limited in range or confined to a prescribed field of action or operation. Similar view was adopted by the Indian High Court in Surya Mohan Thakur vs State of Bihar (1951 AIR (Pat) 4621 where it was held that special law means law enacted for special cases and in special circumstances as distinguished from the general law which applies generally. It is the considered view of this Division that the 2001 Act falls within the meaning of special law since this legislation was enacted for with a specific purpose and does not have general applicability.
18. The issue now revolves around interpretation of status of special laws. A special law, no doubt, has a "special status"; thus for instance, if there is a conflict between special law and general law, special law will prevail. But this interpretation is attributable only if the conflict is with "general law" and not when the conflict is with the Constitution.
19. Article 7 of the Constitution provides for "Supremacy of the Constitution", Article 7(2) provides "This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with the Constitution that law shall, to the extent of inconsistency, be void". Article 152(1) of the Constitution provides for certain definitions including the definition of "law". Under Article 152(1), law means "Any Act, ordinance, order, rule, regulation, bye-law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage, having the force of law in Bangladesh". Law, as defined under Article 152 is drafted quite widely and in simple term means "any instrument having legal binding effect" and no doubt, includes "special law". Article 152 does not make a distinction between general law and special law and it is for this reason, the word "any" was used. Our interpretation is this that Article 152 negatives any superior status of "special law" so far it relates to the Constitution.
20. We also take this opportunity to refer to Article 26 of the Constitution. Article 26(1) of the Constitution provides that "All existing laws inconsistent with the provisions of this Part III shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, become void on the commencement of the Constitution". Thus, under the Constitution and in particular, from reading of Articles 7 and 26 affirms the position that Parliament is not at liberty to enact legislation which is either inconsistent with the Constitutional provisions or has the effect of nullifying the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part HI of the Constitution.
21. In the instant writ petitions, the writ petitioners have challenged the constitutionality of certain provisions of the 2001 Act and also challenged the legality of inclusion of their properties in the vested property list. They have also claimed compensation for the alleged wrongful inclusion.
22. Under the 2001 Act, a Tribunal is constituted for taking steps to release %. The petitioners have challenged provisions of the 2001 Act in order to by-pass the statutory requirement of having the disputes heard by the Tribunal. Furthermore, we agree with Mr Hoque that if section 9 of the 2001 Act is declared unconstitutional, then the Tribunal would automatically lack jurisdiction to adjudicate and properties listed in the schedule would be released. As such, we find it prudent to address the issue of constitutionality of the provisions of 2001 Act which are under challenge. The issue relating to legality of inclusion of petitioners' property will be addressed later.
23. In the instant writ petitions, we are dealing with constitutionality of a primary legislation. In case of primary legislation, there is a presumption in favour of constitutionality. This means, primary legislation as a whole or any provision(s) thereof will not be declared unconstitutional unless the writ petitioner can clearly show, beyond doubt, that the same is violative of Article 7 or Part III of the Constitution. It may happen that the argument advanced in favour of declaring a statutory provision unconstitutional is convincing but on a reasonable alternative interpretation, the provision can be concluded to be constitutional; in such a case, it is a settled principle that the Court should apply the doctrine of "reading in" and adopt the interpretation that favours constitutionality.
24. In the writ petitions, sections 9, 13 and 14 of the 2001 Act have been challenged as being void. But void for what? Which provisions of the Constitution have been offended? That is not set out, though the Rule issuing order ought to have it spelt out clearly. The terms of the Rule are defective and vague. It is our unanimous view that when constitutionality of statutory provisions is challenged, it is imperative that Rule should not only seek a declaration that the provision(s) under challenge should be declared unconstitutional but also state which Constitutional provisions are violated and then proceed for a declaration that the provisions impugned are void. We note that both Articles 7 and 26 of the Constitution use the word "void"; the use of this word relates to the "consequence" of any law being either inconsistent with the Constitution or violative of Part III of the Constitution; nothing more. Therefore, the use of the word "void" in the Rule issuing order, without the mandatory requirements of a Rule issuing order, as noted above, is neither here nor there-one of the reason is that the Division Bench would not be imply into the Rule issuing order. In our view, the term of the Rule issuing orders, so far it relates to the statutory provision, is defective. This on its own is sufficient reason for this Division not to intervene. However, given that the writ petitions have been referred before the Larger Bench in view of important questions of law, we nevertheless shall proceed to assess whether the impugned provisions are actually unconstitutional.
25. To begin with, we turn our attention to Ground No. I, as set out in Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2012. Thorough the said Ground, certain sub-provisions of section 2 and sections 7, 8, 9, 13 and 14 were argued to be unconstitutional. The Rule issued in the said writ petition refers to sections 13 and 14 only. Therefore, there is no reason for us to deal with the constitutionality of any provision of the 2001 Act which is not expressly challenged in either of the writ petitions. If we do otherwise, we would imply into the Rule issuing order and would travel beyond the ambit of the Rule. That we cannot do and this is settled by the Hon'ble Appellate Division.
26. The purpose behind enactment of the 2001 Act is particularly important. The 2001 Act was enacted to expedite the return/release certain properties listed as vested properties to the real owners or successors. This would be evident from the Preamble of the 2001 Act, which reads as follows: "অর্পিত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে তালিকাভুক্ত কতিপয় সম্পত্তি বাংলাদেশী মূল মালিক বা তাহার বাংলাদেশী উত্তরাধিকারী বা উক্ত মূল মালিক বা উত্তরাধিকারীর বাংলাদেশী স্বার্থাধিকারী (Successor-in-interest) এর নিকট প্রত্যর্পণ এবং আনুষাঙ্গিক বিষয়াদি সম্পর্কে বিধান প্রণয়নকল্পে প্রণীত আইন। যেহেতু অর্পিত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে তালিকাভুক্ত কতিপয় সম্পত্তি বাংলাদেশী মূল মালিক বা তাহার বাংলাদেশী উত্তরাধিকারী বা উক্ত মূল মালিক বা উত্তরাধিকারীর বাংলাদেশী স্বার্থাধিকারী (Successor-in-interest) এর নিকট প্রত্যর্পণ এবং আনুষাঙ্গিক বিষয়াদি সম্পর্কে বিধান প্রণয়ন সমীচীন ও প্রয়োজনীয়; সেহেতু এতদ্বারা নিম্নরূপ আইন করা হইল। For this purpose, Tribunal has been constituted and the decree of the Tribunal shall be enforced by the concerned Deputy Commissioner in light of section 11 of the 2001 Act. In essence, through this legislation, the Government intended to set up a specialized Tribunal to deal with vested property disputes and at the same time, ensure that the decree holder obtains the benefit of the decree of the Tribunal and in order to do so, placed an obligation upon the concerned Deputy Commissioner to enforce the decree. The main idea behind enactment of the 2001 Act is that issues pertaining to vested property shall be dealt with by a specialized Court.
27. Section 9 of the 2001 Act is under challenge. The ground of challenge is that section 9 read with section 2(), 2(4i) and 2M confers unfettered power in that among others, the said provision authorizes low profile public servants to include any immovable property in the schedule of vested property. Provision conferring unfettered discretion upon the executives may in certain circumstances be construed as unconstitutional. However, what is important is whether section 9 actually confers such unfettered discretionary power. Section 9 of the 2001 Act is quoted below for ease of reference:

28. Having gone through section 9 of the 2001 Act, what seems to be the case is that it places an obligation upon the Government to publish, within a stipulated time, in the official Gazette a list of প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি; the said provision also contains what information are to be provided in the list to be published. Under section 9(4), in the event any vested property is acquired for public purpose, details pertaining to the acquisition, for instance, compensation paid, must be in the list to be published. Once the list is prepared, section 9(5) of the 2001 Act places an obligation upon the Government to inform the citizens of the list so prepared; this is to facilitate the citizens to take necessary steps. Section 9(6) of the 2001 Act merely states that after publication of the list in the Official Gazette, property not included in the list shall not be treated as vested property and in respect of such property, সরকারের কোন স্বত্ব, স্বার্থ, অধিকার বা দায়-দায়িত্ব থাকিবে না।
29. The term প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি, as set out in section 9 is defined in section 2(ঞ) of the 2001 Act and means vested property, under the laws relating to vested property, which was, prior to the 2001 Act coming into force, under the control or possession of the Government or those properties which are প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য জনহিতকর সম্পত্তি section 2(ক) of the 2001 Act defines vested property to mean property which is vested under the laws relating to vested property and section 2(ট) merely provides that list of প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি is that which is prepared under section 9 of the 2001 Act.
30. In our view, section 9 of the 2001 Act is a step towards release of প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি to the rightful owners. Section 9 merely deals with publication of a list and once published, creates an obligation to inform the citizens of such list so that they can take steps before the appropriate form, being the Tribunal. section 9(6) of the 2001 [(৬) এই ধারার অধীনে 'ক' তফসিলে বর্ণিত এবং গেজেটে প্রকাশিত সম্পত্তির তালিকায় অন্তর্ভুক্ত নহে এমন কোন সম্পত্তি বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না এবং উহাতে অর্পিত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে সরকারের কোন স্বত্ব, স্বার্থ, অধিকার বা দায়-দায়িত্ব থাকিবে না।] is noteworthy in the sense that unless a property appears in the list prepared under section 9, there is no scope to treat any property as vested. Section 9(6) of the 2001 Act therefore puts an end to the power of the Government to include property through publication of a new list.
31. Section 9 of the 2001 Act on its own or read with sections 2(ক). 2(ঞ) and/or 2(ট) do not in any way infringe the fundamental rights of the petitioners in the writ petition. Not only that section 9 on its own or read with sections 2(ক). 2(ক) or 2(ট) of the 2001 Act does not appear to be inconsistent with the Constitutional scheme. Furthermore, having perused the relevant provisions, we fail to see how this provision conferred unfettered discretion upon the Government officials, as alleged or at all. Therefore, there is no scope to hold that section 9 of the 2001 Act is unconstitutional.
32. Section 14 of the 2001 Act has also been challenged by the petitioners on the ground that the said provision confiscates proprietary right. Confiscation of proprietary right, in broad sense takes place when there is deprivation of right to property without due process of law. Acquisition without payment of compensation could be an example of confiscation of proprietary right. The issue is whether section 14 of the 2001 Act has the effect of such confiscation and if so, whether it would be construed as being unconstitutional.
33. Section 14 of the 2001 Act is set out below for ease of reference:
১৪। [(১) [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য। সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ না হওয়া পর্যন্ত উক্ত সম্পত্তি জেলা প্রশাসকের নিয়ন্ত্রণে থাকিবে এবং তিনি প্রচলিত আইন অনুযায়ী উহা ইজারা প্রদান করিবেন।]
(২) উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লিখিত ইজারা প্রদত্ত সম্পত্তির দখল প্রত্যর্পণের জন্য ট্রাইব্যুনালের ডিক্রী থাকিলে, তদানুযায়ী ডিক্রী প্রাপককে ধারা ১১ তে বর্ণিত পদ্ধতিতে উক্ত সম্পত্তির দখল বুঝাইয়া দিতে হইবে।
34. Section 14 of the 2001 Act merely sets how any particular প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি would be dealt with prior to release to the rightful persons. প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি, simply put, means vested property which is under the control or possession of the Government but that which is returnable. Section 14(1) has two parts; the first part is that any প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি, till released shall be under the control of Deputy Commissioner and the second part provides that প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ না হওয়া পর্যন্ত the concerned Deputy Commissioner shall lease the property.
35. প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি by necessary implication means those properties under the control of the Government. The Government is represented by the Deputy Commissioner under section 14. The Deputy Commissioner is the highest administrative executive in any district. It is only logical that the control over such property, till released, be with him. Section 14(1) does not end with control. It deals with utilization. It would make no sense if property remains unutilized, particularly given the scarcity of land. Therefore, section 14(1) places obligation upon the concerned Deputy Commissioner to lease the property; this obligation ensures maximization of utilization of resources and at the same time, ensures revenue. Section 14(1) of the 2001 Act is extremely rational. Section 14(2) of the 2001 Act provides further facility to the person in whose favour প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি  is released by the Tribunal. Under section 14(2) of the 2001 Act, even if the property is leased out, once the Tribunal passes as decree, the concerned Deputy Commissioner shall take steps to hand over possession of the property to the ডিক্রী প্রাপক. This provision ensures that the decree holder does not have to initiate any further proceedings to have the property under his possession. This provision it seems has been enacted to reduce the multiplicity of proceeding.
36. In light of the aforesaid, section 14(1) and (2) of the 2001 Act are rational and cannot be construed to result in confiscation of proprietary right, as alleged. Section 14 of the 2001 Act is not, in our view, unconstitutional. However, we wish to note that the power of the Deputy Commissioner, জেলা প্রশাসক, under section 14(1) should be exercised with caution so that it does not permit any public servant to infringe any fundamental right to property and if there be any infringement of any fundamental right, it should not be a bar to seek remedy under act, 102(1) of the Constitution.
37. At this juncture, we wish to attend to one ancillary submission made by the learned Counsels for the petitioners. It was submitted that under the 2001 Act only মালিক and none other has the right to apply for release; this in effect curtails the proprietary right of others who might have acquired interest. Section 10 of the 2001 Act had been referred to substantiate this submission. Section 10 of the 2001 Act reads as follows:
১০। (১) [ধারা ৯ এর অধীন গেজেটে প্রকাশিত ক তফসিলভুক্ত অর্পিত সম্পত্তির মালিক উক্ত সম্পত্তি তাহার অনুকূলে প্রত্যর্পণের জন্য, উক্ত সম্পত্তির তালিকা প্রকাশের ৩[৩০০ (তিনশত)। দিনের মধ্যে, ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট আবেদন করিতে পারিবেন এবং আবেদনের সহিত তাহার দাবীর সমর্থনে সকল কাগজপত্র সংযুক্ত করিবেন। The word মালিক as used in section 10 of the 2001 Act is a defined term. section 2 (d) of the 2001 Act defines the term মালিক. Under section 2, মালিক includes the main owner or his/her successor in interest or in their absence "Co-sharer in possession by lease or in any form". Section 10(1) cannot be read in isolation; it has to be read in light with section 2 (d). That being the case, anyone who is a মালিক within the meaning of section 2 (d) i.e. main owner or his/her successor in interest or in their absence "Co-sharer in possession by lease or in any form" may apply for release. Accordingly, we find no substance in the argument advanced by the learned Counsels for the petitioners that only main owners have the right to relief under the 2001 Act.
38. The petitioners have also challenged section 13 of the 2001 Act. The said provision deals with প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত মামলার abatement, কার্যধারা বন্ধ ও ট্রাইব্যুনালে দাবী উত্থাপন, The relevant part of section 13 of the 2001 is set out below for ease of reference:
১৩। (১) [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা] সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে যদি কোন আদালতে এমন দেওয়ানী মামলা অনিষ্পন্ন থাকে যাহাতে উক্ত তালিকায় অন্তর্ভুক্ত কোন সম্পত্তিতে স্বত্ব দাবী করিয়া বা উহা অর্পিত সম্পত্তি মর্মে দাবী করিয়া কোন প্রতিকার প্রার্থনা করা হইয়াছে, বা যদি তত্ত্বাবধায়কের নিকট এমন কোন কার্যধারা অনিষ্পন্ন থাকে যাহাতে উক্ত সম্পত্তিকে ি[প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা হইতে অবমুক্তির আবেদন করা হইয়াছে, তাহা হইলে-
(ক) [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা] সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে উক্ত মামলায় উক্ত সম্পত্তি যতটুকু জড়িত ততটুকু বাবদ মামলাটি আপনা আপনি abeted হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে;
(খ) এইরূপ abetment এর জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট আদালত কর্তৃক আনুষ্ঠানিক আদেশ প্রদানের বাধ্যবাধকতা থাকিবে না, এবং উক্ত তারিখে পর এইরূপ সম্পত্তির বিষয়ে উক্ত আদালত প্রদত্ত কোন আদেশ (আনুষ্ঠানিক abetment আদেশ ব্যতীত) কার্যকারিতা থাকিবে না; এর
(গ) উক্ত তালিকা সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে তত্ত্বাবধায়ক উক্ত কার্যধারা কার্যক্রম বন্ধ করিবেন এবং উক্ত তারিখের পর এইরূপ সম্পত্তির বিষয়ে তত্ত্বাবধায়ক প্রদত্ত আদেশ (কার্যক্রম বন্ধকরণের আদেশ ব্যতীত) এর কার্যকারিতা থাকিবে না।
(২) উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লিখিত সম্পত্তির মালিক উহা প্রত্যর্পণের জন্য বা উক্ত সম্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে ধারা ৬ প্রযোজ্য হইলে সংশ্লিষ্ট স্বার্থবান ব্যক্তি উহা [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা] হইতে অবমুক্তির জন্য বা জনস্বার্থে অধিগ্রহনকৃত অর্পিত সম্পত্তির বিপরীতে প্রদেয় ক্ষতিপূরণের জন্য ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট, এবং কোন সম্পত্তি প্রত্যপর্ণযোগ্য জনহিতকর সম্পত্তি হইলে উক্ত ধারায় উল্লিখিত ব্যক্তি জেলা প্রশাসকের নিকট, আবেদন করিতে পারিবেন।
(৩) এইরূপ আবেদন উপস্থাপন ও নিষ্পত্তির ও সংশ্লিষ্ট ডিক্রী বাস্তবায়নের ক্ষেত্রে ধারা ১০, ১১ এবং ক্ষেত্রমত ধারা ১৫ এর বিধানাবলী প্রযোজ্য হইবে।
39. The issue regarding section 13 is simple. Simply put, the issue is whether abetment of proceedings could be construed as unconstitutional. The effect of abetment of proceeding under the 2001 Act is that the proceeding in continuation will no longer continue before the Court concerned but will be heard by the Tribunal. It is in this context, we would wish to point out that "abetment of proceeding" in the absence of alternative forum and "abetment of proceeding" where this is alternative forum have different implications. In the former case, the effect of abetment may tantamount to curtailment of right to seek protection of law which could be argued to be unconstitutional. However, in the latter case (as in the present context), it simply implies a transfer of proceeding; the dispute relating to returning of property, which was pending before a particular Court, will now be heard by the Tribunal under the 2001 Act. This does not amount to any Constitutional violation(s) unless the Tribunal lacked the power of effective adjudication. In the present context, lack of power of effective adjudication may arise from the lack of authority to decide title of property, lack of authority of the Tribunal to consider relevant documents, lack of authority of the Tribunal to take account of executive order(s) or Judgments passed earlier, etc.
40. The Tribunal constituted under the 2001 Act is a special forum, specifically established to expedite the disposal of the disputes pertaining to vested property. Sections 6 and 12 are of particular importance. The relevant part of section 6 and section 12 are set out as follows:
৬। [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকায়। নিম্নবর্ণিত সম্পত্তি অন্তর্ভুক্তি করা যাইবে না, যথা:-
(ক) কোন সম্পত্তি অর্পিত সম্পত্তি নহে এই আইন প্রবর্তনের পূর্বে যথাযথ আদালত চূড়ান্ত সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিয়া থাকিলে সেই সম্পত্তি;
(খ) এই আইন প্রবর্তনের পূর্বে যে কোন সময় তত্ত্বাবধায়ক কর্তৃক অর্পিত সম্পত্তির তালিকা হইতে অবমুক্ত করা হইয়াছে এরূপ কোন সম্পত্তি;
১২। এই আইনের অধীনে কোন সম্পত্তি [প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য] সম্পত্তির তালিকা) হইতে অবমুক্তির সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করা হইলে-
(ক) উক্ত সম্পত্তি ধারা ৬ তে উল্লিখিত প্রকারের সম্পত্তি হওয়ার বিষয়ে চূড়ান্ত হইবে; এবং
(খ) ..............
41. Thus, the effect of section 12, read with section 6 of the 2001 Act is that if any property is wrongly included in the list of vested property despite the fact that the property is released through executive order or declared not to be a vested property by a competent Court, then Tribunal has jurisdiction to hold that inclusion of such property is unlawful. Though this is not directly on the issue of "abetment of proceeding", these two provisions clearly indicate that the Tribunal has the power to take account of Judgments passed or executive orders issued.
42. The Tribunal was set up under section 16 of the 2001 Act and section 17 deals with the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Section 17(2) clearly provides that unless the issue relates to property in the schedule, the Tribunal shall summarily reject the application filed. This means that the Tribunal is constituted only for the purpose of dealing with property listed in the Schedule prepared under the 2001 Act. Section 17 is to be read with section 10 which provides for, among others, the timeframe within which application before the Tribunal would need to be filed for release of property, the procedure, the Tribunal would follow in adjudication of any dispute referred to it. We note that section 10 requires application before the Tribunal to be substantiated by supporting documents, if any. This means that the applicant filing the application for release can enclose any such documents that may be relevant in support of release of the property. Document includes, title deeds, evidence of possession etc. Since Tribunal can consider judgments passed by civil Court, such judgment is also within the purview of documents. After consideration of the documents and after hearing the parties, the Tribunal would either refuse or allow the application. In case of the latter, once the Tribunal passes the decree by allowing the application, the concerned Deputy Commissioner is statutorily obligated to hand over the possession within specified time, unless the decree is stayed by the Appellate Tribunal under the 2001 Act. What is clear is that the procedurally, the Tribunal is empowered to significant extent to deal with the issue. Not only that, the Tribunal's decree is binding and statutorily enforceable by the Deputy Commissioner; no intervention of the applicant is necessary.
43. In respect of cases under the 2001 Act, what is relevant is title and possession. True, the Tribunal can consider any documents but the issue is whether the Tribunal is empowered to deal with title of the property. if after considering everything, Tribunal is not empowered to decide on the title, then it would have been argued that the adjudicating power of the Tribunal is illusory or inadequate requiring intervention. But that in our view is not the case. The Tribunal, after hearing is required to form two opinions: (i) whether the property in question should be released; and (b) if so, whether the release should be in favour of the applicant. In order to decide on the issue set out in (i) in the paragraph, the Tribunal can, by necessary implication determine title of the property in question. This is a sensible interpretation. We find support in our conclusion in the Judgment passed by this Division in Civil Revision No. 545 of 2021 wherein the High Court Division held—
"...However, in deciding whether such properties should be released in favour of the said claimant or applicant, the Tribunal is required to determine whether the said claimant or applicant has established his prima facie title in the said property, and this obligation of the Tribunal to determine prima-facie title become more relevant when we see sub-clause (Gila) of sub-section (8) of section 10 of the said Act..."
<u>44. From the aforesaid, in our view, it is clear that the Tribunal constituted under the 2001 Act is fully competent to deal with all aspects in order to decide whether decree of release should be passed in favour of the applicant. Therefore, in the context of the 2001 Act, the provision dealing with "abetment of proceeding" cannot be construed as unconstitutional since alternative and competent forum is available to decide the issue of release. As we said before, the proceeding would be automatically abated which will permit the litigant to refer the dispute to the Tribunal formed for this purpose. The concept is akin to "transfer of case". No one would be left without an effective forum. Not only that, judgments passed earlier in respect of the property in question, by competent Civil Court can be taken into account. The 2001 Act does not invalidate the judgments passed, if any. That being the case, we are inclined to hold that section 13 of the 2001 is not unconstitutional.</u>
45. We now focus on certain peculiar factual aspect pertaining to Writ Petition No. 17187 of 2012. In the said writ petition, the writ petitioner, after coming to know that the property was listed in the Gazette, filed an application before the Tribunal under section 10(1) of the 2001 Act and the case has been registered as Tribunal Case No. 1370 of 2012. Subsequently, according to the petitioner, when steps were taken for eviction, his Advocate informed him that Tribunal lacked authority to prevent eviction. This, as it appears, compelled the petitioner to file the instant writ petition. The petitioner challenged not only the vires of the law but also the inclusion of the property in question in the Schedule of vested property. Rule was issued accordingly. This means that the petitioner brought the subject matter before Tribunal Case No. 1370 of 2012 to this Division for hearing. We would just wish to add that had the petitioner pursued his case before the Tribunal and if the Tribunal passed decree in favour of the writ petitioner, he would have been able to be in possession by now, though the concerned Deputy Commissioner as the 2001 Act imposes obligation upon the Deputy Commissioner to enforce the decree of the Tribunal within a stipulated time.
46. We have perused the factual aspects set out in Writ Petition No. 10164 of 2012. We find nothing in the pleading that justifies as in assuming the role of the Tribunal with the view to decide whether the inclusion in the list was justified. The writ petitioner can very well agitate his grievance before the concerned Tribunal, if necessary.
47. Before we part with the Judgment, we wish to point out that the issues raised in the writ petitions are purely legal. The factual aspects are not strictly relevant for disposal of the writ petitions. As such, we did not elaborate in our Judgment, the factual aspects leading to finding of the writ petitions.
48. In light of the aforesaid, we find no merit in the Rules. The Rules are accordingly discharged without any orders as to costs. Communicate the Judgment and Order at once.
End.

Land Survey Tribunal, Gopalganj and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Nazrul Islam Talukder, J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, this Rule Nisi, at the instance of the petitioner, was issued calling upon the Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 20-10-2019 (Decree signed on 21-10-2019) passed by the Bicharak of the Land Survey Tribunal, Gopalganj, i.e. the respondent No.1 in Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1319 of 2015 (Annexure-B and B-1) not decreeing the suit as a whole (suit decreed in part) should not be declared to have been passed illegal, in operative and have no legal effect and/or pass such other or further or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The above-mentioned writ petition has been filed challenging the judgment and decree dated 20-10-2019 passed by the learned Bicharak of the Land Survey Tribunal, Gopalganj, in Land Survey Tribunal Case No.1319 of 2015. 

3. The learned Advocates for the petitioner and the respondents conjointly, submits that this writ petition may be disposed of directing the learned Judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal to dispose of the appeal if filed by the petitioner since Land Survey Appellate Tribunal has already been established in the respective districts through Gazette notification. 

4. It may be noted that due to non-existence of appellate forum at the relevant time of passing the decree, the petitioner could not prefer appeal challenging the said judgment and decree. Thus, having no alternative forum, the petitioner filed this writ petition challenging the said judgment and decree and obtained the present Rule Nisi. 

5. Now, by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2023, the appellate forum has been established and on 23-7-2023, the name of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, has been Gazetted. In the circumstances, this Court delivered a judgment and order on 4-12-2023 analogously disposing of Writ Petition Nos. 5135 of 2018, 12559 of 2022, 11772 of 2022, 3743 of 2018, 12797 of 2022, 16281 of 2016, 2210 of 2022 and 7203 of 2022 allowing the respective writ petitioners to prefer appeals before the newly established Land Survey Appellate Tribunals of the respective districts with a direction to the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal to consider their appeals and applications for condonation of delay, if filed, in accordance with section 14 read with section 29 of the Limitation Act. 

6. In the said judgment and order dated 4-12-2023, this Court observed as under: "From the above order, it is apparent that due to non-existence of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, the Apex Court extended the force of order of status quo till 3 (three) months from the date of establishment of the said Appellate Tribunal. But here in these matters, 3 months limitation period have already been passed from the date of establishment of appellate forum. Yet on identical circumstances, we consider that due to non existence of Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, the writ petitioners could not challenge the impugned judgment and decree or order and this situation led them to file writ petitions obtaining Rules Nisi in their respective writ petitions. Thus, they have remained under the litigations before this Court so long. 
Now, since the appellate forum has been established, the petitioners are at liberty to prefer the appeal." 

7. In view of the above-mentioned judgment and order dated 4-12-2023, the Rule Nisi issued in the present writ petition is disposed of with the following directions: 
(i) The petitioner is at liberty to prefer appeal before the Land Survey Appellate -Tribunal with an application for condonation of delay and, if so filed, the Appellate Tribunal shall consider the application as well as the appeal in accordance with section 14 read with section 29 of the Limitation Act. 
(ii) The petitioner and the respondents are at liberty to take back all the original certified copies annexed with the respective writ petitions or affidavits in opposition or application(s) or affidavit(s) on furnishing photocopies thereof duly attested by the respective learned Advocates. 
(iii) The parties are directed to maintain status-quo in respect of position and possession of the land in question till disposal of the case/appeal if any. 
(iv) The learned judge of the appellate tribunal is directed to dispose of the case/appeal if any within 1(one) year from the date of receipt of this judgment and order. 

8. With aforesaid observations and directions, this Rule is disposed of. 

Communicate the judgment and order to the learned Judge of the concerned Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Imtiaz Moinul Islam with Mosfeq Kabir, Advocate ------- For the Petitioner
Md Kamruzzaman Mollah, Advocate—For the Respondent No.6.
parties:
Dhaka North City Corpo ration ------ Petitioner
Vs.
District Judge, Dhaka and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
By invoking section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, (shortly the Arbitration Act), when Dhaka North City Corporation (hereinafter referred to either as DNCC or the petitioner-DNCC) approached this Court questioning the legality and propriety of formation of an arbitration tribunal, which was constituted pursuant to the Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 666 of 2007 (shortly, Arbitration Misc case) and, also, the Order (without No.) dated 30-11-2020 passed by the Chairman of the reconstituted arbitration tribunal, Dhaka in reference to the above-mentioned Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 asking the petitioner-DNCC to appear before it, a Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why constitution of the aforesaid arbitration tribunal (respondent No. 2) shall not be declared to be illegal and, also, an interim Order was passed restraining the respondent No. 2 (arbitration tribunal) from proceeding any further with the aforesaid arbitration proceedings initiated by respondent No. 6 (hereinafter referred to either as M/s Diba Enterprise or the initiating party, a party who is desirous of initiating the arbitration) till disposal of the instant Rule. 

2. The fact of the case, briefly, is that the petitioner-DNCC desired private sector participation in the activities of Inter-District Bus Terminals (Group A-Mirpur Bus Terminal) and therefore called Tender Bid in 2003 and a pre-bid meeting was held by. DNCC with the respondent No. 6 and other bidders on 12-7-2013. Respondent No. 6 eventually won the tender and, accordingly, on 24-9-2003, DNCC entered into a contract to share the collected revenue with respondent No. 6, for an initial period of 3 (three) years with a stipulation to extend it on yearly basis only on mutually agreed terms and conditions. By the end of the three-year period respondent No. 6 failed to clear his total dues and requested for extension of time and waiver of payment on the plea of force majeure situations, like Hartal, Strike, Eid, SAARC Summit etc. A Joint Committee was formed, wherein respondent No. 6 was included, who found that 257 days were wasted and DNCC waived Taka 45,65,434 and also gave an extension of 365 days to respondent No. 6 making the end date 30-9-2007, but respondent No. 6 failed to pay the dues of DNCC and the Government Tax and VAT within the extended time even. As on 30-9-2007, respondent No. 6 owed DNCC Taka 1,31,77,416 as revenue of DNCC and Taka 79,37,952 as the Government tax and VAT totaling Taka 2,11,15, 368 (Taka two crore eleven lacy fifteen thousand three sixty eight) plus interest. The petitioner-DNCC filed Certificate Case No. 775 of 2007 as revenue of DNCC and the Government taxes and, also, on 23-6-2007, invited a new tender to lease out the Mirpur Bus Terminal to private operators as the contract with respondent No. 6 was coming to an end. Respondent No. 6 did not take any step to pay the revenue due to DNCC and the taxes due to Government, but instead filed two applications on 29-7-2007 and on 16-8-2007 under sections 12 and 7A of the Arbitration Act respectively in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka to stop the tender process. The section 12 application was registered as Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007. Thereafter, on 4-10-2010 the learned District Judge. Dhaka appointed Mr Tofailur Rahman, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, as arbitrator for DNCC and Mr AKM Faiz, an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, as arbitrator for respondent No. 6, who then appointed Bangladesh Supreme Court's Senior Advocate Mr Rafiqur Rahman as the Chairman of the tribunal towards formation of the arbitration tribunal. Since the arbitration tribunal was constituted, the learned District Judge, Dhaka disposed of the said Arbitration Misc Case on 31-8-2015. In the meantime on 15-10-2013, respondent No. 6 wrote to DNCC requesting to settle the matter out of Court and to withdraw the Certificate Case No. 775 of 2007. DNCC being fair and cooperative gave respondent No. 6 a clean opportunity to settle the dues of DNCC and accordingly called a meeting on 13-7-2015. However, the out of Court settlement never reached any conclusion as respondent No. 6 did not agree to pay the dues. Suddenly, on 29-1-2019, respondent No. 6 filed an application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act for re-appointment of arbitrators in the aforesaid Arbitration Misc Case by praying for restoration of the same and the petitioner-DNCC filed written objection on 18-3-2020. Subsequently, on 16-9-2020, the heirs of the sole proprietor of respondent No. 6 filed 2 applications; one for substitution and another for acceptance of a power of attorney given by 2 heirs to another heir to represent them. While the application for restoration was pending, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, vide his Order No. 89 dated 16-9-2020. substituted the heirs as the petitioners of the said Arbitration Misc Case and allowed the power of attorney in the said Arbitration Misc Case. Thereafter vide his Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020, the learned District Judge, Dhaka appointed new arbitrators, and when vide Order dated 30-11-2020 the newly-formed arbitration tribunal (respondent No. 2) notified the petitioner-DNCC about the formation of the fresh arbitration tribunal, it came to know about it on 7-12-2020 and approached this Court questioning the jurisdiction of the newly-formed arbitration tribunal. 

3. By filing an affidavit-in-opposition, respondent No. 6 states, amongst others, that he entered into a contract on 24-9-2003 with the erstwhile Dhaka City Corporation (DCC) containing a stipulation that upon completion of initial 3 (three) years, the parties by mutual agreement may extend the same for further 3 years and the non-operation days for an event of force majeure (hartal etc) shall be automatically extended. During operation of the Mirpur Bus Terminal at the tenure of initial 3 years, 152 days elapsed inoperative due to strike and unpredictable political turmoil. Care-taker regime took power in 2007 and conducted Government machineries, including erstwhile DCC, in an extreme high handed manner. DCC instead of extending for 3 further years as per contract, extended for only one year which expired on 30-9-2007. Respondent No. 6 filed the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 under section 12 of the Arbitration Act for appointment of arbitrator upon serving notice and, thereafter, DCC (which later became DNCC) filed a Certificate Case No. 775/2007 against respondent No. 6. In the Arbitration Misc Case No.666 of 2007, respondent No. 6 had mentioned the name of Mr Shamsuddin Chowdhury, Barrister-at-law, an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (as he then was) as their arbitrator, who later on was elevated as Justice of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and DNCC mentioned the name of Mr Tofailur Rahman, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as their arbitrator. In that context, the learned District Judge, Dhaka appointed Mr Tofailur Rahman, a Senior Advocate, as arbitrator for DNCC and Mr AKM Faiz, Advocate Supreme Court, as the arbitrator for respondent No. 6. Both the said arbitrators then appointed Senior Advocate Mr Rafiqur Rahman as the Chairman of the tribunal and. that is how, the arbitration tribunal was constituted. Thereafter, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of DNCC and respondent No. 6 discussed scope of amicable settlement, as previously there were instances of amicable settlements of the disputes regarding Mohak hal i Bus Terminal and Sayedabad Bus Terminal for self-same matter with Panama Trading as the petitioner, and the award was given in favour of that Panama Trading (Arbitration Misc Case No. 650 of 2007 and Arbitration Misc Case No. 651 of 2007). Hence, when the CEO assured that the Certificate Case against respondent No. 6 will be withdrawn to solve the dispute amicably, respondent No. 6 filed application before arbitration tribunal for not pressing the arbitration proceeding, which was signed by the representative of DNCC. But after the arbitration proceedings were non-prosecuted, DNCC did not file any application for withdrawal of the Certificate Case against respondent No. 6. In the meantime, the CEO was transferred to the Ministry of Agriculture and respondent No. 6 was pursuing DNCC to implement the promise given by DNCC, but it was delaying giving false promises to respondent No. 6. Meanwhile, when the said Arbitration Misc Case came up in the cause list of the learned District Judge mistakenly for filing award, the learned District Judge noted that there is no provision for filing award under section 12 of the Arbitration Act and hence, the Court disposed of the said Arbitration Misc Case. Even after the regular Government was formed in the country, when DNCC did not take any initiative for withdrawing the Certificate Case, respondent No. 6, invoking section 12 of the Arbitration Act, filed a fresh application in the said Arbitration Misc Case on 29-1-2019 to the District Judge Court, Dhaka for re-appointment of arbitrators, and DNCC filed a written objection on 18-3-2020 wherein DNCC admitted that there was mutual understanding of settlement. Unfortunately, respondent No. 6, Mr Abul Basher, the sole proprietor of Diba Enterprise. died due to Covid-19 on 15-6-2020 before hearing of the application and, consequently, his heirs and successors filed an application for substitution which was allowed by the Court on 16-9-2020. Thereafter, in the said Arbitration Misc Case the learned District Judge appointed two arbitrators, namely, Mr AKM Zahir Ahmed for respondent No.6 and Mr Ikteder Ahmed for DNCC directing the arbitrators to appoint a Chairman, and the arbitrators appointed retired Justice Mr Md Azizul Hague as the Chairman of the tribunal, following which the new tribunal was formed and, thereafter, the Chairman of the tribunal invited parties for preliminary hearing by the impugned notice dated 30-11-2020. 

4. Mr Imtiaz Moinul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner-DNCC, takes me through sections 15 to 20 of the Arbitration Act, and submits that section 20 being the appropriate provision for challenging constitution or jurisdiction of an arbitration tribunal, question of preferring civil revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) or invoking Article 102 of the Constitution is misconceived. He next submits that section 20 of the Arbitration Act is totally an independent provision and is no way connected with the provisions of section 19 of the Arbitration Act. In a bid to buttress up his above count of submissions, he places the relevant provisions of the UK's Arbitration Act, 1996 and India's Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 as well as Judgment passed by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of SBP vs Patel AIR 2006 SC 450 together with the authoritative book on arbitration written by Dr. PC Markanda, and submits that arbitration tribunal is not competent to rule on its formation when the arbitrators of the concerned arbitration tribunal were appointed by the Court. He next refers to the case of Ghulant Mohiuddin Bhutto vs Rokeya Din ALR On-Line 2019, and submits that as per the principles laid down therein, the petitioner-DNCC has invoked this Court's jurisdiction under section 20 of the Arbitration Act. 

5. He then takes this Court through the statements made in the application under section 12 dated 29-7-2007 filed by respondent No. 6 before the District Judge Court, Dhaka, and submits that the respondent No. 6 filed the said application on 29-7-2007 without issuing statutory notice of 30 days and hence the total proceedings of Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 666 of 2007 is corum non judice, and as per the decision in Genesis Case 9 BLC 636 and the decision of 19 DLR (SC) 266 when no statutory notice is given for arbitration, there shall not be any cause of action to initiate a legal proceeding; since in this case there is a patent lack of jurisdiction, no amount of waiver can cure that defect even if DNCC submitted to the proceeding and, therefore, the arbitration tribunal constituted by the Order dated 4-10-2010 was also illegal. Then, by placing the provisions of section 15 of the Arbitration Act, he submits that the tribunal having been constituted on 4-10-2010, remained inept for 9 years without discharging, their duties; hence the course for respondent No. 6 was to adopt the procedures prescribed in section 15 of the Arbitration Act by, at first, trying to jointly terminate the mandate of the said arbitrators with DNCC and failing which, by filing an application under section 15 (2) of the Arbitration Act to the learned District Judge. But respondent No. 6 without taking such steps unlawfully approached the learned District Judge who erroneously appointed fresh arbitrators, as a result of which there are now 2 unlawfully constituted tribunals to arbitrate the same dispute, which is preposterous, Mr Islam continues to submit. 

6. Then, he takes me through the Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka and the Order dated 30-11-2020 passed by the arbitration tribunal, Dhaka with reference to the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007, and submits that both the Orders are illegal, because there is no valid arbitration agreement as the arbitration agreement was executed on 24-9-2003 under the Arbitration Act, 1940 but the Arbitration Act, 1940 was repealed and has been invalid from 10-4-2001 and hence the arbitration agreement is void under section 20 of the Contract Act, 1872 for mistake of fact by both parties and thus it is a good season under section 17(a) and section 43(1)(a)(ii) of the Arbitration Act to declare the constitution of arbitration tribunal illegal. By taking me through the provisions of section 87(2) of the Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009 and section 3(3) of the Arbitration Act, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the petitioner-DNCC filed Certificate Case No. 775 of 2007 as revenue of DNCC and Government taxes are recoverable as public demand under section 87(2) of the Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009; and section 3(3) of the Arbitration Act itself states that where under any Act, a dispute cannot be referred to arbitration, such dispute will not be arbitrated under the Arbitration Act and, indeed, respondent No. 6 had invoked Order VII, rule 11 for quashing the Certificate Case No. 775 of 2007 but the said petition was rejected by the Certificate Court as the option to dispute public demand is before Certificate Court, not arbitration tribunal. He submits that since the role of Umpire is now extinct under the present Arbitration Act and the Chairman is just another arbitrator when it comes to deciding the dispute, the arbitration agreement is incapable of being performed and is contrary to existing law as it gives the Umpire the ultimate authority to decide and pass award on the dispute, but the existing law being section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act and the doctrine of fairness dictate that an award will be given by majority votes. He next submits that respondent No. 6 referred to the extension of contractual term as a dispute to the arbitration tribunal but extension of time is not a condition of the contract dated 24-9-2003 and is therefore not enforceable. He submits that the reference made to the arbitration tribunal is not a matter that has been submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement and thus three is a good reason under section 17 (e) of the Arbitration Act to declare the constitution of arbitration tribunal unlawful. Mr Islam then submits that the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 was finally disposed of on 31-8-2015 and the learned District Judge, Dhaka became functus officio for the said matter and, hence, the application for restoration filed by him on 29-1-2019 is bad in law and, more importantly, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, without restoring the said case, first substituted heirs of original petitioner and allowed power of attorney on 16-9-'2020 and then by Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 restored the case which are all erroneous, arbitrary and unlawful, and this is a good reason under section 17(b) of the Arbitration Act to declare the constitution of arbitration tribunal, Dhaka illegal and void ab initio. He submits that not only vide his Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020, the learned District Judge restored the dead-case but also he reappointed 2 new arbitrators quoting that DNCC lawyer orally did not object to re-appointment at the hearing, whereas there exists a written objection filed by DNCC on 18-3-2019 and, therefore, the total process is ex-facie illegal and arbitrary and this is a good reason under section 17(b) of the Arbitration Act to declare the constitution of arbitration tribunal, Dhaka illegal. He next submits that the Order dated 30-11-2020 passed by the arbitration tribunal, Dhaka in connection with Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 was received by the petitioner-DNCC on 7-12-2020 but this Court was on holiday since 17-12-2020 and, as such, there is no delay or lathes in filling this instant petition. He submits that if the arbitration tribunal sits and continues, then the petitioner will have to pay arbitrator fees, office expenses and other miscellaneous cost and arbitration will continue for a long time making DNCC's revenue stuck for a prolonged period, so preferring this instant application saves a lot of cost and money. 

7. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for setting aside the Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 as well as the Order dated 30-11-2020 passed by the arbitration tribunal. Dhaka (respondent No. 2) in connection with the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 and, thereby, obtaining a declaration from this Court that the constitution of the aforesaid arbitration tribunal is illegal and the said arbitration tribunal does not have any jurisdiction to conduct any arbitration between the petitioner-DNCC and respondent No. 6. 

8. Mr Md Kamruzzaman Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 6, takes me through the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, and submits that from the style of couching the prayer by the petitioner, it appears that the petitioner is actually aggrieved by certain Orders passed by the learned District Judge and, as such, since the instant application has been filed under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, which does not confer any civil revisional power, the 1st part of the Rule, which seeks to impugn the Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 666/2007, is beyond the purview of or outside the jurisdiction of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, as any grievance against the aforesaid Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge needs to be agitated in a different appropriate legal forum. He then submits that the jurisdiction of arbitration tribunal emanated/originated from the Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge and the arbitration agreement. He submits that the Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge in the said Arbitration Misc Case is within the authority of a learned District Judge given by section 12 of the Arbitration Act and, thus, there is no infirmity in that impugned Order. 

9. Mr Mollah, without prejudice to the above submission, next submits that even in civil proceedings under the CPC, non-pressing or non-prosecuting an application does not constitute legal bar in initiating a fresh suit, inasmuch as until the dispute is decided with finality on merit, the principle of res judicata does not become applicable. By referring to the case of 2019 ALR (HCD) Online 174 = 71 DLR 577, Chulain Mohiuddin vs Mrs Rokeya Din and others, he submits that the grounds agitated by the petitioner for challenging the jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal does not, on the face of it, satisfy the collective criteria as required under section 20 of the Arbitration Act. He places before this Court the provisions of sections 17 and 19 of the Arbitration Act and submits that any objection to jurisdiction to the arbitration tribunal should be agitated before the arbitration tribunal at first, and since the petitioner has not exhausted that route, this petition is not maintainable. By taking this Court through the texts of the Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, he contends that the learned Advocate for the petitioner-DNCC has consented to appoint new arbitrators, and since both the parties have agreed to appoint the new arbitrators, upon termination of appointments of previous arbitrators, the petitioner's application is liable to be rejected outright. 

10. The learned Advocate for respondent No. 6 next places before this Court the provisions of section 7 of the Arbitration Act, and submits that since there is an arbitration clause in the contract, without exhausting the arbitration, filing of the Certificate Case by DNCC demanding money, which being a dispute of the arbitration, is illegal. In respect of the opinion of Dr. PC Markanda stated in his book on arbitration and the observations made by the Supreme Court of India in the cases reported in 4 SCC (2000) 272 and 3 SCC (2011) 258, Mr Mollah submits that these are not in accordance with the Arbitration Act of Bangladesh and, as such, not relevant in this case. In respect of legal maxim 'nemo judex in causa sua' meaning no one can be the Judge in his own cause, is not proper in case of Arbitration Act which is a special law, which delegates power to the arbitration tribunal, Mr Mollah submits. 

11. He next takes this Court through the documents which are to be deemed to have formed part of this contract agreement, and submits that from the Minutes of Pre Bid Meeting held on July 12, 2003, particularly from the Queries and Response made therein, it is evident that after initial contract period of 3 (three) years, the contract can be extended for further 3 years at a time, and as the decision of the Pre Bid Meeting is a part of this contract agreement and 3 (three) years instead of 1 (one) year have been allowed, DNCC shall have to extend further 3 years if the operator in the meantime has no fault during his initial 3 years. He submits that the Arbitration Act empowers the District Judge and the arbitral tribunal to pass ad-interim Orders/injunctions under sections 7A and 21 of the Arbitration Act respectively and there is no scope for the High Court Division to invoke power for passing any ad-interim Order or Order of injunction, but the petitioner wrongly pointed out that under section 53 of the Arbitration Act all the Courts have been given power for passing any ad-interim Order or Order of injunction because in section 2 of the Arbitration Act the District Judge and Additional District Judge have been defined as Court, not the High Court Division. He further submits that section 20 of the Arbitration Act does not empower granting any temporary injunction. fie submits that when unfortunately the respondent Mr Abul Basher, the sole proprietor of Diba Enterprise, died due to Covid 19 before hearing of the application and his heirs and successors filed an application for substitution and the Court allowed the substitution application before allowing the application for re-opening the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666/2007, it may at best be termed as a procedural irregularity but it does not amount to an error of law and, hence, the same is not unlawful which can be challenged and, as such, there is no substantial ground or element to file this application. 

12. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the respondent prays for discharging the Rule and vacating the Order of temporary injunction, and also for passing an Order that the Certificate Case No. 775/2007, now pending before the Certificate Officer, Dhaka, is not maintainable. 

13. Upon hearing the learned Advocates for both the sides, on perusal of the petitioner's application as well as the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 6 together with their annexures and having read the relevant statutory laws and case-laws cited from the various Law Journals, it appears to this Court that the following issues are to be adjudicated upon by this Court; (1) whether the facts and circumstances of this case fit into the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, in other words, whether the instant application is maintainable and (2) whether this Court is competent to pass necessary consequential Order/s and Direction/s, if this application is found to be maintainable. 

14. Let me take up the first issue, namely, (1) whether the facts and circumstances of this case fit into the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. For an effective adjudication of the issue, section 20 of the Arbitration Act is quoted below:-
20. Powers of the High Court Division in deciding jurisdiction—(1) The High Court Division, may, on the application of any of the parties to the arbitration proceeding, after serving notice upon all other parties, determine any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal. 
(2) No application under this section shall be taken into account, unless the High Court Division is satisfied that—
(a) The determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs. 
(b) The application was submitted without any delay; and (c) There is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court. 
(3) The application shall state the reasons on which the matter should be decided by the High Court Division. 
(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section, the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award. 

15. From a bare reading of the afore-quoted provision of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, it plainly appears to this Court that the High Court Division has been invested with the power to determine any issue regarding jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal in question, subject to the conditions that the application fulfills the stipulations laid down in sub-sections (2) & (3) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. 

16. At this juncture, this Court needs to see, at first, whether the question that has been brought to the notice of this Court can be termed as a jurisdictional issue and, secondly, whether the instant application satisfies the requirements of sub-sections (2) & (3) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. 

17. Let me first focus on the term `jurisdiction'. Nowhere in the Arbitration Act or any other laws of the land, including General Clauses Act, 1897, the word 'jurisdiction' has been defined. The word 'jurisdiction' derives from the Latin `juris' (law)  + `dictio' (declaration). As per Oxford Dictionary. meaning of the word 'jurisdiction' is 'the power of a Court to hear and decide a case or make a certain Order' and, also, "administration of justice and exercise of judicial authority" as well as "the territory over which such power extends" and the meaning provided by Black's Law Dictionary is 'a Court's power to decide a case or issue a decree'. Common synonyms of the word 'jurisdiction' are authority, command, control, dominion, power and sway. Having been provided with the aforesaid meanings and definitions by the globally recognized general dictionaries and Law Dictionaries, this Court holds that 'jurisdiction' means the legal power/authority of a Court or a judicial forum to try and adjudicate upon cases/disputes of certain types within a particular geographic area. 

18. In the case in hand, the question that the arbitration tribunal lacks jurisdiction has been raised by the petitioner-DNCC on the following grounds; (1) that the arbitration tribunal in question, formed on the basis of the 2 (two) Orders (the first one is dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge of Dhaka by which two fresh arbitrators were appointed with a direction upon them to appoint a Chairman of the arbitrator and the second one is dated 30-11-2020 passed by the reconstituted arbitration tribunal) which are impugned herein, is not a tribunal in the eye of law as there already exists an arbitration tribunal on the self-same dispute which was constituted by the same Court of the learned Distract Judge of Dhaka, (2) that the arbitration clause is created under the repealed Arbitration Act of 1940 which is a mistake of fact committed by both parties and, consequently, .the same is void under section 20 of Contract Act 1872; and since survival of said arbitration clause will directly contradict with section 37(1) of the 2001 Act which says majority decision out of two arbitrators and one Chairman will prevail, but the arbitration clause in question says Umpire's decision will be final, thus. this arbitration clause is not enforceable as the 2001 Act made the "Chairman" just another arbitrator when it comes to voting on decision whereas previous 1940 Act made "Umpire" the tie-breaker and (3) that before filing section 12 application, since no notice was issued upon the petitioner-DNCC for appointment of arbitrators, the learned District Judge of Dhaka being not competent to entertain the said application, the constitution of arbitration tribunal by him was illegal. 

19. I am taking up the petitioner-DNCC's second and third grounds, at first, together for the reasons to be known eventually. From the Order sheets and papers of the Lower Court's Record (LCR), it appears that the Arbitration Misc Case No. 666 of 2007 was filed on 29-7-2007 by the Diba Enterprise (respondent No. 6 herein), and the DNCC (the petitioner herein) entered its appearance on 09-8-2007. Thereafter, the petitioner-DNCC submitted before the Court of the learned District Judge of Dhaka many pleadings which include various applications, written statement and written objections, and after making continuous appearances before the said Court for nearly three years, the petitioner-DNCC suggested the name of an arbitrator from its side and finally the Court vide its Order No. 42 dated 18-3-2010 granted the aspired relief by appointing 2 (two) arbitrators, namely, Mr Shamsuddin Chowdhury, Senior Advocate and Mr Tofailur Rahman, Senior Advocate as the arbitrators of the arbitration tribunal and, thereafter, the aforesaid Order was modified on 4-10-2010 by substituting Mr AKM Faiz, an Advocate of the Supreme Court for Mr Shamsuddin Chowdhury. Before and after passing the aforesaid Orders dated 18-3-2010 and 4-10-2010, the petitioner-DNCC has never raised the question before the Court of the District Judge of Dhaka either about non-receipt of the notice for appointment of arbitrator under section 12 of the Arbitration Act nor about the commission of alleged mistake of facts by the parties because of mentioning the Arbitration Act as the Act of 1940 and using the word 'Umpire' instead of the Chairman' of the tribunal. As per the provisions of section 6 of the Arbitration Act, a party to the arbitration is debarred from raising any objection as to non-compliance of any provisions of the Arbitration Act at a belated stage i.e. when a party to an arbitration moves forward with the arbitration proceeding despite knowing that his opponent is guilty of non-compliance with any legal requirement of the Arbitration Act, and if the said party later on raises any .objection at a stage where compliance or non-compliance of the said legal requirement does hardly matter, the law dictates the concerned adjudicating fora (i.e. the High Court Division, the Court and the arbitration tribunal) not to take the said omission into consideration. 

20. In this case, the Court, by the conduct of the parties, has proceeded on a presumption that the parties have agreed to arbitrate on the dispute under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001 inasmuch as when respondent No. 6 approached the Court upon invoking section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and the present petitioner-DNCC initially submitted the name of Mr Shamsuddin Chowdhury, as an arbitrator from its side before the District Judge Court of Dhaka and, thereafter, replaced him by Mr AKM Faiz, any one with ordinary prudence shall be of the view that the parties have mutually consented to take recourse to the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and, with regard to the issue of the legal requirements of issuance of notice to other party, in absence of any objection from the petitioner-DNCC's side, it was very usual for the Court to think that either the said legal requirement has been complied with by the initiating party or it has been waived by the other party. Therefore, this Court does not find any substance in the petitioner-DNCC's aforesaid pleas. 

21. Regarding the first ground (i.e. questioning the arbitration tribunal's jurisdiction on the plea that there already having an arbitration tribunal, constitution of second tribunal was illegal), this Court finds that it is an admitted fact that vide the Orders dated 18-3-2010 and 4-10-2010 passed by the learned District Judge of Dhaka, arbitration tribunal was constituted with two arbitrators, namely, Mr Tofailur Rahman, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and Mr AKM Faiz, an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and, thereafter, these two arbitrators appointed Mr Rafiqur Rahman, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the Chairman of the tribunal. Now, the question comes up for consideration as to whether with the passing of the Order/s as to appointments of the arbitrators, the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 666 of 2007 was disposed of finally, or in an application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, there remains something for the Court to deal with, even after appointments of the arbitrators towards formation of the arbitration tribunal. To this end, it would be helpful for this Court to be acquainted with the provisions of section 12 of the Arbitration Act which are quoted below:-
12. Appointment of arbitrators—
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the parties are free to agree on a procedure for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators. 
(2)  ----------- 
(3) Failing any agreement referred to in sub-section(1)— 
(a) in an arbitration with a sole arbitrator, if the parties fail to agree on the arbitration within thirty days from receipt of a request by one party from the other party to so agree the appointment shall be made upon request of a party—
(i) by the District Judge in case of arbitration other than international commercial arbitration, and 
(ii) by the Chief Justice or by any other Judge of the Supreme Court designated by the Chief Justice in international arbitration. 
(b) In an arbitration case of commercial with three arbitrators, each party shall appoint one arbitrator, and the two appointed arbitrators shall appoint the third arbitrator who shall be Chairman of the arbitral tribunal. 
(4) If the appointment procedure in sub-section (3) applies and 
(a) a party fails to appoint an arbitrator within thirty days of the receipt of a request to do so from the other party or,

(c) by the District Judge except in case of international commercial arbitration, and 
(d) by the Chief Justice or by any other Judge of the Supreme Court designated by the Chief Justice in case of international commercial arbitration. 
(5) The third arbitrator appointed under clause (b) of sub-section (4) shall be the Chairman of the said tribunal. 
(6) If more than one arbitrators are  appointed under sub-section (4), the District  Judge or the Chief Justice or any other Judge of the Supreme Court designated by the Chief Justice as the case may be, shall appoint one person from among the said arbitrators to be the Chairman of the arbitral tribunal.   
(7) Where. under an appointment procedure agreed upon by the parties—
