(b) the parties, or the arbitrators, fail to reach an agreement under the same procedure; or 
(c) a person or any third party fails to perform any function assigned to him under that procedure, unless the agreement on the appointment procedure provides other means to take the necessary measure for securing the appointment, a party may apply to-
(d) the District Judge except in case of international commercial arbitration and the District Judge shall appoint the Chairman of the tribunal along with the other arbitrators, 
(e) the Chief Justice or any Judge of the Supreme Court designated by  the Chief Justice in case of international commercial arbitration and the Chief Justice or the Judge of the Supreme Court as designated by the Chief Justice shall appoint the Chairman of the  tribunal alone with other arbitrators.

22. If the provisions of all the sub-sections of section 12 of the Arbitration Act and the clauses thereunder are read together, the plain meaning that derives is that while the parties to a contract have been given the liberty to mutually determine the procedures of appointments of arbitrators. however, in the absence of such a procedure, the initiating party shall issue a notice giving 30 (thirty) days time to the other party for formation of a tribunal either by appointing a single arbitrator for both the sides, if it is agreed that the proposed arbitration tribunal shall consist of one arbitrator, or by appointing one arbitrator from each side who shall then on consensus appoint a Chairman, if it is agreed by the parties that the arbitration tribunal shall be comprising three arbitrators. Up to this stage, if the parties can act amicably, they do not need to approach the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh for formation of an international commercial arbitration tribunal or to the District Judge Court for formation of a domestic arbitration tribunal. However, issuance of the notice for formation of the arbitration tribunal may trigger two contingencies, namely, either the other party does not respond to the proposal for formation of the tribunal, or the 2 (two) arbitrators (who have been appointed by each side) are unable to find a mutually agreed Chairman. Either way, the parties would have no other option than to end up in the High Court Division/District Judge Court. Thereafter upon receipt of the application from either party, the High Court Division/District Judge Court in the scenario of disagreement between two arbitrators as to appointment of Chairman will appoint a Chairman for the tribunal of its own choice within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the section 12 application and. in the scenario of non-responding to the notice of the initiating party the High Court Division/the District Judge Court shall constitute the tribunal either by appointing a single arbitrator of its own choice in the case of one-member tribunal or by appointing two arbitrators and the Chairman of its own selection in the case of a 3 (three)-member tribunal within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the section 12 application. 

23. Usually the initiating party of the arbitration approaches the High Court Division/ the District Judge Court proposing name of an arbitrator. However, the High Court Division/the District Judge Court is not bound, be it for formation of a single-member tribunal or a three-member tribunal, to include the said proposed person in formation of the tribunal inasmuch as when the parties mutually form the tribunal, the law prescribes that the appointments of arbitrator/s are to be made as per the choices of the parties to arbitration but whenever there will be a disagreement among the arbitrators as to appointment of the Chairman, it is the High Court Division/the District Judge Court which has exclusively been empowered to appoint the Chairman, either upon taking or without taking name/s from the parties to the arbitration. However, eventually if both the parties come to an agreement as to appointment of the Chairman during pendency of the section 12 application, then, the case being redundant should be non-prosecuted. Similarly, in the case of appointment of a single arbitrator for formation of a one-member tribunal if the initiating party comes up with name of an arbitrator and the other party does not appear before the High Court Division/the District Judge Court, it shall appoint the arbitrator of its own choice by ignoring the name supplied by the initiating party, so that the other party does not consider the tribunal to be partisan. The same principle shall also be applied for formation of a three-member tribunal by the High Court Division/the District Judge Court in a scenario when the other party does not supply the name of an arbitrator from its side upon receipt of notice containing the name of the arbitrator from the initiating party. The rationale behind non-inclusion of the name supplied by the initiating party in the one/three-member tribunal to be formed by the High Court Division/the District Judge Court is to provide security/protection to the other party through elimination of the possibility of bias, for it is of fundamental importance that justice must not only be done, but also be seen to be done; that is to say, if the High Court Division/the District Judge Court forms the one/three-member tribunal in the absence of the other party, the other party should not feel itself sided/cornered when it will appear before the tribunal. The scheme of the law regarding formation of an arbitration tribunal is such that when the parties to the arbitration form a three-member arbitration tribunal upon appointing two arbitrators from each sides without the Court's aid, none of the arbitrators shall he considered biased merely because of being appointed by the parties to the arbitration, but since the scenario becomes different because of non-appointment of an arbitrator from the other side despite receiving the notice issued by the initiating party, the said presumption, in the absence of the other party, does not become applicable in the case of formation of the tribunal by the High Court Division/the District Judge Court, be it for constitution of a one-member tribunal or a three-member tribunal. 

24. In other words, even when the other party appears before the Court pursuant to section 12 application for formation of a one-member tribunal, the Court should not form the tribunal on the basis of the names supplied by the parties. However, pursuant to filing a section 12 application by the initiating party for formation of a three-member tribunal, when the other party having appeared before the High Court Division/the District Judge Court proposes the name of an arbitrator, then, the parties may form the proposed three-member tribunal on their own outside the Court by non-prosecuting the section 12 application, unless the two arbitrators find themselves in disagreement in appointing the Chairman. If, however, the parties insist upon the concerned Court to form a three-member tribunal, then the said Court shall be at liberty to form the three-member tribunal either by inclusion of the names proposed by the parties or by ignoring the names suggested by the parties and thereby including the persons of the choice of the Court concerned in the said three-member tribunal. 

25. While, at first sight, the provisions of sub-section (1) to (5) of section 12 of the Arbitration Act regarding appointment of the two arbitrators and the Chairman of the arbitration tribunal may seem to be cumbersome, however, its sub-sections (6) & (7) make it abundantly clear that it is the High Court Division/the District Judge Court which shall appoint the entire members of a three-member tribunal (or more than three-member tribunal with odd number, such as five-member tribunal or seven-member tribunal and so on). That is to say, sub-section (6) of section 12 of the Arbitration Act dictates that if the High Court Division/the District Judge Court requires to appoint more than 2 (two) arbitrators with odd numbers [such as, 3 (three), 5 (five), 7 (seven) and so on], the concerned Court itself shall appoint a Chairman out of the said odd-numbered arbitrators, and shall not leave the issue of appointment of the Chairman for consideration of the Court-appointed members (arbitrators) of the tribunal. And, as per the provisions of sub-section (7) of section 12 of the Arbitration Act, it is incumbent upon the High Court Division/ District Judge Court to appoint 2 (two) arbitrators and one Chairman of a three-member tribunal in a scenario when there is an agreed procedure in place but one of the parties to the arbitration fails to comply with the said procedure or either both the parties or arbitrators fail to observe any one condition/rule of the said procedure or a third party, upon whom a certain duty is imposed, fails to perform its functions. The instances are that (i) when as per the agreed procedures, the parties were obliged to appoint the arbitrators from a particular profession but they fail to comply with it or (ii) total non-cooperation by the other party to proceed with the arbitration as per agreed procedure, such as the other party's inaction as to exhaustion of formation of mediation before stepping into the phase of arbitration or (iii) the parties have appointed arbitrators from their respective sides but they could not proceed further due to disagreement on certain issues, which are not related to the appointment of the Chairman and so on. 

26. It follows that the choices of the parties regarding appointment of arbitrator/s are open only in two scenarios; the first scenario is when there is a procedure of arbitrators' appointment in place and the parties amicably form the tribunal as per the procedures laid down therein and, the second one is, in absence of such a procedure, when both the parties form the arbitration on consensus following initiating party's issuance of notice upon the other party. However, in absence of the procedure of arbitrator's appointment if other party does not respond to the notice issued by the initiating party or though there is a procedure in place but both the parties or arbitrator/s do not or one of the parties does not intend to follow the procedure, in the said events, the High Court Division/ the District Judge Court assumes the authority to appoint all the arbitrator/s and the Chairman towards formation of the arbitration tribunal. 

27. In this case, therefore, it was incumbent upon the learned District Judge to constitute the arbitration tribunal within 60 (sixty) days from the date of registering the section 12 application on 29-7-2007 as Arbitration Misc. Case No. 666 of 2007, upon appointing two arbitrators and one Chairman as per the Court's choice. In a section 12 application, a learned District Judge is expected to confine itself within the very limited necessary works, such as, passing appropriate Orders/Directions for ensuring the presence of the other party and, then, disposing of the case by formation of the arbitration tribunal, however, in this case, the learned District Judge, Dhaka passed as many as 92 (ninety two) Orders to dispose of the case. Upon skimming through the entire Order-sheets of the case, it surfaces that as many as 11 (eleven) learned District Judges had the occasion to have dealt with the case one after another and most of them did not care to look into the Orders passed by his/her predecessors and, consequently, they indulged themselves in passing contradictory Orders and Directions.

The section 12 application, which was filed by the initiating party on 29-7-2007, states the name of Mr Shamsul Huda, a retired Hon'ble Justice of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, as the arbitrator of the initiating party. However, the initiating party when on 22-1-2008 came up with an application invoking section. 15 of the Arbitration Act for changing the name of the arbitrator previously proposed by the initiating party, the Court allowed the application and Mr AKM Faiz, an Advocate of the Supreme Court, replaced the previous arbitrator Mr Shamsul Huda/Shamsuddin Chowdhury [it is not clear, whether the initiating party had primarily appointed Hon'ble Justice (retired) Mr Shamsul Huda or Hon'ble Justice (retired) Mr Shamsuddin Chowdhury, which ought to have been correctly recorded by the learned District Judge]. Let me examine whether it was a proper step for the initiating party to invoke section 15 of the Arbitration Act in the stated circumstances. For this purpose, it shall be beneficial if the provisions of section 15 of the Arbitration Act can be acquainted, which are quoted below: 
15. Termination of arbitrator's mandate.—(1) The mandate of an arbitrator shall terminate, if 
(a) he withdraws himself from office: 
(b) he dies; 
(c) all the parties agree on the termination of his mandate; or 
(d) he is unable to perform his functions of his office or for other reasons fails to act without undue delay and withdraws from his office or the parties agree on the termination of his mandate. 
(2) If any arbitrator, who has incurred disqualifications referred to in clause (d) of sub-section (1), fails to withdraw himself from his office and all the parties fail to agree on his termination, then on the application of any party within the prescribed period by rules—
(a) the District Judge, in case of other arbitrations excepting international commercial arbitration;

(3) --------------
(4) --------------  

30. From a minute reading of the above-quoted provisions as well as taking into consideration the interpretation of the provisions regarding appointments of the arbitrators laid down by this Court hereinbefore, it appears that the provisions of section 15 of the Arbitration Act comes into operation with its two-fold applicability only after formation of the tribunal, be it constituted by the parties amicably or by the High Court/District Judge Court. So, following constitution of the tribunal (and, thus, not before the tribunal's constitution), at first, application/use of the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 15 of the Arbitration Act attracts the arbitrators who are currently performing their functions and, also, the parties of the arbitration and, in the event of failure of the aforesaid persons of the arbitration, the second part of the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 15 of the Arbitration Act becomes applicable at the instance of any stakeholder, subject to observing the procedures prescribed in section 16 of the Arbitration Act, which runs as follows: 
16. Substitution of an arbitrator whose mandate has been terminated.—(1) Where the mandate of an arbitrator terminates, a substitute arbitrator shall be appointed according to the provisions applicable to the appointment to the arbitrator whose mandate has been terminated. 
(2) In the absence of any agreement between the parties—
(a) the substitute arbitrator shall, at the discretion of the arbitral tribunal continue the hearings from the stage at which the mandate of the arbitrator has been terminated. 
(b) Any order or decision of the arbitral tribunal shall not be invalid before the termination of the mandate of an arbitrator due to such termination. 

31. After formation of the arbitration tribunal, thus, the parties to the arbitration, upon exhausting the procedures set out in sub-section (1) to (3) of section 14 of the Arbitration Act, may again come back to the High Court Division either under section 14(4) for preferring an appeal on the grounds specified in section 13 of the Arbitration Act, and the said case shall be registered as Arbitration Miscellaneous Appeal. Similarly, pursuant to formation of arbitration tribunal, when there will be a cause of action under section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act for the stakeholders of the arbitration (namely, arbitrators, the initiating party and the other party) to approach the High Court Division or the District Judge Court, the case shall be registered as a new Arbitration Miscellaneous Case. 

32. Thus, at this stage (at the time of passing Order No. 14, when no tribunal was formed) the initiating party was not obligated to invoke section 15 of the Arbitration Act, because a usual application would have served the purpose of the initiating party albeit there is no legal requirement to submit a name by the initiating party before the Court.

The learned District Judge Mr SM Kuddus Zaman (as he then was), rightly observed that in a section 12 application, under the Arbitration Act of 2001, there is no provision for filing Award following making appointments of arbitrators by the Court towards formation of the arbitration tribunal, albeit his predecessor (who had been performing the functions of the learned District Judge previously) had appointed only two arbitrators overlooking the appointment of the Chairman of the arbitrator. It is evident from the Order-sheets that his predecessors wasted the Court's valuable time for nearly 8 (eight) years by repeatedly fixing the date Tor submission of award' and, also, by entertaining frequent applications under section 7A of the Arbitration Act one after another. Let it be known by the learned District Judges of the country that an application under section 7A of the Arbitration Act must be registered as a separate 'Arbitration Miscellaneous Case' with distinctive number maintaining a separate Court Record. However, in order to save the Court's invaluable time and for the sake of convenience, both the Misc Cases (one under section 12 and another under section 7A of the Arbitration Act) may be enlisted in the cause list of the Court on the same date one after another and, if the facts and circumstances of the cases permit, both the cases can be disposed of simultaneously by a single Order. 
Order # 89 
16-9-2020 
অদ্য শুনানীর জন্য দিন ধার্য্য আছে। দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ হাজিরা দিয়াছে। দরখাস্তকারী আবুল বাশার এর মৃত্যুতে তৎওয়ারীশ মোসাঃ ছানোয়ারা বেগম গং কার্যবিধির ২২ আদেশ ৩(১) ধারামতে এক দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া বর্ণিত কারণে বাদী/দরখাস্তকারীর স্থলাভিষিক্ত করার প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে এবং ফিরিস্তিযোগে আমমোক্তার নিয়োগ করায় উক্ত আমমোক্তারনামা গ্রহণ করার প্রার্থনা করিয়া পৃথক এক দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়াছে। কপি জারী হয়েছে। প্রতিপক্ষ পক্ষে একদরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া আপত্তি দাখিলের জন্য সময়ের প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে।
Heard the learned lawyers for the both sides at length and perused the petition for time & petition under order 22 rule 3(1) of the CPC for substitution of heirs of heirs of deceased petitioner stating that above petitioner has died. 
Both petitions are allowed. 
Let the heirs of deceased petitioner be substituted in this case as prayed for. To 14-10-2020 for hearing of the case. 
Amend the petition and register accordingly. Dictated & corrected by me. 

36. After the case had finally been disposed of following formation of an arbitration tribunal, the learned District Judge Mr Mohammad Showkat Ali Chowdhury (as he then was) was not competent to entertain the application for substitution; rather he ought to have directed the petitioners to approach the tribunal, be that a tribunal of two members or three members, conducting the arbitration at that point of time. 

Order # 91 
5-11-2020  
অদ্য শুনানীর জন্য দিন ধার্য্য আছে। দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ ও প্রতিপক্ষ পক্ষে হাজিরা দিয়াছে।
Today is fixed for hearing of the petition dated 29-1-2019 filed by the petitioner for restoration of instant case. But it appears that by order No. 89 dated 19-9-2020 the Court substituted the heirs of the deceased petitioner. Since the heirs of the deceased petitioner is substituted, the instant case is restored. 
Thereafter the record is taken up for hearing of the petition dated 29-1-2019 for appointment of new arbitrators after recalling the Order No. 42 dated 19-3-2010. Heard the learned Advocate for both sides. 
The learned Advocate for the OP submits that he has no objection if Hon'ble Court appoints new arbitrators by recalling the Order No. 42 dated 18-3-2010. As such, the petition dated 29-1-2019 filed by the petitioner is allowed & the Order No. 42 dated 18-3-2010 is recalled. 
Accordingly, Mr AKM Zahir Ahmed, retired District & Sessions Judge, 3/17, Iqbal Road Seltak Chowdhury Vila, Apartment No. 2/B, 1st Floor, Mohammadpur, Dhaka is appointed arbitrator for the petitioner & Mr Ikteder Ahmed, Former Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Chamber-1/B, Eastern Housing Apartment Siddeshwari, Dhaka-1217, Ce11-01715100314 is appointed arbitrator for the OP for settlement of the dispute of this case through arbitration according to law after appointing third arbitrator who will be the Chairman of the Arbital Tribunal. 
Let the learned arbitrators be informed of the appointment for initiation of arbitration proceeding according to law. 
Dictated & corrected by me. 

37. The afore-quoted Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020 has been taken by the petitioner-DNCC as the basis for challenging the jurisdiction of the tribunal on the ground that while an already-constituted tribunal is in existence, there can not be another arbitration tribunal on the self-same dispute. Let me now examine the said arguments advanced by the petitioner-DNCC. 

38. By this Order, the learned District Judge, Dhaka appointed two new arbitrators in a section 12 application (Miscellaneous Case), which had been disposed of long ago. While there are certain types of Miscellaneous Cases where the Court might be competent to reopen an already-disposed of case in exceptional circumstances, but where the law dictates that after disposing of a particular type of Misc Cases, the jurisdiction to deal with the said type of Misc. Cases passes onto another forum and/or the concerned litigant requires to exhaust certain procedures, there is no authority for the Court/High Court Division to reopen or restore the said type of cases. A Misc. Case under section 12 of the Arbitration Case falls in a category of such Misc Cases, which can not be reopened/restored, once the aspired remedy of appointment of arbitrators have been granted and then the arbitral tribunal have also been constituted. Because following constitution of an arbitration tribunal, while for challenging (raising objection) against an arbitrator, a specific procedure is laid down in sections 13 and 14 of the Arbitration Act, which prescribe to approach the arbitration tribunal at first and, if rejected by the tribunal, to the appellate forum. However, after formation of the tribunal for changing/ terminating an arbitrator, it is the arbitrator under challenge who shall withdraw himself, or the parties to the arbitrators shall agree to effect termination of the arbitrator/s in question; and in case the arbitrator/s in question could not be terminated, any one among the arbitrators or parties to the arbitration may approach the High Court Division/District Judge Court invoking section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act for such termination. 

39. However, in the case in hand, it is not the case that because of non-registering a new Arbitration Misc Case there occurred some irregularities; rather an illegality has been committed for not exhausting the stipulations provided in sub-section (1) of section 15 of the Arbitration Act as well as non-compliance with the provisions of section 16(1) of the Arbitration Act. From a careful examination of the application under section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act, it appears to this Court that though the petitioner termed the application as an application under section 15 of the Arbitration Act, but nowhere in the said application anything is stated about termination of the existing arbitrators nor did this Court find a single word about taking any step under sections 15(1) and 16(1) of the Arbitration Act and, further, from perusal of the Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, this Court finds (even any one with ordinary prudence shall find) that the learned District Judge did not pass any Order as to terminating the arbitrators who were appointed previously. It was contended by the initiating party that the first arbitration proceeding was non-prosecuted by the initiating party, but no evidence as to non-prosecution of the said proceeding has been submitted before this Court nor is it evident from the LCR that the petitioner filed any application before the tribunal for non-prosecution of the arbitration proceeding. On the contrary a written objection filed by the DNCC is available in LCR which categorically raises objection about the initiating party's prayer for constitution of a new arbitration tribunal. 

40. So, the above examination of the facts and law leads this Court to hold that formation of the tribunal in question vide the two impugned Orders, namely, the Order dated 5-11-2020 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka and the Order dated 30-11-2020 passed by the Chairman of the reconstituted arbitration tribunal, was done illegally and, therefore, the newly constituted arbitration tribunal, not being an arbitration tribunal in the eye of law, does not have jurisdiction to deal with and adjudicate upon the dispute between the petitioner-DNCC and M/s Diba Enterprise (respondent No. 6). 

41. Now the question comes up for consideration as to whether this jurisdictional issue could have been dealt with by the arbitration tribunal itself; in other words, whether the arbitration tribunal is the proper forum to deal with the issue of tribunal's jurisdiction under section 17 read with 19 of the Arbitration Act, or whether the High Court Division is the appropriate forum to adjudicate upon the issue of jurisdiction under section 20 of the Arbitration Act. For obtaining the answers, this Court should look at the provisions of sections 17, 19 and 20 sequentially. At first, the provisions of section 17 are quoted below: 
17. Competence of arbitration tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction. Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, the arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction on any questions including the following issues, namely—
(a) whether there is existence of a valid arbitration agreement; 
(b) whether the Arbitral Tribunal is properly constituted; 
(c) whether the arbitration agreement is against the public policy; 
(d) whether the arbitration agreement is incapable of being performed; and, 
(e) whether the matters have been submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement. 

42. From a bare reading of the afore-quoted provisions of the Arbitration Act, it appears that section 17 of the Arbitration Act amply empowers the arbitration tribunal to make a decision on any issue relating to the tribunal's jurisdiction, including the issues enumerated in Clauses (a) to (e) thereunder, if the parties to the arbitration have not incorporated any stipulation in the arbitration agreement negating the invocation of section 17 of the Arbitration Act. 

43. Section 19 of the Arbitration Act runs as follows: 
19. Objection as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal.--(1) An objection that the tribunal does not have jurisdiction shall be raised not later than the submission of the statement of defence. 
(2) An objection during the course of the arbitral proceedings that the tribunal is exceeding the scope of its authority shall be raised as soon as the matter alleged to be beyond the scope of its authority is raised. 
(3) The arbitral tribunal may in either of the cases referred to in sub-sections (I) and (2) admit a later plea if it considers the delay justified. 
(4) The arbitral tribunal shall decide on an objection referred to in sub-sections (1) and (2) and where the arbitral tribunal takes a decision rejecting the plea, it shall continue with the arbitral proceedings and make an award. 
(5) A party shall not be precluded from raising such a plea merely because that he has appointed, or participated in the appointment of an arbitrator. 

44. From a minute reading of the above-quoted provisions, it appears to this Court that section 19 of the Arbitration Act provides the time-limits of raising the jurisdictional issues as well as the scope of its authority before the arbitration tribunal and, also, provides the information as to whether the tribunal should proceed with its functions after rejecting the application challenging tribunal's jurisdiction and, also, whether a party who had suggested the name of an arbitrator is competent to raise the jurisdictional issue. When a party to the arbitration intends to challenge jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal, the time-limit is upto the date of submission of the Statement of Defence and if the party wants to question the tribunal's authority as to its scope to deal with any procedural/ substantive issue, the time-limit is taking immediate step, meaning that when the concerned party who claims to have noticed that the tribunal has exceeded the scope, the said party shall have to approach the tribunal without squandering any time. However, the tribunal is invested with the power to condone the delay in an appropriate case. 

45. Now, comes the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. The said provisions being quoted hereinbefore, are not needed to reproduce here for the second time. 

46. A combined reading of sections 17, 19 and 20 of the Arbitration Act makes it abundantly clear that the sections are not at all connected with or dependent on each other and are absolutely independent of each other. By referring to the case of Ghulam Mohiuddin Bhutto vs Mrs Rokeya Din and others ALR Online 2019 = 71 DLR 577, the respondent No. 6 seeks to make out a case that the tribunal is the only forum for the petitioner-DNCC to challenge the tribunal's jurisdiction. However, from a minute reading of the afore-mentioned case-law, this Court does not find merit in the said submission for, in the said case the petitioner's circumstances while attracted the provisions of section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act to some extent, its facts also were relevant to the provisions of section 17(b) and section 20 of the Arbitration Act. And, the petitioner's application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act was rejected not on the ground that the petitioner can not come to the High Court Division directly, rather on the ground of non-fulfillment of the requirements set out in sub-section(2) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. Because, entertainment of an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act depends on having the satisfaction by the High Court Division that the stipulations engraved in Clauses (a) to (c) of section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act have been complied with. Per contra, the learned Advocate for the petitioner-DNCC sought to rely on the observations made by Supreme Court of India in the case of SBP vs Patel AIR 2006 SC 450 as well as on the commentaries made by renowned Law Academician Dr. PC Markanda in his authoritative book on arbitration that when the arbitration tribunal is formed by a competent Court, the tribunal's jurisdictional issue should be raised before the competent Court, not before the tribunal. However, since from the wordings employed in section 17(c) of our Arbitration Act, it is amply clear that a party is well competent to raise the issue before the arbitration tribunal as to whether the arbitration tribunal is properly constituted, be it by the parties amicably or by the Order of the Court, this Court is not inclined to concede to the said arguments. But it will, of course, be a better course of action for the parties to the arbitration to approach the High Court Division invoking section 20 of the Arbitration Act, if the petitioner is able to satisfy the High Court Division that (a) the determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs, (b) the application was submitted without any delay and (c) there is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court. It is to be borne in mind that the phrases and words used in the Arbitration Act of foreign countries might be different. A plain reading of section 32 of the 1996 Arbitration Act, of UK states that to prefer an application to the Court challenging jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal, either it has to be made with the agreement in writing of all the other parties to the proceedings or it has to be made with the permission of the tribunal. But our Parliament, after due consideration, precisely and intentionally excluded these 2 conditions, making section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 an all-in-all independent provision, not connected with or dependent upon exhausting or seeking permission from the arbitration tribunal in question. Therefore, it is indeed the facts of each case that will determine whether a party will challenge the jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal under section 17 read with section 19 or section 20 of the Arbitration Act. 

47. So, it is abundantly clear that for the purpose of having an adjudication on the issue as to having the jurisdiction of arbitration tribunal, our Arbitration Act provides a concurrent jurisdiction, namely, the arbitration tribunal itself and the High Court Division and, accordingly, a party to the arbitration proceeding is at liberty to approach either the arbitration tribunal or the High Court Division depending on the facts and circumstances of a particular case, and when a party decides to invoke section 20 of the Arbitration Act to approach the High Court Division challenging the jurisdiction of the tribunal, it is necessary for the said party to satisfy the High Court Division that (a) the determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs, (b) the application was submitted without any delay and (c) there is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court. The same ratio was laid down by this Court in the case of Chulain Mohiuddin Bhutto vs Mrs Rokeyet din and others, ALR Online 2019 though the facts of the case were different and the observations were made in a different context. 

48. In this case, the petitioner-DNCC being competent to avail any of the two fora, namely, the arbitration tribunal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act and the High Court Division under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, has rightly invoked section 20 of the Arbitration Act given the peculiarity of the facts of the case. Because, it was not possible for the petitioner to ascertain as to which tribunal should be approached, that is to say, the tribunal that was formed previously or the newly constituted tribunal. 

49. Upon carrying out examinations of the facts and circumstances of this case carefully, this Court finds that all the three conditions as laid down in Clauses (a) to (c) of section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act, have been satisfied by the petitioner, as it is apparent that the petitioner-DNCC is bleeding money each day because of being stuck with this case and preferring this section 20 application saved a huge amount of cost and the petitioner-DNCC preferred this instant application within the shortest period of time after obtaining internal approval and, finally, since the reasons, raised by the petitioner-DNCC in support of this section 20 application, have been found by this Court to be good reasons, therefore, this Court holds that the facts and circumstances of this case were fit for invoking the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, and hence the present petition is maintainable. 

50. Now, the second issue, namely, whether this Court is competent to pass necessary consequential Order/s, may be taken up. 

51. The reason behind framing the second issue is to determine the next course of actions to be taken by the District Judge Court, Dhaka, the arbitration tribunal and the parties to the arbitration, pursuant to this Court's declaration that the newly constituted arbitration tribunal is not a lawful tribunal in the eye of law; otherwise, the parties, being confused, may indulge them-selves in multifarious litigations. It is the view of this Court that since there is no prohibitory provisions in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) in taking recourse to the provisions of the CPC, any provisions of the CPC may be resorted to resolve a dilemma, if the Courts and the tribunal ever need it. To this end, section 24 may be quoted, which runs as follows; 24. The arbitral tribunal not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure and the Evidence Act—The arbitral tribunal shall not be bound to follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Evidence Act in disposing of a dispute under this Act. 

52. From a plain reading of the above-quoted provisions, it is not difficult to understand that the Legislature's intention behind incorporation of the provisions of section 24 in the Arbitration Act is to discourage the Courts and arbitration tribunal to apply the provisions of CPC, so that an arbitration proceeding is disposed of quickly. However, it shall be a serious misconstruction of the provisions of section 24 of the Arbitration Act, if it is inferred that the scheme of the aforesaid provision is to negate the employment of the provisions of the CPC in an appropriate case in the aid of expeditious disposal of an arbitration proceeding. Therefore, this Court holds that the provisions of the CPC will be applicable by the Courts and the arbitral tribunal in conducting an arbitration proceeding subject to the condition that employment of the CPC's provision shall help the arbitration tribunal and the concerned Court to conclude the arbitration proceeding quickly. More importantly, the High Court Division being endowed with the supervisory duties to take care of the judicial functions of the sub-ordinate Courts of the country by Article 109 of our Constitution, this Court finds it appropriate to pass necessary Directions upon all the District Courts of the country and, also, upon the 'Judicial Administrative Training Institute of Bangladesh' which is responsible for required training of the judicial officers of the country upon preparing necessary appropriate syllabus and topics in the training course for each of the phases of the service term of a judicial officer. 

53. Given the scenario of this case, this Court finds that if the necessary Orders and Directions are not passed by this Court upon the District Judge Court, the tribunal and the parties to the arbitration, there shall be a long delay in concluding the instant arbitration proceeding: Hence, this Court finds that if the provisions of section 151 of the CPC are resorted to conclude the arbitration proceeding speedily, then, there shall be an effective and meaningful disposal of the instant Rule. Accordingly, the following Observations, Orders and Directions are passed upon the relevant parties. 

54. Observations as to the next course of actions for the parties to the arbitration: (1) The parties to the arbitration shall be at liberty to approach the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka invoking section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act for appointment of any arbitrator in place of late learned Senior Advocate Dr. Rafiqur Rahman who expired during Covid-19, if upon exhausting the provisions of section 16 of the Arbitration Act (in reference to section 15(1)(b) of the Arbitration Act), they fail to agree upon appointment of the Chairman of the tribunal. 
(2) They shall further be at liberty to notify (either jointly or separately) the existing two arbitrators, namely, Mr Tofailur Rahman, Bar-at-Law, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and Mr AKM Faiz, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh about commencement of the arbitration at their earliest convenience.  
(3) After communicating with them, if any of them withdraws himself from office or expresses his inability to perform his functions, the parties shall be free to invoke section 16 of the Arbitration Act and, in the event of their failure to appoint an arbitrator on consensus, they can file an application to the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka under section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act. 
(4) The parties, however, shall be compe-tent to mutually agree to terminate the appointments of Mr Tofailur Rahman and Mr AKM Faiz upon invoking the provisions of Clauses (c) and (d) of sub-section (1) to section 15 of the Arbitration Act. And, if they succeed to terminate both the existing arbitrators, they shall also be competent to form a new arbitration tribunal on their own, upon mutually appointing two new arbitrators who thereafter shall appoint a Chairman of the tribunal within the shortest possible time. 

55. Direction upon the learned District Judge, Dhaka: (1) If the parties of this arbitration come up with an application under section 15(2) or under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, the learned District Judge, Dhaka is directed to dispose of the said application on fast track basis, within a maximum period of 60 (sixty) days. (2) The learned District Judge, Dhaka is directed that if an application under section 15(2) of the Arbitration Act is filed with a statement that there is only one arbitrator willing to perform his functions, in that scenario, appointment of one arbitrator and the Chairman shall be made vide a single Order. 
(3) If the application is filed under section 12 of the Arbitration Act on the averments that while the office of the Chairman has become vacant due to the death of Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the other two arbitrators have expressed their inability to perform their respective functions, in that scenario, the learned District Judge, Dhaka shall appoint all the three members of the tribunal, upon selecting one of them as the Chairman of the tribunal. To clarify this Direction, all that this Court intends to state that if any of the parties come up with the name of an arbitrator, the learned District Judge is not obliged to include him in the arbitration tribunal. Therefore: he should not appoint only two arbitrators (i.e. on the basis of the usual practice that one name is to be supplied by the petitioner and the other is to be appointed by the Court), rather the learned District Judge shall appoint three arbitrators of his own choice, upon investing the duties of chairmanship among one of the aforesaid three arbitrators, and dispose of the case finally. 
(4) The learned District Judge, however, shall be at liberty to appoint anyone or all of the arbitrators, who were appointed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka vide Order No. 91 dated 5-11-2020, [namely. Mr AKM Zahir Ahmed, retired District & Sessions Judge, Mr Ikteder Ahmed, former Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, and Hon'ble Justice (retired) Azizul Hague] if they are alive and health-wise fit and willing to take up the job. 

56. Directions upon all the learned District Judges of the country: 
They are directed to arrange an in-house meeting with the learned Judges with the rank of District Judges and Additional District Judges in their respective office rooms with an agenda of learning about the ratio laid down in this case, so that they are not mistaken in dealing with any applications under the Arbitration Act. In other words, they should know that all the applications under sections 7A, 10, 12, 15, 21(4), 42(1), 44, 50(1) and 53 of the Arbitration Act shall be registered as a separate application (Misc Case); secondly, upon appearance of the other party in an application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, they shall constitute the full tribunal including the Chairman, in the case of the tribunal to be consisted of more than 2 (two) arbitrators, within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the application and, thirdly, they should prefer to appoint the arbitrators of their own choice and, finally, they should apprise themselves about the other observations made in this Judgment. 

57. Direction upon the Registrar-General of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh: 
(1) The Registrar General of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is directed to disseminate this Judgment to all the 64 (sixty four) learned District Judges of the country. 
(2) He is further directed to ensure that the learned District Judges of the country have arranged the in-house meeting in their respective Offices within 60 (sixty) days of the receipt of this Order. 

58. Direction upon the Hon'ble Chairman of the Judicial Administrative training Institute of Bangladesh (JATI): 
She is directed to do the needful to include the Arbitration Act and the ratio of this Judgment in the lectures fixed for the trainees of the rank of the District Judges. 

59. Direction upon the concerned Office (which is responsible for dealing with Arbitration, Admiralty and Company Matters) of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh: 
Office is directed to send down the LCR at once to the office of the learned District Judge, Dhaka and, also, directed to communicate a copy of this Judgment to the (I) Hon'ble Chairman of JATI, (2) The Registrar General of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and (3) The learned District Judge, Dhaka. 

With the above observations, Directions, this application is disposed of, however, without any Order as to costs. 

End.
