full_judgment:
This Application brought under section 20(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001("Act") requires several other provisions of the Act to interface both with section 20 and variously with each other. It is deemed prudent at the outset, accordingly, for the text of each such provision to be laid out as follows for greater ease of subsequent reference: 
"20. Powers of the High Court Division in deciding jurisdiction.—(1) The High Court Division, may on the application of any of the parties to the arbitration agreement, after serving notice upon all other parties, determine any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal. 
(2) No application under this section shall be taken into account, unless the High Court Division is satisfied that—
(a) the determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs; 
(b) the application was submitted without any delay; and 
(c) there is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court. 
(3) The application shall state—the reasons on which the matter should be decided by the High Court Division. 
(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award. 

21. Powers of the arbitration tribunal to make interim orders.—(1) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, the arbitral tribunal may, at the request of a party, order a party to take any interim measure of protection as the arbitral tfibunal may consider necessary in respect of the subject matter of the dispute, and no appeal shall lie against this order. 
29. Statements of claim and defence.—(1) Within the period of time determined by the tribunal, the claimant shall state the facts supporting his claim, the points at issue and the relief or remedy sought, and the Respondent shall state his defence in respect of these particulars, unless the parties have otherwise agreed. 
35. Powers of the arbitral tribunal in case of default of the parties.—(1) The parties shall be free to agree on the powers of the arbitral tribunal in case of a party's failure to do anything necessary for the proper and expeditious conduct of the arbitration. 
(2) Where under sub-section (1). of section 29—
(a) any claimant fails to communicate his statement of claim, the tribunal shall terminate the proceedings, ... 
(5) If without showing sufficient cause a party fails to comply with any order or directions of the arbitral tribunal, the arbitral tribunal may make an order to comply with such order or directions within such time as it may deem fit." 

2. The Petitioner. hKash Limited prefers the instant Application challenging the jurisdiction of the sole arbitrator to conduct the arbitration proceedings between the Petitioner and the Respondent No. 1 and adjudicate on the same and to pass, in particular, Order No. 6 dated 31-1-2022 rejecting the application of the Petitioner to terminate the arbitration proceedings despite the mandatory requirement to terminate the proceedings under the Act and Order No. 7 dated 31-1-2022 also rejecting the Petitioner's application to vacate a section 7A (under the Act) order of status quo of the District Judge, Chattogram dated 21-11-2021 and the modification instead of vacating the section 7A order to the extent that the parties shall maintain status quo till 12-2-2022 (the next hearing date of the arbitration proceedings) in the circumstances that the initial section 7A order of status quo had already become redundant and superfluous. 

3. The facts essential for the disposal of this Application are that through a Distributor Agreement dated 25-6-2012 (`Agreement'), the Petitioner and the Respondent No. 1 agreed to appoint the Respondent No. 1 as a distributor of the Petitioner in order to establish and operate agent network and provide bKash's products and services throughout Khulshi, Bayazid Bostami and Halishahar territory in Chattogram City through distribution houses namely Prime AMR Exchange, Prime AMR Exchange-2 and Prime AMR Exchange-3 in Chattogram. 

4. Since the Respondent No. 1 was not adhering to the Petitioner's instructions and was seen to be in breach of the Agreement, the Petitioner issued three warning letters dated 16-7-2019 to the Respondent No. 1 for Prime AMR Exchange, Prime AMR Exchange-2 and Prime AMR Exchange-3 to which the Respondent No. 1, Distributor replied on 18-8-2019 refuting the Petitioner's allegations. Thereafter, the Petitioner having issued a show cause notice dated 2-10-2019 contending the failure of the Respondent No. 1 to maintain adequate investment to sustain its distributorship obligations, the latter replied to the said notice on 14-10-2019 attributing the insufficiency of invested funds to an alleged robbery incident. The Petitioner contesting the veracity of the excuse given of the robbery issued another show cause notice dated 11-11-2019. 

5. Replying to the show cause notice dated 11-11-2019, the Respondent No. 1 on 25-11-2019 sought time to provide the evidence of the robbery but eventually failed to do so. Thereafter, on 4-12-2019 an account closing letter was issued by the Petitioner regarding the account/wallet pertaining to Khulshi territory only with effect from 10-12-2019 the account was closed consequently on 2-2-2020. This prompted an eventual amendment agreement to be executed between the two parties titled the First Amendment Agreement to the Distributor Agreement on 12-8-2020 through which both parties agreed to discontinue the distributorship for Khulshi territory. It suffices to note here that the distributorships for the Halishahar and Bayeid Bostami areas remained untouched by the First Amendment Agreement for which the Petitioner pursued separate and different courses of action against the Respondent No. 1. 

6. It is against this backdrop that the Respondent No. 1 issued a notice of arbitration dated 29-4-2021 which was received by the Petitioner on 5-5-2021. Thereafter, the Petitioner replied to the said notice on 19-6-2021 pursuant to which the current sole arbitrator was appointed. This led the Respondent No. 1 to file Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 2021 under section 7A of the Act before the District Judge Court. Chattogram praying for an order of status quo in relation to distributorship service operations under various heads but covering too inter alio Bayazid Bostami and Halishahar areas till disposal of the arbitration and to secure too during such period the currency of the Agreement against any potential move of the Petitioner to terminate the same till disposal of the arbitration. The District Judge accordingly passed an ad interim order of status quo dated 5-5-2021. 

7. On 30-10-2021, the counsel for the Respondent No. 1 filed before the sole arbitrator an application seeking a three-week extension to submit the statement of claim as was granted-in-part by the tribunal on 4-11-2021 and was decided, amongst others, that:—
i. the Respondent No. 1 will file a statement of claim on or before 13-11-2021; 
ii. the Petitioner will file the statement of defence and counter-claim (if any) on or before 4-12-2021; and 
iii. the Respondent No. 1 could file a rejoinder and statement of defence to the counter-claim, if any, on or before 11-12-2021. 

8. Thereafter on 21-11-2021, vide Order No. 14 passed in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 2021, the District Judge, Chattogram decided to extend the order of status quo until such time as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 (filed by the Respondent No. 1 to secure the appointment of an arbitrator) was disposed of with a view to avoiding conflicting outcomes being arrived at in these two cases. Here the Petitioner contends that Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 in effect came to an end once the sole arbitrator entered appearance in the arbitration proceedings under consideration. 

9. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner, Mr.Tanjib-ul Alam submits against this backdrop that in gross abuse of the order of status quo of the District Judge dated 21-11-2021 and in violation of Order No. 2 dated 4-11-2021 of the sole arbitrator, the Respondent No. 1 did not submit any statement of claim till 10-1-2022. As a result on 10-1-2022, the Petitioner submitted two applications before the sole arbitrator, namely, (i) an application for vacating the orders of status quo dated 21-11-2021 and 5-5-2021, and (ii) an application for terminating the arbitration proceedings. 

10. Within eight days of receiving the Petitioner's applications, the Respondent No. submitted the statement of claim along with an application for condonation of delay and admission of the statement of claim on 18-1-2022. On 22-1-2022, the Petitioner submitted a written objection to the application for condonation of delay from the Respondent No. 1. Moreover, the Respondent No. 1, once again not adhering to the timeline as set by the sole arbitrator, submitted an application praying for time to submit written objections against the applications submitted by the Petitioner. 

11. The hearing consequently took place on 26-1-2022 where the Petitioner's counsel emphasized that when in an arbitration the claimant fails to submit the statement of claim within time as decided by the arbitrator the Act mandates the termination of the arbitration proceedings without conferring any discretion on the tribunal to decide otherwise. It was further emphasized that in view of the District Judge's order dated 21-11-2021 in Arbitration Misc. Case No. 128 of 2021, there is no order of status quo current at that time since Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 had came to an end owing to assumption of responsibilities by the sole arbitrator. 

12. The sole arbitrator through Order No. 6 dated 31-1-2022 rejected the application for termination of the proceedings by reference to section 29 of the Act on the purported grounds that "the word 'shall' does not always necessarily mean mandatory and 'may' is not always interpreted to be directory or discretionary". The sole arbitrator further fixed the date for the next hearing to be 12-2-2022 for framing of issues and commencement of hearing and also directed the Petitioner to submit any statement of defence and counterclaim within two weeks. Furthermore, through Order No. 7 of the same date, the arbitrator decided to modify, as the Petitioner submits, a non-existing status quo order, thereby, directing the parties to maintain status quo till 12-2-2022 on the ground that the original order was a harmless one and none of the parties is likely to be irreparably prejudiced if that order subsists while the arbitration proceeding is pending. 

13. Here, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam, as aided by the learned Advocate Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam, submits that the sole arbitrator decided not to terminate the arbitration proceedings despite his mandate under the Act to do so on the indefensible ground that the word "shall" does not necessarily have the connotation of mandatoriness attached to it but can instead have a certain element of laxity attached to it if need be. Here, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam emphatically argues that there are numerous precedents in support of the rule of statutory interpretation that when the meaning of a word is unambiguous and clear, it should be given its ordinary and natural meaning and that this is one such case where that cardinal rule holds true. The meaning of the words of section 35(2)(a) read with section 29(1) of the Act in that sense is submitted to be clear and unambiguous, thereby, not requiring any exceptional explanation or interpretation as provided by the sole arbitrator in the present instance. Accordingly, the Petitioner views the act of the sole arbitrator not to terminate the arbitration proceedings as a clear example of bias on his part necessitating such a decision to be declared by this Court as wholly out of jurisdiction. As such, the Petitioner would also have the Arbitrator declared as consequentially having no jurisdiction to preside over the arbitration proceedings further to the Order Nos. 6 and 7 being declared as been made without jurisdiction. 

14. The first aspect of the case taken up for consideration by this Court pertains to Order No. 6 dated 31-1-2022 of the sole arbitrator in which the Petitioner challenges the jurisdiction of the arbitrator to reject the application of the Petitioner to terminate the arbitration proceedings involving the Petitioner and the Respondent No. 1 on the grounds that "the word 'shall' does not always necessarily mean mandatory and may is not always interpreted to be directory or discretionary". 

15. By reference to the Application and submissions made by the Petitioner's learned Advocate Mr. Tanbjib-ul Alam aided by Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam this Court has taken particular note of the interplay of sections 29(1) and 35(2)(a) of the Act. Indeed, this Court accepts the fact that the cardinal rule of statutory interpretation applicable and attracted to this case is that when the meaning of a word is unambiguous and clear it should be given its ordinary and natural meaning and that in the circumstances the word "shall" as appears in both sections 29 and 35(2)(a) will be taken to mean mandatory. It has not also escaped this Court's attention that the Respondent No. 1 has sought to interpret the provisions of the Act in light of the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 without pinpointing the fact that there are some material differences in the provisions of these two pieces of legislation. Section 25 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides for a determination of a defaulting act, i.e., the filing of a statement of claim, to be contingent upon sufficient cause not being shown for such failure. However, the corresponding provision of the Act leaves no such scope for the claimant to show sufficient cause for failure to submit such statement of claim leading to the termination of proceedings mandated under section 35 of the Act. The judgment of the Bombay High Court in Wanbury Ltd vs Candid Drug Distributions, Arbitration Petition No. 1461 of 2014 cited by the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 1, Mr. Mukunda Chandra Debnath as was delivered in light of the fact that the provisions of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 allowed for sufficient cause to be shown is accordingly distinguished by Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam as not being applicable in the present fact and circumstances. Therefore, this Court finds, since the Act does not permit of sufficient cause to be shown, there is no scope to consider the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 or the aforementioned judgment to be of persuasive nature in providing in any way greater content or the meaning to sections 29 and 35(2(a) of the Act. Furthermore, this Court opines that the entire purpose of the enactment of the Act is to ensure speedy disposal of disputes and, therefore, section 29(1) has been drafted in a manner as leaves no scope for procrastination in such dispute resolution mechanism. It follows that like section (1), section 35(2)(Ka) of the Act is equally of mandatory application permitting an arbitrator to terminate any proceeding where any claimant fails to communicate the statement of claim. Moreover, section 35(5) provides that the arbitration tribunal may order compliance with its orders within such time as deemed fit. Predicated on the golden rule of interpretation of statutes that words prima facie must be given their ordinary meaning, if section 35(2)(a) and section 35(5) are considered together, it would be seen that the former mandates the arbitrator to terminate the proceedings whereas the latter one only gives power to the arbitrator to secure compliance in limited circumstances. This case reveals to this Court the phenomenon also of the double imperative when one considers the provisions of section 35(2)(a) in correlation to section 29(1) of the Act. A perusal of the facts reveals to this Court that by reason of its preoccupation with section 35 the tribunal lost sight of the root provision under section 29 of the Act mandatorily requiring the filing of a claim within the time limit set by the tribunal. There is little doubt in this Court's mind, therefore, that by passing Order No. 6 the sole arbitrator was wholly misguided on these mutually reinforcing clear provisions of applicable law. 

16. The Petitioner has also challenged the jurisdiction of the arbitrator to pass Order No. 7 dated 31-1-2022 modifying the District Judge's order of status quo dated 21-11-2021 to the extent that the parties shall maintain status quo till 12-2-2022, i.e., until the next hearing date of the arbitration proceedings. It is to be noted that upon rejecting the application for termination of the proceedings the sole arbitrator further fixed 12-2-2022 as the next date of hearing for framing of issues and commencement of hearing and also directed the Petitioner to submit any statement of defense within two weeks. Fundamentally further, as the Petitioner contends, through Order No. 7 dated 31-1-2022 the arbitrator decided to modify a non-existing status quo and directed the parties to maintain such status quo till 12-2-2022. This Court accepts the argument that the arbitrator indeed modified a non-existing status quo order in the facts and directed the parties to maintain the status quo till 12-2-2022. In this regard the sole arbitrator is found to have acted beyond his jurisdiction and acted in violation of section 21(1) of the Act under which a tribunal can only exercise its jurisdiction to issue an interim order only upon an application by the party seeking such an order. In the instant case, the claimant Respondent No. 1 neither submitted any application for status quo nor any application for extension of an order of status quo. As such, this Court finds by passing the order of status quo suo motu and rejecting the application for vacating the order of status quo the sole arbitrator exceeded his authority to do so and, thereby, the said order is found to be manifestly issued beyond jurisdiction. 

17. It is at this juncture that this Court emphasizes the fact that the instant Application has been brought under section 20 of the Act which provides, 
"(1) The High Court Division, may, on the application of any of the parties to the arbitration agreement, after serving notice upon all other parties, determine any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal." 

18. The question posed this Court at the outset is, therefore, the extent of its own jurisdiction under section 20 to scrutinize the orders passed by an arbitral tribunal or, as in this case, the sole arbitrator. The word "jurisdiction" has been defined in Stroud's Judicial Dictionary thus: 
"Jurisdiction' is a dignity which a man hath by a power to do justice in causes of complaint made before him (Termes de la Ley). In its narrow and strict sense, the `jurisdiction' of a validly constituted court connotes the limits which are imposed upon its power to hear and determine issues between persons seeking to avail themselves of its process by reference (i) to the subject matter of the issue or (ii) to the persons between whom the issue is joined or (iii) to the kind of relief sought, or to any combination of these factors. In its wider sense, it embraces also the settled practice of the court as to the way in which it will exercise its power to hear and determine issues which fall within its 'jurisdiction' (in the strict sense) or as to the circumstances in which it will grant a particular kind of relief which it has 'jurisdiction' (in the strict sense) to grant, including its settled practice to refuse to exercise such powers, or to grant such relief in particular circumstances." 

19. The Supreme Court of India, in the case of National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd vs Siemens Atkeingesellschaft as reported in 2007(1) Arb. LR 377 (SC) held that the "expression `jurisdiction' is a word of many hues. Its colour is to be discerned from the setting in which it is used." In Shaqafath Ali Khan and Ors. vs Imdad Jah Bahadur and On as reported in (2009) 5 SCC 162 the Supreme Court of India held that: 
"A civil revision application although must necessarily having regard to the terminologies used in Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure involve the question of jurisdiction, the question which would arise is as to what are the jurisdictional questions. A jurisdictional question may arise not only when a court acts wholly without jurisdiction but also in a case where jurisdictional errors are committed while exercising jurisdiction. There are various facets of 'jurisdictional errors'. Taking into consideration any irrelevant fact or non-consideration of a. relevant fact would involve jurisdictional issue." 

20. Furthermore, Section 20(4) provides that, "(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section, the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award". In this regard it is apparent to this Court that sections 20(1) and 20(4) read together permit of the word "jurisdiction" in section 20(1) to refer to a tribunal's jurisdiction not only in regards to its constitution and formation but also to the extent and scope of the tribunal's power of determination. If section 20(1) merely referred to jurisdiction with regards to the formation of a tribunal then the provisions on a tribunal's determinative power in section 20(4) would not have necessarily followed in the scheme of section 20 as a whole. In this regard, it has been affirmed in a myriad of cases including Abu Khair Md. Nazmul Huq and Ors. vs Government of Bangladesh and Ors. as reported in EX/BDHC/0055/2022 that a statute must be read as a whole and not in part. In light of the above, it can be deduced, therefore, that how jurisdiction is exercised is also a matter which definitely falls within an expansive treatment of the word "jurisdiction" in section 20(1) to include the authority and scope of a tribunal to pass any order in the concerned arbitration. 

21. This Court accepts the submission of Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam that under section 20 the High Court Division has been empowered to determine 
any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and such a power is an independent power so conferred upon this Court as held in the case of Dhaka North City Corporation vs District Judge, Dhaka reported in (2023] 27 ALR (HCD) 234. Accepted too is the submission that under section 21 of the Act, unlike section 37 of Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, no provision for appeal has been provided against an interim order passed by an arbitral tribunal. Predicated on the above this Court also finds merit in Mr. Alam's submission that the legislature intended, as evident in section 20(4), that section 20 of the Act would enable this Court to examine an order passed by an arbitral tribunal or a sole arbitrator on the question of jurisdiction. Carrying forward such line of reasoning it is this Court's view further that section 20 empowers this Court to examine whether an arbitration tribunal is stepping outside its jurisdiction by passing a patently illegal order and, thereby, causing miscarriage of justice. In this context this Court finds that the word "jurisdiction" is not merely to be taken as being confined to gauging the validity of the arbitration agreement, proper constitution of the arbitral tribunal or whether the matters have been submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement, but also must necessarily extend to cover the determination of the question relating to the scope of jurisdiction and mode of exercise of the same by a tribunal. 

22. In light of the aforementioned provisions of law, it is considered important by this Court to determine the ambit of the word "jurisdiction" of the arbitration tribunal. If the arbitration tribunal has exceeded its jurisdiction and, therefore, made a determination which is in essence a nullity, then this Court would indeed have the jurisdiction to determine any question regarding that purported determination. The House of Lords in its landmark judgment in Anisminic Ltd vs Foreign Compensation Commission [1969] 1 All ER 208 ("Anisminic") has dealt with this very question of jurisdiction. Lord Reid at page 212, paragraph H, provided a non-exhaustive list of instances where the decision made by a tribunal, i.e., the Foreign Compensation Commission in England in that instance, may be rendered outside jurisdiction in the following terms:—
`But there are many cases where, although the tribunal had jurisdiction to enter on the enquiry, it has done or failed to do something in the course of the enquiry which is of such a nature that its decision is a nullity. It may have given its decision in bad faith. It may have made a decision which it had no power to make. It may have failed in the course of the enquiry to comply with the requirements of natural justice. It may in perfect good faith have misconstrued the provisions giving it power to act so that it failed to deal with the question remitted to it and decided some question which was not remitted to it. It may have refused to take into account something which it was required to take into account. Or it may have based its decision on some matter which, under the provisions setting it up, it had no right to take into account. I do not intend this list to be exhaustive. But if it decides a question remitted to it for decision without committing any of these errors it is as much entitled to decide that question wrongly as it is to decide it rightly." 

23. It is pertinent to note at this juncture that any authority or body, be it an administrative tribunal or otherwise, as is empowered to act in any manner as affects any individual's or any entity's rights and interest has a concomitant obligation to exercise such power judicially, i.e.. fairly. When such power is administrative or arbitral, it does not make such power any less judicial if its exercise affects rights of a person. 

24. The next stage of the evaluation of the principles of Anisminic is the decision in Re Racal Communications Ltd. reported in [1981 AC 374 where Lord Diplock in the House of Lords upheld the opinion of Lord Denning thus:—
"The breakthrough made by Anisminic was that, as respects administrative tribunals and authorities, the old distinction between errors of law that went to jurisdiction and errors of law that did not was for practical purposes abolished. Any error of law that could be shown to have been made by them in the course of reaching their decision on matters of fact or of administrative policy would result in their having asked themselves the wrong question with the result that the decision they reached would be a nullity." 

25. Anisminic has been relied upon in O'Reilly and others vs Mackman and others [1982.1 3 All ER 1124, where at 1129 it has been observed that:—
"that the courts had theretofore imposed upon themselves so far as determinations of inferior courts and statutory tribunals were concerned, by drawing esoteric distinctions between errors of law committed by such tribunals that went to their jurisdiction, and errors of law committed by them within their jurisdiction. The breakthrough that the Anisminic case made was the recognition by the majority of this House that if a tribunal whose jurisdiction was limited by statute or subordinate legislation mistook the law applicable to the facts as it had found them, it must have asked itself the wrong question, i.e., one into which it was not empowered to inquire and so had no jurisdiction to determine. Its purported 'determination', not being a 'determination' within the meaning of the empowering legislation, was accordingly a nullity." 

26. One is reminded too of Lord Lane's evaluation of Anisminic in Pearlman vs Keepers and Governors of Harrow School 119791 QB 56 (CA) that a court as this will always retain the power to quash a decision of an inferior tribunal which has acted in excess of its jurisdiction including a case where, as Lord Reaid emphasized in Anisminic, the purported determination of the tribunal turns out to be a nullity because it cannot be properly called a determination at all. Moreover, Lord Reid in Anisminic made an observation regarding the jurisdiction of the courts to enquire into the decisions made by tribunals. It was held that if there is a provision which is reasonably capable of having two meanings, that meaning shall be taken which preserves the ordinary jurisdiction of the court. As such, this Court finds merit in Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam's submission that when there is a decision of the arbitration tribunal where the tribunal has decided a matter for exceeding its jurisdiction this Court has jurisdiction under section 20 of the Act to adjudicate on that issue. 

27. Predicated on the above the statutory task of this Court is now to ascertain to its satisfaction that this section 20(1). Application does indeed meet the section 20(2) requirements, thereby, meriting due consideration by this Court under the following heads: 
(a) The determination of the jurisdictional question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs: 

28. The Respondent No. 1, in the guise of restraining the Petitioner, bKash from stopping a host of market services and operational activities as claimant, has effectively sought a perpetual injunction on termination of the Agreement entered into between the Petitioner and the said Respondent. It is to be noted that the Petitioner did not take any steps for termination of the Agreement itself and, as such, this could not, therefore, be a subject matter of 'arbitration pursuant to clause 18.1 of the Agreement further to which the sole arbitrator was appointed. Hence, the sole arbitrator did not have any jurisdiction to decide on the matter of restraining the Petitioner from termination of the Agreement. As such, the sole arbitrator did not have jurisdiction to pass any order which would otherwise allow the relief as sought by the Respondent which is outside the ambit of jurisdiction of the sole arbitrator. Besides, as has been contended by Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam, the Respondent, taking advantage of the order of status quo, has resorted to dilatory tactics leading to a protracted process before the tribunal and the courts resulting in financial loss to the Petitioner which is left impaired to effectively and profitably compete in the market for lack of proper presence of a distributor. Besides, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam apprehends, if the arbitration is allowed to proceed and an award is made by the same tribunal, the Petitioner will have to challenge the award on the same grounds at a later stage after incurring substantial cost in the arbitration. As such, the Petitioner submits that the determination of the question of jurisdiction at this point is likely to produce substantial savings in costs and this Court ought to exercise its jurisdiction to determine the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal. This Court finds no reason to question such line of submission by Mr. Alam and has, therefore, been inclined to exercise its power of oversight under section 20(1) through this judgment. 
(b) The application was submitted without any delay: 

29. The impugned orders being Order No. 6 and Order No. 7 were passed by the sole arbitrator on 31-1-2022 and the Application was filed on 8-2-2022. After receiving the Orders Nos. 6 and 7, both dated 31-1-2022, it is found that immediate steps were taken by the counsel for the Petitioner to advise the Petitioner and receive necessary instructions. Thereafter, the counsel drafted the Application and submitted the same before this Court within seven days without undue delay. 
(c) There is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court: 

30. Highlighted under this head by Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam is the fact there is no forum for the Petitioner to appeal against the impugned order(s) under the Act. It is that element of finality of the Orders complained of and the very peremptory nature and effect of the same that is now satisfactorily and aptly agitated as a strong ground ensuring the maintainability of this Application under Section 20(2)(c). Accordingly, it is submitted that the question as to whether the sole arbitrator has exceeded his jurisdiction in passing the offending Orders ought to be determined under section 20 of Act. 

31. This Court is satisfied that the preliminary statutorily designated ingredients as identified above are in indeed present in this section 20 Application. Resultantly, the said Application having survived this initial elimination round it now falls upon this Court to piece together its views and findings on the extent to which the sole arbitrator travelled beyond his jurisdiction in passing the Order Nos. 6 and 7. 

32. Upon a review of the facts and the grounds agitated to support the Petitioner's cause of action, this Court remains satisfied that the sole arbitrator has exceeded his jurisdiction in several ways, namely, by passing an order on an issue even when there was no extant cause of action or dispute, through deciding against the termination of the arbitral proceedings despite being mandated to do so by the Act, extending the order of status quo despite there being no application or prayer from the Respondent No. 1 to do so, and, consequentially, by losing sight of the fact that the current case is not one where specific performance can be ordered. 

33. As evident from the discussion above, an entire set of background facts have been placed before this Court with a view to ascertaining whether the sole arbitrator acted beyond his jurisdiction meriting a section 20 intervention by this Court. It is evident from the First Amendment to the Agreement dated 12-8-2020 that the distributorship for Khulshi area only has been terminated. However, no dispute or cause of action has arisen in relation to the accounts pertaining to the Halishohor and Baizid area which nevertheless have been made subject to an order of status quo passed by the District Judge, Chattogram. It appears also that the District Judge passed a final order of disposal of the section 7A of the act application by tagging the matter with another proceeding under section 12 of the Act at a time when the sole arbitrator had already been appointed. Accordingly, when the sole arbitrator extended the order of status quo (through Order No. 6) in absence of any application to do so he also went beyond his jurisdiction since the dispute which has arisen is not in relation to Prime AMR Exchange 2 or 3 for Baizid or Halishohor area. 

34. On the issue of the termination of arbitration proceedings, this Court notes that section 35(2) of the Act provides that where under section 29(1) "any claimant fails to communicate his statement of claim, the tribunal shall terminate the proceedings". From a plain reading of section 35(2) it appears that the section mandatorily sanctions the termination of the proceedings contingent upon the claimant's failure to submit its claim etc. within the time determined by the tribunal and that there are no two ways about it. The use of the word "shall" as opposed to "may" is clearly in evidence of the fact that a failure by the claimant to submit the statement of claim within the time specified does not leave the arbitrator with any discretion and scope not to terminate the proceedings. Sections 29(1) and 35(2)(a) represent a composite whole that may aptly be termed as a double imperative the failure to comply with which shall invariably prove to be fatal for the claimant. There is no statutory mechanism available at circumventing this statutorily entrenched double imperative not even by reference to the section 35(5) avenue of limited redress. Let it be noted that the discretionary relief that may be obtained through section 35(5) does not extend so far as to neutralize in any way the absolute and mandatory effect of the section 29(1) and 35(2)(a) provisions. Section 35(5) has a sphere of operation limited by and outside of or beyond the firm statutory tenets of section 29(1) and 35(2)(a). In other words, it is a residual power given to the tribunal under section 35(5) to provide discretionary redress leaving untouched and not encroaching upon the firm, absolute, and reinforcing provisions of sections 29(1) and 35(2)(a). 

35. Furthermore, the Respondent No. 1 has sought to substantiate its case through attempting to explain the tenor and purport of section 35 by references to ostensibly corresponding provisions of and case law based on the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 in which, however, a significant distinguishing feature has been overlooked by the learned Advocate for the said Respondent. The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides that, "unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where, without showing sufficient cause—(a) the claimant fails to communicate his statement of claim in accordance with sub-section (1) of section 23, the arbitral tribunal shall terminate the proceedings." The words "without showing sufficient cause" mark the point of material difference and deviation between the two aforementioned sections, essentially meaning that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides the arbitrator with a discretion to determine as to whether there was sufficient cause for the failure to submit the statement of claim which is wholly absent in the Act. 

36. Also the District Judge. Chattogram passed the order dated 21-11-2021 of status quo in the following manner, অত্র আদালতের সালিশী মিছ-১৩৪/২০২১ নং মামলার সালিশী কার্যক্রম বিজ্ঞ জেলাজজ আদালত, ঢাকাতে চলমান থাকায় উক্ত সালিশী কার্যক্রম নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত অত্র সালিশী মিছ মামলায় প্রদত্ত বিগত ৫-৫-২০২১ ইং তারিখের স্থিতাবস্থার আদেশ বলবত থাকিবে। It appears from the order that status quo had to be maintained until the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 came to an end. The said case was filed by the Respondent No. 1 for the appointment of an arbitrator by reference to section 12 of the Act. However, on account of the supervening development of the Respondent No. 2 entering appearance as the sole arbitrator, the said Miscellaneous Case had, in this Court's opinion, come to be subsumed under the arbitration proceedings presently underway. Under such circumstances, the status quo came to be non-existent and redundant once the sole arbitrator had entered appearance. Moreover, and as otherwise statutorily prescribed, there was no application on behalf of the Respondent No. 1 to modify or extend the order of status quo. Rather, there was an application filed by the Petitioner for vacating the order of status quo which could either be allowed or rejected. However, the Respondent No. 2, sole arbitrator went beyond his jurisdiction by opting instead to modify the said order as operated to the benefit of the Respondent No. 1. 

37. Under such facts and circumstances, it is found that the sole arbitrator travelled beyond his jurisdiction by passing Order Nos. 6 and 7 both dated 31-1-2022 and which are, hereby, set-aside. This Court resultantly terminates the appointment of the sole arbitrator and Mr. Akhtar Imam, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh is, in the alternative, appointed as new sole arbitrator. Mr. Akhtar Imam's appointment proceeds upon this Court's overall satisfaction as to his ability to discharge such responsibility in an independent and impartial manner within the scheme of the arbitration as already underway between the parties. 

38. In the result, the Petitioner's Application is allowed, subject to the findings, observations, and directions above. 

There is no Order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Kashefa Hussain, J:  Since all these writ petitions involved similar questions of law and facts therefore sake of convenience these are all taken up together for hearing and now being disposed of by this common judgment. 

The judgments and decrees, which are called in question in the instant writ petitions, are narrated in the table below for ready reference:- 
S.L. Nos.	Writ Petition Nos.	Judgment and decree dated	Land Survey Tribunal Case Nos.	Land Survey Tribunals (LST) concerned
1.	4259 of 2022	31.01.2022	983 of 2013	LST, Barisal
2.	416 of 2020	19.10.2020	53 of 2017	LST, Gaibandha 
3.	6417 of 2022	19.11.2020	40 of 2020	LST, Kurigram
4.	11921 of 2019	26.08.2019	593 of 2014	LST, Sherpur
5.	14014 of 2019	17.09.2017	482 of 2014	LST, Sirajgonj
6.	9823 of 2017	19.05.2014	01 of 2013	LST, Faridpur
7.	11633 of 2022	30.08.2022	2215 of 2015	LST, Chandpur
8.	6880 of 2021	22.02.2021	189 of 2013	LST, Barisal
9.	12123 of 2019	13.01.2019	4311 of 2013	LST, Kishoreganj

All these writ petitions arise out of judgment and decrees passed by the land survey tribunals and all arise out of suits filed in land survey Tribunals. When the matters were taken up for hearing our attention was drawn to some judgments passed by other Benches of this division involving similar matters and issues arising out of judgment and decrees or judgment and orders passed by the Land Survey Tribunal. For our convenience we have particularly perused the judgment tiled in writ petition No. 11463 of 2016 and another in writ petition No. 515 of 2017 inter alia another decision. In these writ petitions Rule were disposed of primarily on the ground of writ not being maintainable pursuant to enactment of Section 145 B of the S.A.T Act. 

Section 145 B provides for setting up Laud Survey Appellate Tribunal. The objective of enacting section 145 B is that any person aggrieved by any judgment and decree or order passed by any land survey tribunal may file an appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. The Overall view taken in these judgments while disposing of these writ petitions are that judgment and decrees and orders passed by the Tribunal involving question of law and fart needs reassessment of evidence and other factors which is not possible or permissible in writ and therefore writ is not maintainable. 

We have also perused the writ petition before us which involves similar question and issues of law and fact. For sake of convenience we are inclined to take up writ petition No. 4259 of 2022 which arises out of a judgment and decree in which Rule was issued in the following terms: 
"Let a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent No. 5 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 25.01.2022 (decree sinned on 31.01.2022) passed by the learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal, Barishal decreeing the suit of the plaintiff in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 983 of 2013 (Annexure-A) to the writ petition should not be declared illegal, improper, unjust, erroneous, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper." 

Upon perusal of the writ petition it also appears that the judgment and decree passed by the tribunal inherently and primarily involve question of facts and evidences which need reassessment inter aria other relevant procedures. Drawing support from the judgment in writ petition No. 11463 of 2016 and writ petition No. 515 of 2017 including some other judgments with which we are in respectful agreement with, we are of the considered view upon examination and scrutiny of all the writ petitions before us that these judgments involves question of law and fact which call for reassessment of evidences including exhausting other procedures which is not possible in writ jurisdiction. 

We are also of the considered view these writ petitions arc not maintainable. Moreover the government has already by enactment of Section 145 B of the S.A.T Act provided for establishment of Land Survey Appellate Tribunals. Although the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal has not been formally constituted but nevertheless we are of the considered view that since a law has been passed in this regard by way of Section 145 B of the S.A.T Act therefore we are not in a position to entertain these matters in writ jurisdiction. As mentioned above all these matters involve question of law and evidential facts that need reassessment including exhausting other procedures which are not possible in writ jurisdiction. Moreover also by way of enactment of Section 145 B of the S.A.T Act writ petition is not maintainable. 

Therefore also drawing support from the judgments passed by other Benches of this Division and relying on the observations made above we are inclined to dispose of the Rules. 

In the result, all these Rules are disposed of. The petitioners are at liberty to prefer appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal whenever the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal may be constituted. Meanwhile status-quo or stay whatsoever granted during the issuance of the Rule shall continue till tiling of appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. 

Let the L.C.R which have already been sent and tagged with the concerned writ petitions, be sent down to the concerned Tribunals. 

Communicate this order at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman, J: This rule, was issued challenging the validity of order dated 30-12-2021 passed under Nothi Number CEVT/ Case (Cus)-675/2021/4047 by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka (respondent number 1 herein) dismissing the appeal affirming order number 68/Bond Circle-6(A)/2021 dated 8-12-2021 passed by the Commissioner, Customs Bond Commissionerate, Dhaka (respondent number 2 herein) imposing penalty of Taka 2,16,00,000 with customs duty, tax and other charges of Taka 3,94,04,192.62 (Taka 6,10,04,192.62 in total) upon the petitioner under section 111 read with Clauses 60, 61, 62 and 90 of the Table appended to section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 (in short, the Act, 1969) without disposing of the application filed under section 194(1) thereof. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule, in brief, are that the petitioner is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and is engaged in business of Printing and Packaging under the name and style of M/s Mantaka Printing and Packaging Limited. In course of its business, the petitioner-company also obtained a bond license bearing number 1068/CusPBW/2016 dated 11-4-2016 from respondent number 2. He (respondent 2) formed an Audit Team and the team physically inspected the factory and warehouse of the petitioner-company on 29-5-2021, where it was detected that 8,12,082.50 KGs raw materials were illegally removed from the warehouse and another 42,401.71 Kgs were kept to remove in the same manner. The value of the removed raw materials was Taka 9,94,69,705.21 and customs duty, tax and other, charges on the same was calculated Taka 3,94,04,192.62. 

3. Pursuant to the audit report, respondent number 2 issued a notice upon the Managing Director of the petitioner-company on 4-7-2021 asking him to show cause as to why the amount of Taka 3,94,04,192.62 should not be realized as customs duty and taxes under section 111 of the Act, 1969 and as to why the penalty should not be imposed upon the company under section 13(3) and Clauses 60, 61, 62 and 90 of the Table appended to Section 156(1) of the Act, 1969 (vide Annexure-A to the writ petition). 

4. The petitioner replied to the notice on 6-7-2021 denying all the material allegations made therein contending, inter alia, that on the day of inspection on 24-5-2021 the factory was open from 9-00 am to 5-00 pm and due to pandemic situation, the production was also stopped at that time. The audit team visited the factory at about 7-30 pm while only the security guards were present at the factory premises. It was further contended that the utilization permission (UP) number 51/2021 and twelve bills of entry number as mentioned in the show cause notice were not of the petitioner-company. The audit team found shortage of raw materials against a wrong UP number, which was not issued in the name of the petitioner-company. The allegation of illegal removal of raw materials was not correct and sustainable. 

5. On receipt of the reply, respondent number 2 issued second show cause notice on 14-9-2021 bringing the same allegations against the petitioner-company simply omitting the number .of the bills of entry and amending the UP number as mentioned in the first notice. The petitioner replied thereto on 15-9-2019 denying the allegations of illegal removal of raw materials from the warehouse, and prayed to recall the show cause notices exonerating it from the allegations. 

6. After hearing, respondent number 2 passed an adjudication order on 8-12-2021 imposing penalty upon the petitioner-company with a direction to pay customs duty and taxes in addition to the penalty as already stated. The order was communicated to the petitioner on 9-12-2021. 

7. In that event, the petitioner-company preferred Customs Appeal Number (Cus) 675 of 2021 dated 21-12-2021 in the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka (in short, the Tribunal) against the adjudication order and filed an application under section 194(1) of the Act, 1969 praying for dispensation with the statutory deposit of the demanded duty and taxes, and penalty on the ground of hardship (vide Annexure:F-1). 

8. The Tribunal heard the application hit without disposing of the same summarily dismissed the appeal by order dated 27-12-2021 (vide Annexure-G) giving rise to the instant writ petition. 

9. Respondent number 2 contests the rule by filling an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition stating that the petitioner imported raw materials under bond facilities. On the basis of an allegation against the petitioner-company, a preventive team of his office inspected the factory as well as the bonded warehouse on 29-5-2021 and detected shortage of 8,12,082.50 KGs raw materials and also found another 42,801.71 KGs kept to be removed illegally from the warehouse. The value of the raw materials was Taka 9,94,69,705.21 and chargeable duty and taxes thereon was calculated Taka 3,94,04,192.62. The petitioner is liable to pay the said amount of duty and taxes under section 111 of the Act, 1969 and also liable to pay the penalty under Clauses 60, 61, 62 and 90 of the Table appended to section 156(1) of the Act, 1969. Respondent number 2 gave notice, heard the petitioner and rightly passed the adjudication order. Considering the provisions of law, the Tribunal (impliedly) rejected the application filed under section 194 of the Act and dismissed the appeal. 

10. Mr Mintu Kuamr Mondal, learned advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Members of the Tribunal without disposing of the application filed under section 194(1) of the Act, 1969 and applying their judicial minds and exercising their discretionary power passed the impugned order dismissing the appeal holding that the allegation brought against the petitioner-company was proved and thereby committed illegality. 

11. Mr Mondal further submits that the Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction dismissing the appeal straightway without settling the issue of statutory deposition and without hearing the parties on merit. The impugned order is, therefore, not an order under the provision of section 1968 of the Act, 1969. Under the facts and circumstances of the present case, the Tribunal ought to have considered that the petitioner-company was suffering from financial hardship due to unpaid bank-loan, fire-disaster and the ongoing pandemic situation, under which it had to pray for admission of the appeal exempting the statutory deposit. 

12. In support of his submission, Mr Mondal refers to the cases of Shahadat Hossain (Md) vs National Board of Revenue and others 65 DLR 522 and NOL (Bangladesh) Ltd. Chittagong vs Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong and others 27 BLC 58. 

13. Per contra, Mr Amit Talukder, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for respondent number 2 refers to the decision of the larger bench of this division presided over by Zubayer Rahman Chaowdhury, J passed in the case of Nila Packing and Accessories Ltd vs Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal and another with eleven other cases in bunch and submits that the second proviso to section 194 of the Act, 1969 leaves no room for doubt that the power to dispense with the deposit, either unconditional or with any condition has been left to the sole discretion of the Tribunal. In the case in hand, the Tribunal logically exercised its discretion and rightly dismissed the appeal. There is nothing to interfere with the impugned order and, as such, the rule is liable to be discharged. 

14. Mr Talukder further submits that this court has no jurisdiction to substitute its own decision for that of the Tribunal granting exemption on the application of hardship filed by the appellant. The second proviso to section 194 of the Act confers absolute power on the Tribunal to decide the question of hardship considering each and every case on merit. In the present case, the Tribunal impliedly rejected the hardship application and consequently dismissed the appeal. Since the petitioner preferred the appeal without making the statutory deposit, the Tribunal rightly dismissed the same. 

15. We have considered the submission of the learned Advocate and that of the learned Deputy Attorney-General and also gone through the record as well as the decisions cited. 

16. It appears that the petitioner preferred the appeal and on the same day filed an application for exemption from statutory deposit under the second proviso to section 194(1) of the Act on the ground of hardship as taken therein. The Tribunal upon hearing the appellant, summarily dismissed the appeal by the impugned order. On a plain reading of the order, it further appears that the Tribunal heard the appellant but without disposing of the application for dispensing with the statutory deposit, dismissed the appeal on merit holding that the petitioner admitted the allegations and hence those were proved beyond doubt. 

17. The main issue requires to be decided in this writ petition is whether the Tribunal can summarily dismiss an appeal on merit without giving any expressed decision on the application for granting exemption from the statutory deposit as mandated by section 194(1) of the Act, 1969. 

18. In order to get the reply, let us go through the text of section 194 of the Act, which reads as follows: 
"194.— Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied —(1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196A against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer fifty per cent of the duty demanded or fifty per cent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be: 
Provided that such person may, instead of depositing the amount of the penalty as aforesaid, deposit only fifty percent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance: 
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty imposed will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. 
(2) If, upon an appeal it is decided that the whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty or penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be." 

19. The above quoted law requires the appellant to deposit the duty demanded or penalty imposed at the time of filing the appeal, or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority, at any stage before disposal of the appeal, deposit fifty percent of the duty demanded or penalty imposed, or both as the case may be. In the case of appeal against a penalty, the first proviso to Sub-Section (1) allows the appellant to deposit fifty percent of the penalty in cash and furnish a bank guarantee for the balance while the second proviso confers power on the appellate authority to dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or with such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. 

20. In the present case, the Tribunal did not express any single word in the impugned order whether the application for dispensation with the statutory deposit on the ground of hardship was rejected or not. But under the facts and circumstances of the case coupled with the financial crisis during the pandemic, the Tribunal could have permitted the appellant to deposit the demanded amount at any specific date before disposal of the appeal. 

21. Learned Deputy Attorney-General, with reference to the decision of the larger bench passed in the bunch cases of Ni/n Packing and Accessories Ltd. vs Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal and others, submits that it is the discretion of the Tribunal to dispense with the deposit either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. We have no scope to disagree with the decision of the larger bench. In the cited case the larger bench relied on the case of Pandyan Insurance Company Limited vs KJ Khambatta and others, reported in AIR 1955 (Bombay) 241 and observed: 
"It is the cardinal rule of interpretation that the words used in a Statute are to be interpreted as it is, and not what they ought to be. The Legislature, in their wisdom, and in our view quiet correctly, stipulated that the discretion to allow dispensation with the deposit is vested only with the Tribunal. This is apparent from the very last sentence, which reads, "it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or submit to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose." (emphasis added on the word "it") By using the word "it", the Legislatures have very clearly expressed their intention that it is the Tribunal and the Tribunal alone which is vested with the sole authority to dispense with the deposit or otherwise accept an appeal upon such conditions as it deems fit to impose with regard to such deposit.. The use of the word "it", in our view, implies that the jurisdiction or authority of this Court to interfere in matters of granting exemption on the ground of hardship has been excluded...." 

22. It appears that the petitioners in their respective writ petitions made submission before the larger bench relying on the judgment of the Appellate Division passed in Dhaka Warehouse Ltd and another vs Assistant Collector of Customs and others disposed of with three others cases in bunch and reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 227, wherein the Appellate Division observed: 
"Payment of the demanded sum, a condition precedent as required under section 194 of the Act for filing an appeal, would have surely caused a great hardship to the appellants. The appellants' prayer for exemption from depositing demanded sum rather arbitrarily rejected by the appellate authority." 

23. In the above cited case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd, the Appellate Division considering the hardship in depositing the demanded duty, directed the High Court Division to hear the writ petition filed against the order of the Tribunal dismissing the customs appeal for non-deposit due to hardship. The above case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd was distinguished by the larger bench in the following manner: "...the aforesaid decision of the Apex Court is distinguishable from the present case before us for the simple reason that in the decision referred to above, no exemption was granted and the appellants' application of hardship was rejected summarily. In the present writ petitions, the petitioners were granted exemptions, albeit of varying degrees. It is the non-deposit of the exempted amount which led to the rejection of the appeals by the Tribunal." 

24. The larger bench further observed: 
"When a Tribunal is set up under an Act for adjudicating the disputes between the contending sides relating to the rights and privileges conferred under the Act, unless otherwise provided by law, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal is exclusive. However, this should not be inferred as a total ouster of the Court's jurisdiction. Where the Tribunal exceeds its authority or where it fails to exercise its power in accordance with law or where it has acted malafide, in such cases, this Court can and should interfere."  

25. It appears from the above quoted two passages that in the cases of larger bench, the Tribunal allowed the appellants' applications of hardship and directed them to make deposits of varying degrees, which they failed to comply with. In the present case, the Tribunal did not at all consider the appellant's application on hardship even did not pass any order disposing of the same. The present case is thus sharply distinguishable with that of the larger bench. It rather matches the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. In fact, the case in hand is better, because in the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd. the applications were rejected, but in this no order was passed on the application for exemption. 

26. Under the facts and circumstances of the present case, the Tribunal ought to have dispensed with the deposit either unconditionally or subject to such condition as it may deem fit to impose or to allow time to deposit the demanded amount by the appellant at any time before disposal of the appeal. 

27. Moreover, any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Commissioner of Customs, may prefer an appeal before the Tribunal under section 196A of the Act, 1969 by depositing the demanded amount as required under section 194(1) of the Act or he may file application for granting exemption for payment of the demanded amount due to hardship under its second proviso. According to section 196B of the Act the Appellate Tribunal, after giving the parties to the appeal, an opportunity of being heard, would pass such order or orders thereon, as it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or refer the case back to the authority which passed such decision or order with such directions as the Tribunal may think fit, for a fresh adjudication or decision, as the case may be, after taking additional evidence, if necessary. 

28. In the case of Shahadat Hossain vs National Board of Revenue and others 65 DLR 522, the High Court Division observed: 
"With the above discussions of law and facts, the questions as raised in the aforesaid appeals are answered in the following terms: 
(1) An order of the Tribunal rejecting an appeal as being not maintainable for non-deposit of 50% of 'the duty demanded or penalty imposed in accordance with the provisions of section 194 of the said Act is not an order under section 196B of the said Act. Accordingly, no appeal against such orders shall lie before the High Court Division under section 196D of the said Act. Thus, the Customs Appeal No. 17 of 2008 is dismissed as being not maintainable. 
(2) The order of the Tribunal dismissing the appeal before it for default or the order rejecting an application for restoration of the said Appeal is not an order under section 196B of the said Act. Accordingly, no appeal against such order(s) shall lie before the High Court Division under section 196D of the said Act. Thus, the Customs Appeal No.22 of 2007 is also dismissed as being not maintainable. 
(3) However, the order passed by the Tribunal under section 193C(3) in confirming, modifying, annulling the decision of the Review Committee or sending the case back to the Review Committee on remand is an order under section 196B and hence Appeal against such order passed by the Tribunal shall lie before the High Court Division under section 196D of the said Act. Thus, Customs Appeal No. 25 of 2008 is maintainable and the same is allowed. Customs Authority is directed to accept CRF value for the final assessment and release the bank guarantee of the appellant within 30(thirty) days from receipt of the copy of this judgment and order." 

29. In the case of NOL (Bangladesh) Ltd., Chattogram vs Commissioner of Customs, Chattogram and others 27 BLC 58, the High Court Division observed: "On reading the provision of section 194 of the Customs Act it appears that both 1st proviso and 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Customs Act given discretion upon the Customs Authority to consider the hardship of the appellant. Since the petitioner filed application under section 194 asserting hardship and furnish 100% bank guarantee for the entire penalty amount, the respondent No.1 would have exercised its jurisdiction by accepting the said bank guarantee. Discretion of bank does not mean arbitrary exercise of power and rather discretion have to apply judiciously...." 

30. From a plain reading of the impugned order, it also appears that in the present case, the Tribunal without issuing any notice upon the parties dismissed the appeal summarily on merit in violation of the provision of section 196 B of the Act, 1969. The Tribunal thus acted in violation of the law. 

31. In view of the discussions made above, we find substance in the submissions of the learned advocate for the petitioner-company and thus we are inclined to give a chance to the company to press its appeal on merit by depositing a certain percent of the demanded duty and taxes and the imposed penalty. 

32. Accordingly, the rule is made absolute. The order dated 30-12-2021 passed under Nathi Number CEVI/Case(Cus)-675/2021/ 4047 by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka dismissing the appeal without disposing of the application filed under section 194(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority, and the application for hardship is allowed in a different form. The petitioner is directed to deposit 10% of the demanded amount of duty and taxes, and the imposed penalty within 60 (sixty) days and the Tribunal is directed to hear and dispose of the appeal in accordance with law within 6 (Six) months from receipt of this order. 

Communicate a copy of this judgment to respondent number 1. 

End.

full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub, J: Since common question of law and facts are involved in all these 3(three) writ petitions as such, those have been heard together and are being disposed of by this single judgment. 

2. In all these 3(three) writ petitions filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh respective Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inaction and failure of the respondents concerned in considering the lands in question as "commercial" land instead of "Vitta/Bari" and in commencing the tenure for the compensation of immovable property under section 9(l)(ka) of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act, 2017 from 13-9-2020 to 13-9-2021 in writ petition No.7409 of 2023, from 31-10-2020 to 1-11-2021 in writ petition No.11432 of 2022 and from 11-4-2020 to 10-4-2021 for the properties in question proposed to be acquired in LA Case Nos. 06, 08, 09 and 12 all of 2020-2021 respectively and fixing award of compensation vide Memo Jari No. 62(353) dated 2-10-2022 relating to RS Dag No.267 under Chariashikar Mouza, Memo Jail No. 65(250) dated 4-10-2022 relating to RS Dag No.101 of Dhopakandi Mouza, Memo Jari No.67(433) relating to RS Dag No.1332 under Chariashikar Mouza and Memo Jari No.60(298) dated 2-10-2022 in connection with RS Dag Nos. 249, 250, 251 and 300 of Dhopakandi Mouza under Ullapara Upazilla, District-Sirajgonj as per compensation rate of 2014, should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect. 

3. At the time of issuance of the Rules, directions were given upon the respective contending parties to maintain status-quo in respect of possession and position of the case properties and the buildings situated thereon, for a prescribed period. 

4. However, challenging the ad-interim orders of direction the respondent concerned moved the Hon'ble Appellate Division by filing Civil Petition to Leave to Appeal Nos. 3250 and 3251 both of 2022 and No. 1932 of 2023. The Appellate Division upon hearing the respective contending parties ultimately, disposed of the applications vide order dated 12-10-2023 without interfering into the ad-interim orders with direction upon this Bench to hear and dispose of the Rules on merit. 

5. In writ petition No.7409 of 2023 facts, in brief, are that the petitioner is a businessman who carries on business in the name of M/s. Alom Chairman Market by establishing market/bazar of verities items and receives rental subscription from the respective shopkeepers and bank authority. He became the owner of 0566 decimals of land of RS Dag No.267 under Chariashikar Mouza and 0466 decimals of land of RS Dag No. 101 under Dopakandi Mouza vide separate kabalas and got mutation with the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Ullapara vide mutation Case Nos.215 and 213 both of 2019 with Holding Nos.2367 and 746 respectively identifying the class of the case land as "ফসলী/বানিজ্যিক” (Annexure-B). 36. Article 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, as embodied in Chapter III of the Constitution guarantees right to property but subject to restrictions imposed by law. However, said right is extinguished by way of compulsory acquisition, nationalization or requisition under the authority of law. Vide Article 42(2) when a law/statute, promulgated by the Legislature in exercise of power as provided under Article 42(1), provides for compensation, it should either fix the amount of compensation or prescribe the principles on which, and the manner in which the compensation is to be assessed and paid. Said law cannot be called in question in any court of law on the ground that its respective provision for compensation is inadequate. 

37. Article 42 is quoted below:—
"42. (1) Subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalised or requisitioned save by authority of law. 
[(2) A law made under clause (1) of this article shall provide for the acquisition, nationalization or requisition with compensation and shall fix the amount of compensation or specify the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be assessed and paid ; but no such law shall be called in question in any court on the ground that any provision of the law in respect of such compensation is not adequate.] 

38. The Parliament in view of Article 42(1) promulgated "স্থাবর সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহন ও হুকুম দখল আইন, ২০১৭" (Act No. 21 of 2017) (in short, the Act, 2017) relating to acquisition and requisition of immovable property and to provide for matters connected therewith and ancillary thereto.

39. Under the Act of 2017 the process of acquisition commences with the publication of notice under section 4(1) by the Deputy Commissioner " জেলা প্রশাসক" as defined in section 2(5) in the prescribed form and manners, in connection with the properties proposed to be acquired. 

40. Section 4(1) is quoted below:— 
"৪। স্থাবর সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহণের জন্য প্রাথমিক নোটিশ জারি:
(১) জেলা প্রশাসকের নিকট কোনো স্থাবর সম্পত্তি জনপ্রয়োজনে বা জনস্বার্থে আবশ্যক মর্মে প্রতীয়মান হইলে তিনি উক্ত সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহণের প্রস্তাব করা হইয়াছে উল্লেখ করিয়া উক্ত সম্পত্তির উপর বা সম্পত্তির নিকটবর্তী সুবিধাজনক স্থানে, নির্ধারিত ফরম ও পদ্ধতিতে, নোটিশ জারি করিবেন।"

41. However, prior to publication of the said notice the Deputy Commissioner is required under section 4(3)(ka) to prepare an inventory, making video with photograph of the actual position and nature of the property proposed to be acquired along with the buildings situated thereon, and or crops and trees which are standing on the said property proposed to be acquired. 

42. Vide section 4(3)(kha), subsequent to issuance of notice under section 4(1) the Deputy Commissioner concern shall prepare "a joint inventory" "যৌথ তালিকা" in the prescribed manner with the participation of the requiring body as well as the person interested in the property who are to remain present on the respective date and at the respective time. 

43. Section 4(4) provides that while preparing the said joint inventory if found any change of classification of the record of the proposed acquired property, the Deputy Commissioner concern has to endorse his decision to that effect. 

44. At the same time, vide section 4(5) the Deputy Commissioner shall endorse his findings in the said joint inventory whether any house or structure has been or is being constructed with a view to cause prejudice to the public interest. 

45. Section 4(6) stipulates that after preparation of joint inventory under section 4(3)(kha) it shall be displayed in the notice board of the local head office or at any conspicuous place of the respective project site for public gaze. 

46. As per section 4(7) after initiation of proceeding for acquisition under section 4(3)(ka) if it is found that any construction of building is or is being made with a view to change the nature/ classification of the property, said change of classification shall not be enlisted in the said যৌথ তালিকা. For non-inclusion of such change in the inventory list is subject to appeal under section 4(8) before the Commissioner and his decision is final under section 4(10).
